Hofer–Wysocki–Zehnder · Polyfold and Fredholm Theory, Part I · the formal proof in words

Polyfold Theory, proof by proof

The formal proof of Hofer–Wysocki–Zehnder’s Polyfold and Fredholm Theory, Part I, retold as mathematics: every definition as the formalization makes it, every proof step by step as the Lean proof goes, and on every step of substance a trace tag naming the declaration that proves it.

109,293 lines of Lean3,741 trace tags3,127 declarations citedLean 4.33.1 · Mathlib · November 2026

A trace tag looks like this: Chapter1/ChainRuletheorem_1_21, a file of the project and the declaration in it that proves the sentence. Each part opens on its own; use the contents or the links at the end of a part.

Part I. The sc-calculus (HWZ Chapter 1, §§1.1–1.4)

Chapter 1 of Part I fixes the vocabulary of the whole theory: sc-Banach spaces, sc-operators, sc-subspaces and quotients, sc-Fredholm operators and their stability under \(\mathrm{sc}^+\)-perturbations, partial quadrants, \(\mathrm{sc}^0\) and \(\mathrm{sc}^1\) maps, the tangent construction and the inductive definitions of \(\mathrm{sc}^k\) and sc-smooth, the relation between sc-differentiability and classical differentiability on the levels (Propositions 1.16–1.19 and Corollary 1.20, quoted from the 2010 paper), the chain rule, the degeneracy index of a point of a partial quadrant and boundary recognition. The formal proof establishes all of it, Proposition 1.19 and Corollary 1.20 under the text’s own hypothesis (\(C^{l+1}\) from \(U_{m+l}\) to \(F_m\) for \(l \le k\)), by the 2010 paper’s induction \((\mathrm S_k)\) on elementary maps (§I.17). Example 1.2, the weighted Sobolev spaces, is not formalized.

Two decisions shape everything. First, an sc-Banach space is an indexed family of Banach spaces \(E_m\) with injective compact inclusions \(E_{m+1} \to E_m\), not one space with a chain of subspaces (§I.1). “The point \(x\) of \(E_0\) lies in \(E_m\)” then means that \(x\) is in the image of \(E_m\), and every map has level maps \(f_m : E_m \to F_m\) determined by injectivity. Second, the text’s standing hypothesis “\(U\) relatively open in a partial quadrant” enters the proofs of §§1.2–1.3 only through two facts about each level set \(U_m\): it is the intersection of an open and a convex set, and derivatives within it are unique. These two facts make up the notion of an sc-domain (§I.10), which the tangent construction and the level shift preserve by a two-line argument, so the inductions of §1.2 run on sc-domains, and the text’s tuples \((U, C, E)\) are a special case.

Four proofs take a different road from the text’s. The chain rule replaces the two integrals of §1.4.2 by the one-dimensional mean value inequality along a segment, and does not need the first integral at all (§I.12). The compactness argument behind Propositions 1.16–1.18, the subsequence \(h_n \to h\) in \(E_m\) for unit vectors \(h_n \in E_{m+1}\), is isolated once as the compact-open lemma, and its \(C^k\) version replaces the multilinear maps \(\Gamma(x)\) and the differentiation under the integral sign of the 2010 paper (§I.13). Theorem 1.25, which the text quotes from another paper, is proved by the argument of §2.3, for \(\mathrm{sc}^1\) germs (§I.19). And the induction \((\mathrm S_k)\) behind Proposition 1.19 runs on the order \(s\) over all elementary maps \(d^jf(\pi_0 z)(\pi_1 z, \dots, \pi_j z)\) at once, rather than on a description of the \(2^{k+1}\) components of \(T^{k+1}f\) (§I.17). Smaller departures are flagged where they occur: the complement in Proposition 1.10 is built from a right inverse rather than a lifted basis; the regularizing step of §1.4.1 is a bootstrap; \(k = k'\) in Lemma 1.24 is derived from the lemma, not proved first. What Mathlib lacked, the Riesz–Schauder theorem, the stability of Fredholm operators under compact perturbations and the invariance of the Fredholm index, is proved in §I.7; the index statements of the exposition’s Lemma 2.D and Proposition 1.10 follow in §I.6 and §I.9. The lemmas that the exposition adds to make the text’s remarks precise are proved where they belong: uniqueness of the sc-structure in finite dimensions (§I.1), sc-splittings as sc-projections (§I.3), the smooth points of a quotient (§I.5), the shift and tangent of a tuple (§I.10), compact-open continuity and sc¹ = \(C^1\) on quadrants in finite dimensions (§I.11).

I.1 Scales and sc-Banach spaces (Definition 1.1)

The scale. A scale of Banach spaces consists of real Banach spaces \(E_m\), one for each \(m \in \mathbb N\), together with continuous linear maps \(\mathrm{incl}_m : E_{m+1} \to E_m\) that are injective and compact operators Chapter1/ScBanachScScale. Compactness is Mathlib’s: the preimage of some neighbourhood of \(0\) is mapped into a compact set Mathlib/Analysis/Normed/Operator/Compact/BasicIsCompactOperator. The composite inclusion \(\iota_m : E_m \to E_0\) is defined by recursion, \(\iota_0 = \mathrm{id}\) and \(\iota_{m+1} = \iota_m \circ \mathrm{incl}_m\) Chapter1/ScBanachScScale.toBase; it is injective Chapter1/ScBanachScScale.toBase_injective, and the composite \(E_{m+k} \to E_m\) is defined likewise Chapter1/ScBanachScScale.inclK and is compatible with \(\iota\) Chapter1/ScBanachScScale.toBase_inclK. The text’s \(E_m\) is here the image \(\iota_m(E_m) \subseteq E_0\); the text’s \(E_m \supset E_{m+1}\) is the inclusion of images, and “\(x \in E_m\)” for \(x \in E_0\) is “\(x \in \operatorname{range} \iota_m\)”. The smooth points \(E_\infty\) form the subspace of \(E_0\) of points that lift to every level, \(E_\infty = \bigcap_m \operatorname{range}\iota_m\) Chapter1/ScBanachScScale.smooth Chapter1/ScBanachScScale.mem_smooth_iff, and \(E_\infty \cap E_m\) is its preimage in \(E_m\) Chapter1/ScBanachScScale.smoothLvl; a smooth point of \(E_m\) lifts to every \(E_{m+k}\) Chapter1/ScBanachScScale.exists_inclK_of_mem_smoothLvl.

The density axiom. An sc-Banach space is a scale in which \(E_\infty \cap E_m\) is dense in \(E_m\) for every \(m\) Chapter1/ScBanachScBanach. This is condition (2) of Definition 1.1 exactly as the text states it. The weaker statement that \(E_{m+k}\) has dense image in \(E_m\) follows Chapter1/ScBanachScBanach.denseRange_inclK Chapter1/ScBanachScBanach.denseRange_incl; it does not obviously imply the axiom, which is why the strong form is the definition.

Why a family. Nothing in Chapter 1 uses more than the family: the text’s identification of \(E_{m+1}\) with a subset of \(E_m\) is the injectivity of \(\mathrm{incl}_m\), a field of the structure, and its “the inclusion is continuous” is part of compactness. The gain is that each level is a Banach space in its own right, with its own norm, and Mathlib’s analysis applies on each level without carrying a filtration along.

The constant structure. For a finite-dimensional normed space \(V\) the family \(E_m = V\) with identity inclusions is a scale: the identity of a finite-dimensional space is a compact operator Mathlib/Analysis/Normed/Operator/Compact/FiniteDimensionisCompactOperator_id_iff_finiteDimensional Chapter1/ScBanachScBanach.constScale. Here \(\iota_m\) is the identity Chapter1/ScBanachScBanach.constScale_toBase, every point is smooth Chapter1/ScBanachScBanach.constScale_smoothLvl, and density is trivial, so \(V\) is an sc-Banach space Chapter1/ScBanachScBanach.const Chapter1/ScBanachScBanach.const_toBase.

Only the constant structure (Lemma 1.A(2)–(3) of the exposition). The text remarks that a finite-dimensional space has precisely one sc-structure. For families this reads: if \(E\) is an sc-Banach space with \(E_0\) finite-dimensional, the inclusions identify \(E\) with the constant structure on \(E_0\). First, every point is smooth: \(E_\infty\) is a subspace of the finite-dimensional \(E_0\), hence closed Mathlib/Topology/Algebra/Module/FiniteDimensionSubmodule.closed_of_finiteDimensional, and dense by the axiom at level \(0\), hence everything Chapter1/ExpositionLemmasScBanach.smooth_eq_top_of_finiteDimensional. So every \(x \in E_0\) lifts to every level, and \(\iota_m : E_m \to E_0\), injective by construction, is bijective Chapter1/ExpositionLemmasScBanach.toBase_bijective_of_finiteDimensional. A continuous linear bijection between Banach spaces is an isomorphism (open mapping theorem) Mathlib/Analysis/Normed/Operator/BanachContinuousLinearEquiv.ofBijective; the isomorphisms \(\iota_m\) commute with the inclusions by the very definition \(\iota_{m+1} = \iota_m \circ \mathrm{incl}_m\), so they form an sc-isomorphism of \(E\) onto the constant structure on \(E_0\) Chapter1/ExpositionLemmasScBanach.isoConstOfFiniteDimensional Chapter1/ExpositionLemmasScBanach.isoConstOfFiniteDimensional_apply. In particular all the norms \(|\cdot|_m\) are equivalent to \(|\cdot|_0\). The second remark, that on an infinite-dimensional space the constant structure fails the compactness axiom, becomes: if an inclusion \(\mathrm{incl}_m : E_{m+1} \to E_m\) of a scale is onto, then \(E_m\) is finite-dimensional. Indeed \(\mathrm{incl}_m\) is then a continuous linear bijection, hence an isomorphism \(e\), and \(\mathrm{id}_{E_m} = \mathrm{incl}_m \circ e^{-1}\) is compact as a compact operator composed with a bounded one Mathlib/Analysis/Normed/Operator/Compact/BasicIsCompactOperator.comp_clm; a Banach space with compact identity is finite-dimensional Mathlib/Analysis/Normed/Operator/Compact/FiniteDimensionFiniteDimensional.of_isCompactOperator_id Chapter1/ExpositionLemmasScScale.finiteDimensional_of_surjective_incl.

Direct sums. For scales \(E\), \(F\), the family \(E_m \times F_m\) with the product inclusions is a scale: the product of two compact operators is compact, because the preimage of a product of neighbourhoods is mapped into the product of two compact sets Chapter1/ScBanachScBanach.prodScale. Its \(\iota_m\) is the pair of the two Chapter1/ScBanachScBanach.prodScale_toBase, and its smooth points are the pairs of smooth points Chapter1/ScBanachScBanach.prodScale_smoothLvl; since a product of dense sets is dense, \(E \oplus F\) is an sc-Banach space Chapter1/ScBanachScBanach.prod Chapter1/ScBanachScBanach.prod_smoothLvl.

The level shift. The family \(E_{m+1}\) with the inclusions \(\mathrm{incl}_{m+1}\) is a scale \(E^1\) Chapter1/ScBanachScBanach.shiftScale. Its composite inclusion to its base \(E_1\), followed by \(\iota_1\), is \(\iota_{m+1}\) Chapter1/ScBanachScBanach.shiftScale_toBase, and its smooth points at level \(m\) are the smooth points of \(E\) at level \(m+1\) Chapter1/ScBanachScBanach.shiftScale_smoothLvl, so \(E^1\) is an sc-Banach space Chapter1/ScBanachScBanach.shift Chapter1/ScBanachScBanach.shift_toBase Chapter1/ScBanachScBanach.shift_smoothLvl; \(E^k\) is the \(k\)-fold iterate Chapter1/ScBanachScBanach.shiftK.

Level sets. For \(U \subseteq E_0\) the level set \(U_m \subseteq E_m\) is the preimage \(\iota_m^{-1}(U)\) Chapter1/ScSmoothScBanach.lvlSet; \(U_0 = U\) Chapter1/ScSmoothScBanach.lvlSet_zero, \(U_{m+1} = \mathrm{incl}_m^{-1}(U_m)\) Chapter1/ScSmoothScBanach.lvlSet_succ, and level sets preserve inclusions, intersections, openness, closedness and convexity Chapter1/ScSmoothScBanach.lvlSet_mono Chapter1/ScSmoothScBanach.lvlSet_inter Chapter1/ScSmoothScBanach.isOpen_lvlSet Chapter1/ScSmoothScBanach.isClosed_lvlSet Chapter1/ScSmoothScBanach.convex_lvlSet. This is the text’s filtration \(A_m = A \cap E_m\) of a subset. The level sets of \(U_1 \subseteq E_1\), taken in the shifted space \(E^1\), are the \(U_{m+1}\) Chapter1/LevelsScBanach.shift_lvlSet, which is the text’s \((A^1)_m = A_{1+m}\).

I.2 Sc-operators, sc-isomorphisms, sc⁺-operators (Definitions 1.3–1.4)

An sc-operator \(T : E \to F\) is a family of continuous linear maps \(T_m : E_m \to F_m\) commuting with the inclusions, \(\mathrm{incl}^F_m \circ T_{m+1} = T_m \circ \mathrm{incl}^E_m\) Chapter1/ScBanachScOperator. Then \(\iota_m T_m = T_0 \iota_m\) by induction Chapter1/ScBanachScOperator.toBase_comm, so the whole family is determined by the base map \(T_0\) Chapter1/ScBanachScOperator.ext_base: this is the sense in which the text’s single linear map \(T\) “with \(T(E_m) \subset F_m\) and \(T : E_m \to F_m\) continuous” is the same thing. The text’s formulation is also available as a predicate on a continuous linear \(T_0 : E_0 \to F_0\), “for every \(m\) there is a continuous linear \(T_m\) with \(\iota_m T_m = T_0 \iota_m\)” Chapter1/ScBanachIsScOperator, and the two notions pass into each other Chapter1/ScBanachScOperator.isScOperator Chapter1/ScBanachIsScOperator.toScOperator Chapter1/ScBanachIsScOperator.toScOperator_zero. The identity is an sc-operator, sc-operators compose and add Chapter1/ScBanachScOperator.id Chapter1/ScBanachScOperator.comp Chapter1/ScBanachScOperator.add, and they map smooth points to smooth points, since a lift of \(x\) to level \(j\) is carried by \(T_j\) to a lift of \(T_0 x\) Chapter1/ScBanachScOperator.mapsTo_smoothLvl.

An sc-isomorphism is a family of continuous linear equivalences \(E_m \simeq F_m\) commuting with the inclusions Chapter1/ScBanachScIso; it has an underlying sc-operator Chapter1/ScBanachScIso.toScOperator, an inverse Chapter1/ScBanachScIso.symm, composites Chapter1/ScBanachScIso.trans and the identity Chapter1/ScBanachScIso.refl, and \(\iota_m\) commutes with it and with its inverse Chapter1/ScBanachScIso.toBase_comm Chapter1/ScBanachScIso.symm_toBase_comm. The text defines an sc-isomorphism as a bijective sc-operator whose inverse is an sc-operator; the continuity of the inverse on each level, which there follows from the open mapping theorem, is here part of the data.

An \(\mathrm{sc}^+\)-operator \(E \to F\) is an sc-operator \(E \to F^1\) into the shifted space, i.e. continuous linear maps \(S_m : E_m \to F_{m+1}\) commuting with the inclusions Chapter1/ScBanachScPlus. The text’s first condition, \(S(E_m) \subset F_{m+1}\), is contained in the second and is dropped. The inclusion \(F^1 \to F\), level by level \(\mathrm{incl}_m : F_{m+1} \to F_m\), is itself an sc-operator Chapter1/ScBanachScBanach.shiftIncl, and composing gives the sc-operator \(E \to F\) underlying \(S\) Chapter1/ScBanachScPlus.toScOperator Chapter1/ScBanachScPlus.toScOperator_apply. Its level-\(m\) map is the compact \(\mathrm{incl}_m\) after the bounded \(S_m\), hence compact Mathlib/Analysis/Normed/Operator/Compact/BasicIsCompactOperator.comp_clm Chapter1/ScBanachScPlus.isCompactOperator: the text’s remark that \(\mathrm{sc}^+\)-operators are sc-compact. In terms of images, \(S\) raises the level: if \(x \in \operatorname{range}\iota_m\) then \(S_0 x \in \operatorname{range}\iota_{m+1}\) Chapter1/ScFredholmScPlus.toScOperator_mem_range_toBase_succ.

I.3 Sc-subspaces and sc-splittings (Definition 1.5)

For a subspace \(A \subseteq E_0\) its level-\(m\) part \(A_m \subseteq E_m\) is the preimage of \(A\) under \(\iota_m\) Chapter1/ScBanachScBanach.levelSub Chapter1/ScBanachScBanach.mem_levelSub; \(A_0 = A\) Chapter1/ScBanachScBanach.levelSub_zero, the inclusions map \(A_{m+1}\) into \(A_m\) Chapter1/ScBanachScBanach.incl_mem_levelSub, and \(A_m\) is closed when \(A\) is, as the preimage of a closed set under a continuous map Chapter1/ScBanachScBanach.isClosed_levelSub.

\(A\) is an sc-subspace if \(A\) is closed and, for every \(m\), \(A_m\) lies in the closure of \(A_m \cap E_\infty\) Chapter1/ScBanachScBanach.IsScSubspace Chapter1/ScBanachScBanach.IsScSubspace.isClosed. The text asks that \((A_m)\) be an sc-structure on \(A\); of the conditions in that phrase, the closedness of \(A_m\) in \(E_m\) was just proved, and the compactness of the restricted inclusions \(A_{m+1} \to A_m\) is automatic, since the restriction of a compact operator to a subspace, with values in a closed subspace, is compact. This is how the scale structure on a closed \(A\) is built: levels \(A_m\), inclusions the restrictions of \(\mathrm{incl}_m\), injective because \(\mathrm{incl}_m\) is, compact by the remark Chapter1/ScBanachScBanach.ofSubspaceScale. Its composite inclusion is that of \(E\) on the underlying points Chapter1/ScBanachScBanach.ofSubspaceScale_coe_toBase, and its smooth points are the points of \(A_m\) that are smooth in \(E\) Chapter1/ScBanachScBanach.mem_ofSubspaceScale_smoothLvl Chapter1/ScBanachScBanach.ofSubspaceScale_smoothLvl. The density condition of IsScSubspace is then exactly the density axiom for this scale, so an sc-subspace is an sc-Banach space with the induced structure Chapter1/ScBanachScBanach.ofSubspace.

\(E = F \oplus G\) is an sc-splitting if \(F\) and \(G\) are sc-subspaces and, for every \(m\), \(F_m\) and \(G_m\) are complementary subspaces of \(E_m\) Chapter1/ScBanachScBanach.IsScSplitting. The text asks for a topological direct sum \(E_m = F_m \oplus G_m\). Since \(F_m\) and \(G_m\) are closed and complementary, the projection onto \(F_m\) along \(G_m\) is continuous by the closed graph theorem, which is Mathlib’s “closed complemented from complementary closed subspaces” Chapter1/ScBanachScBanach.IsScSplitting.closedComplemented; so nothing is lost by asking only for complementarity. The splitting is symmetric in \(F\) and \(G\) Chapter1/ScBanachScBanach.IsScSplitting.symm.

Sc-splittings are sc-projections (Lemma 2.B of the exposition). The proof of Proposition 1.6 in the text passes from “\(P \circ P = P\), continuous on every level” to “a sc-projection” and an sc-complement \((1 - P)(E)\) without comment. Both directions are proved. (i) Given an sc-splitting \(E = A \oplus B\), on each level \(A_m\) and \(B_m\) are complementary and closed, hence topological complements Mathlib/Analysis/Normed/Module/ComplementedSubmodule.IsCompl.isTopCompl_of_isClosed Chapter1/ExpositionLemmasScBanach.IsScSplitting.isTopCompl, so the projection \(P_m\) of \(E_m\) onto \(A_m\) along \(B_m\) is continuous Mathlib/Topology/Algebra/Module/ComplementSubmodule.projectionL. These projections commute with the inclusions: write \(x = P_{m+1}x + (x - P_{m+1}x)\) with the first term in \(A_{m+1}\) and the second in \(B_{m+1}\) Mathlib/Topology/Algebra/Module/ComplementSubmodule.projectionL_eq_self_sub_projectionL; \(\mathrm{incl}_m\) carries them into \(A_m\) and \(B_m\) (§I.3), where \(P_m\) is the identity, resp. zero Mathlib/Topology/Algebra/Module/ComplementSubmodule.projectionL_eq_self_iff Mathlib/Topology/Algebra/Module/ComplementSubmodule.projectionL_apply_eq_zero_iff, so \(P_m(\mathrm{incl}_m x) = \mathrm{incl}_m(P_{m+1}x)\). Hence the \(P_m\) form an sc-operator \(P\) Chapter1/ExpositionLemmasScBanach.IsScSplitting.scProj Chapter1/ExpositionLemmasScBanach.IsScSplitting.scProj_apply with \(P_m^2 = P_m\) Chapter1/ExpositionLemmasScBanach.IsScSplitting.scProj_idem, \(P_m(E_m) = A_m\) Chapter1/ExpositionLemmasScBanach.IsScSplitting.range_scProj and \(\ker P_m = B_m\) Chapter1/ExpositionLemmasScBanach.IsScSplitting.ker_scProj. (ii) Conversely let \(P\) be an sc-operator with \(P_0^2 = P_0\). Idempotence passes to every level by injectivity of \(\iota_m\), since \(\iota_m P_m P_m x = P_0P_0\iota_m x = P_0\iota_m x = \iota_m P_m x\) Chapter1/ExpositionLemmasScOperator.idem_lvl. The level-\(m\) part of \(P_0(E_0)\) is \(P_m(E_m)\): if \(\iota_m x = P_0 y\) then \(P_0\iota_m x = \iota_m x\), i.e. \(\iota_m P_m x = \iota_m x\), so \(x = P_m x\) Chapter1/ExpositionLemmasScOperator.levelSub_range_eq; the level-\(m\) part of \(\ker P_0\) is \(\ker P_m\) (§I.6, Chapter1/ScFredholmScOperator.ker_lvl). \(P_0(E_0) = \{x : P_0x = x\}\) is closed, and \(\ker P_0\) is closed. Density of smooth points: \(x \in P_m(E_m)\) satisfies \(x = P_mx\) and is the limit of \(P_m z_n\) for smooth \(z_n \to x\), and the \(P_m z_n\) are smooth points of \(P_m(E_m)\) (§I.2); \(x \in \ker P_m\) satisfies \(x = x - P_mx\) and is the limit of \(z_n - P_mz_n\), smooth points of \(\ker P_m\). Finally \(P_m(E_m)\) and \(\ker P_m\) are complementary because \(P_m\) is idempotent Mathlib/LinearAlgebra/ProjectionLinearMap.IsIdempotentElem.isCompl. So \(E = P_0(E_0) \oplus \ker P_0\) is an sc-splitting Chapter1/ExpositionLemmasScBanach.isScSplitting_of_idem, and together: \(E = A \oplus B\) is an sc-splitting iff an idempotent sc-operator has range \(A\) and kernel \(B\) Chapter1/ExpositionLemmasScBanach.isScSplitting_iff_exists_scProj. The text’s \((1 - P)(E)\) is \(\ker P\). The formal Proposition 1.6 (§I.4) builds its complement directly and does not use this.

I.4 Proposition 1.6: finite-dimensional sc-subspaces

Statement. Let \(F \subseteq E_0\) be finite-dimensional. Then \(F\) is an sc-subspace if and only if \(F \le E_\infty\) Chapter1/ScBanachScBanach.proposition_1_6_iff; and if \(F \le E_\infty\) there is a \(G\) with \(E = F \oplus G\) an sc-splitting Chapter1/ScBanachScBanach.proposition_1_6.

The equivalence. If \(F\) is an sc-subspace, the density condition at level \(0\) says \(F \subseteq \overline{F \cap E_\infty}\). But \(F \cap E_\infty\) is a subspace of the finite-dimensional \(F\), hence finite-dimensional, hence closed Mathlib/Topology/Algebra/Module/FiniteDimensionSubmodule.closed_of_finiteDimensional; so \(F \subseteq F \cap E_\infty\), i.e. \(F \le E_\infty\). Conversely, if \(F \le E_\infty\) then \(F\) is closed (finite-dimensional) and every point of \(F_m\) is already a smooth point of \(F_m\), so the density condition holds trivially.

The complement. Mathlib provides a continuous linear projection \(p : E_0 \to F\) with \(p|_F = \mathrm{id}\), from the closed complementation of finite-dimensional subspaces (Hahn–Banach) Mathlib/Analysis/LocallyConvex/HahnBanachSubmodule.ClosedComplemented.of_finiteDimensional. This is the text’s \(P(x) = \sum \lambda_i(x) e_i\). Put \(G := \ker p\). Since \(F \le E_\infty\), the restriction of \(\iota_m\) to \(F_m\) is a bijection onto \(F\) (injective by injectivity of \(\iota_m\), surjective because every point of \(F\) lifts to level \(m\)) Chapter1/ScBanachScBanach.levelRestrict Chapter1/ScBanachScBanach.levelRestrict_bijective Chapter1/ScBanachScBanach.levelEquiv; through this linear isomorphism \(F_m \cong F\) the projection lifts to a continuous linear \(P_m : E_m \to F_m\), \(P_m = (\iota_m|_{F_m})^{-1} \circ p \circ \iota_m\) (continuous because \(F_m\) is finite-dimensional) Chapter1/ScBanachScBanach.finProj. It fixes \(F_m\) Chapter1/ScBanachScBanach.finProj_apply_of_mem, and \(P_m x = 0\) iff \(p(\iota_m x) = 0\) Chapter1/ScBanachScBanach.finProj_eq_zero_iff, so \(G_m = \ker P_m\). Now \(F\) is an sc-subspace by the first part, and \(G\) is closed as a kernel. For the density of \(G_m \cap E_\infty\) in \(G_m\): given \(g \in G_m\), let \(Q := 1 - P_m\) on \(E_m\); then \(Qg = g\), \(Q\) maps \(E_m\) into \(G_m\), and \(Q\) maps smooth points to smooth points, since \(P_m x\) is smooth (\(F \le E_\infty\)) and smooth points form a subspace Chapter1/ScBanachScScale.smoothLvl_submodule_closed_sub. Hence \(g = Qg\) lies in the closure of \(Q(E_\infty \cap E_m) \subseteq G_m \cap E_\infty\), because \(E_\infty \cap E_m\) is dense and \(Q\) is continuous. This is the text’s \(g_n = (1 - P)f_n \to g\). Finally \(F_m\) and \(G_m = \ker P_m\) are complementary because \(P_m\) is a projection onto \(F_m\) Mathlib/LinearAlgebra/ProjectionisCompl_of_proj.

I.5 Proposition 1.7: quotients

Statement. Let \(A \subseteq E_0\) be closed. The quotients \(E_m/A_m\) form an sc-Banach space \(E/A\) Chapter1/ScBanachScBanach.quotient, the quotient maps form an sc-operator \(E \to E/A\) Chapter1/ScBanachScBanach.quotientMap, and, as a statement, there are an sc-Banach space \(Q\) and an sc-operator \(q : E \to Q\) with every \(q_m\) surjective and \(\ker q_m = A_m\) Chapter1/ScBanachScBanach.proposition_1_7. The text assumes \(A\) is an sc-subspace; only closedness is used.

The inclusions. \(A_m\) is closed in \(E_m\) (§I.3), so \(E_m/A_m\) is a Banach space. The map \(E_{m+1}/A_{m+1} \to E_m/A_m\) is induced by \(\mathrm{incl}_m\): it is well defined because \(\mathrm{incl}_m\) maps \(A_{m+1}\) into \(A_m\) Chapter1/ScBanachScBanach.quotIncl Chapter1/ScBanachScBanach.quotIncl_mk. It is injective: if \(\mathrm{incl}_m x \in A_m\) then \(\iota_{m+1} x = \iota_m(\mathrm{incl}_m x) \in A\), so \(x \in A_{m+1}\) Chapter1/ScBanachScBanach.quotIncl_injective. This injectivity is the text’s identification of \(E_m/A_m\) with the subspace \(\{x + A : x \in E_m\}\) of \(E/A\), and it holds precisely because \(A_m\) is the full preimage of \(A\). It is compact: the quotient map \(E_m \to E_m/A_m\) after the compact \(\mathrm{incl}_m\) is compact, and the induced map on \(E_{m+1}/A_{m+1}\) sends the image of a neighbourhood of \(0\) (which is a neighbourhood, since quotient maps are open) into the same compact set Chapter1/ScBanachScBanach.quotIncl_isCompactOperator. So the quotients form a scale Chapter1/ScBanachScBanach.quotientScale, whose composite inclusion sends the class of \(x\) to the class of \(\iota_m x\) Chapter1/ScBanachScBanach.quotientScale_toBase_mk. The text’s argument with a sequence \(x_k + A_{m+1}\) of norm \(\le 1\) and representatives of norm \(\le 2\) is the sequential form of the same fact.

Density. The quotient map \(E_m \to E_m/A_m\) is continuous and surjective, so the image of the dense set \(E_\infty \cap E_m\) is dense. A class \([x]\) with \(x\) smooth is a smooth point of the quotient scale: a lift \(y\) of \(x\) to level \(j\) gives the lift \([y]\) of \([x]\). So the smooth points of \(E_m/A_m\) are dense Chapter1/ScBanachScBanach.quotient. This is the inclusion “\(\{x + A : x \in E_\infty\} \subseteq (E/A)_\infty\)” of the text’s proof, which is all its density claim needs.

The smooth points of the quotient (Lemma 2.C of the exposition). The text also asserts that the two sets are equal. Let \(A\) be an sc-subspace and \(x \in E_0\) with, for every \(j\), a point \(x_j \in E_j\) such that \(\iota_j x_j - x \in A\). We find a smooth \(y\) with \(y - x \in A\) Chapter1/ExpositionLemmasScBanach.exists_smooth_mem_coset. The differences. \(d_j := \mathrm{incl}_j x_{j+1} - x_j \in E_j\) has \(\iota_j d_j = \iota_{j+1}x_{j+1} - \iota_j x_j = (\iota_{j+1}x_{j+1} - x) - (\iota_jx_j - x) \in A\), so \(d_j \in A_j\). A uniform bound for the inclusions. Put \(P_j := \prod_{i<j}\max(1, \|\mathrm{incl}_i\|) \ge 1\) Chapter1/ExpositionLemmasScBanach.inclBound Chapter1/ExpositionLemmasScBanach.one_le_inclBound. By induction, \(\|\iota_jv\| \le P_j\|v\|\) for \(v \in E_j\) Chapter1/ExpositionLemmasScBanach.norm_toBase_le and \(\|\mathrm{incl}^{J+k}_Jv\| \le P_{J+k}\|v\|\) for the composite inclusion \(E_{J+k} \to E_J\) Chapter1/ExpositionLemmasScBanach.norm_inclK_le, each step multiplying by \(\|\mathrm{incl}_i\| \le \max(1, \|\mathrm{incl}_i\|)\) Chapter1/ExpositionLemmasScBanach.norm_incl_le. This replaces the exposition’s \(M_j = \max_{i\le j}\|E_j \to E_i\|\), and avoids comparing levels \(J + k\) with \(j\). Smooth corrections. Since \(A\) is an sc-subspace, \(A_j \cap E_\infty\) is dense in \(A_j\), so there are \(c_j \in A_j \cap E_\infty\) with \(\|d_j - c_j\| \le 2^{-j}/P_j\) Mathlib/Topology/MetricSpace/Pseudo/DefsMetric.mem_closure_iff. Then \(b_j := d_j - c_j \in A_j\) has \(P_j\|b_j\| \le 2^{-j}\). The series. \(\sum_j \iota_jb_j\) converges absolutely in \(E_0\), its terms being bounded by \(2^{-j}\) Mathlib/Analysis/Normed/Group/InfiniteSumSummable.of_norm_bounded; let \(S\) be its sum and \(y := x_0 + S\). Its partial sums lie in \(A\), which is closed, so \(S \in A\) (the additive form of Mathlib/Topology/Algebra/InfiniteSum/NatIntHasProd.tendsto_prod_nat), and \(y - x = (x_0 - x) + S \in A\). \(y\) is smooth. Fix \(J\). The tail \(t := \sum_k \mathrm{incl}^{J+k}_J b_{J+k}\) converges in \(E_J\) (terms bounded by \(2^{-J}2^{-k}\)), and \(\iota_J t = \sum_k \iota_{J+k}b_{J+k}\) because \(\iota_J\) is continuous and linear Mathlib/Topology/Algebra/InfiniteSum/ModuleContinuousLinearMap.map_tsum and \(\iota_J \circ \mathrm{incl}^{J+k}_J = \iota_{J+k}\) (§I.1). The head telescopes: \(\sum_{j<J}\iota_jd_j = \iota_Jx_J - x_0\) (the additive form of Mathlib/Algebra/BigOperators/Group/Finset/BasicFinset.prod_range_div), so \(\sum_{j<J}\iota_jb_j = (\iota_Jx_J - x_0) - \sum_{j<J}\iota_jc_j\), and the last sum is smooth, hence \(\iota_J w\) for some \(w \in E_J\). Splitting \(S\) into head and tail (the additive form of Mathlib/Topology/Algebra/InfiniteSum/NatIntMultipliable.prod_mul_tprod_nat_add) gives \(y = \iota_J(x_J - w + t)\). As \(J\) was arbitrary, \(y \in E_\infty\). As a statement about \(E/A\). The class of \(x\) is a smooth point of \(E/A\) iff for every \(j\) it is the image of a class \([z]\), \(z \in E_j\), i.e. iff \(\iota_jz - x \in A\) for some \(z\) (§I.5 and Mathlib/LinearAlgebra/Quotient/DefsSubmodule.Quotient.eq); by the above this happens iff \(x + A\) contains a smooth point Chapter1/ExpositionLemmasScBanach.mk_mem_quotient_smooth_iff. This is the text’s equality.

I.6 Definition 1.8: sc-Fredholm operators

Level kernels and ranges. For an sc-operator \(T\), the kernel of \(T_m\) is the level-\(m\) part of the kernel of \(T_0\) Chapter1/ScFredholmScOperator.ker_lvl, and the range of \(T_m\) lies in the level-\(m\) part of the range of \(T_0\) Chapter1/ScFredholmScOperator.range_lvl_le; both from \(\iota_m T_m = T_0 \iota_m\) and injectivity.

The definition. An sc-Fredholm splitting of \(T : E \to F\) consists of subspaces \(K, X \subseteq E_0\) and \(C, Y \subseteq F_0\) such that \(E = K \oplus X\) and \(F = C \oplus Y\) are sc-splittings, \(K = \ker T_0\), \(Y = \operatorname{range} T_0\), \(K\) and \(C\) are finite-dimensional, and \(T_m\) restricts to a bijection \(X_m \to Y_m\) for every \(m\) Chapter1/ScFredholmScFredholmSplitting; \(T\) is sc-Fredholm if such a splitting exists Chapter1/ScFredholmIsScFredholm. The text’s condition (3), “\(T : X \to Y\) is an sc-isomorphism”, is here the bijectivity on each level; the continuity of the inverses \(Y_m \to X_m\) is automatic by the open mapping theorem between the closed subspaces \(X_m\) and \(Y_m\), so nothing is lost.

The index. The index of a splitting is \(\dim K - \dim C\) Chapter1/ScFredholmScFredholmSplitting.index, and the index of \(T\) is \(\dim\ker T_0 - \dim(F_0/\operatorname{range}T_0)\) Chapter1/ScFredholmscIndex. They agree: \(K = \ker T_0\), and \(C\) is a complement of \(Y = \operatorname{range}T_0\) in \(F_0\), so \(C \cong F_0/Y\) Mathlib/LinearAlgebra/ProjectionquotientEquivOfIsCompl Chapter1/ScFredholmScFredholmSplitting.index_eq. So the index does not depend on the splitting, which the text does not state.

The remarks after the definition. \(K\) is a finite-dimensional sc-subspace, hence \(K \le E_\infty\) by Proposition 1.6 Chapter1/ScFredholmScFredholmSplitting.K_le_smooth. \(\ker T_m = K_m\) Chapter1/ScFredholmScFredholmSplitting.ker_lvl and \(\operatorname{range} T_m = Y_m\): one inclusion from above, the other because \(T_m\) maps \(X_m\) onto \(Y_m\) Chapter1/ScFredholmScFredholmSplitting.range_lvl. The text’s “\(F = C \oplus T(E_m)\)” (read \(F_m\)) is the level-\(m\) part of the splitting \(F = C \oplus Y\) together with \(\operatorname{range}T_m = Y_m\). Finally, every \(T_m\) is a Fredholm operator in Mathlib’s sense: its kernel \(K_m\) injects into the finite-dimensional \(K\), its range \(Y_m\) is closed, and \(Y_m\) has the finite-dimensional complement \(C_m\) (which injects into \(C\)), so its range has finite codimension Mathlib/RingTheory/Finiteness/CofiniteFG.cofg_of_isCompl Chapter1/ScFredholmScFredholmSplitting.isFredholm, using the criterion of §I.7. This is the fact the text uses in the first line of §1.4.1.

The index on every level (Lemma 2.D of the exposition). \(C\) is a finite-dimensional sc-subspace, so \(C \le F_\infty\) by Proposition 1.6 Chapter1/FredholmIndexScFredholmSplitting.C_le_smooth. For any subspace \(A \le E_\infty\), \(\iota_m\) restricts to a bijection \(A_m \to A\) (injective as \(\iota_m\) is, surjective because every point of \(A\) lifts), so \(\dim A_m = \dim A\) Chapter1/FredholmIndexScBanach.finrank_levelSub_of_le_smooth. Hence \(\dim\ker T_m = \dim K_m = \dim K\), and \(F_m/\operatorname{range}T_m = F_m/Y_m \cong C_m\) (complements, Mathlib/LinearAlgebra/ProjectionquotientEquivOfIsCompl) has dimension \(\dim C\). So \(T_m\) is Fredholm with index \(\dim K - \dim C\) in the sense of §I.7 Chapter1/FredholmIndexScFredholmSplitting.fredholmIndex_lvl, which by the previous paragraph is the index of \(T\) for every splitting Chapter1/FredholmIndexIsScFredholm.fredholmIndex_lvl; on level \(0\) this is the definition, \(\operatorname{ind}(T)\) being the Fredholm index of \(T_0\) Chapter1/FredholmIndexscIndex_eq_fredholmIndex. The text states the splittings on each level but not the index.

I.7 Fredholm operators between Banach spaces: Riesz–Schauder and compact perturbations

Mathlib has a notion of Fredholm operator Mathlib/Analysis/Normed/Operator/Fredholm/BasicIsFredholm: a continuous linear \(u : E \to F\) that is a strict map, with closed range, finite-dimensional kernel, range of finite codimension Mathlib/RingTheory/Finiteness/CofiniteCoFG and closed complemented kernel. It does not have the two theorems that §1.4.1 quotes as classical, that \(1 + \text{compact}\) is Fredholm and that compact perturbations preserve the property. Both are proved here, for real Banach spaces.

The criterion. A continuous linear map with closed range between Banach spaces is a strict map Mathlib/Topology/Maps/Strict/BasicIsStrictMap: by the open mapping theorem its corestriction to the range is an open quotient map Mathlib/Topology/Maps/Strict/ModuleisStrictMap_iff_isOpenQuotientMap_rangeRestrict Chapter1/FredholmPerturbationisStrictMap_of_isClosed_range. Hence a continuous linear map with finite-dimensional kernel, closed range and range of finite codimension is Fredholm, the kernel being closed complemented because it is finite-dimensional Chapter1/FredholmPerturbationisFredholm_of_banach. A finite-rank operator is compact: the image of the unit ball is bounded in the finite-dimensional range, so its closure is compact Chapter1/FredholmPerturbationisCompactOperator_of_finiteDimensional_range.

Riesz–Schauder: the kernel. Let \(c : E \to E\) be compact and \(N := \ker(1 + c)\). On \(N\) the operator \(c\) is \(-\mathrm{id}\), and \(c\) restricts to a compact operator of the closed subspace \(N\) Mathlib/Analysis/Normed/Operator/Compact/BasicIsCompactOperator.restrict; so \(\mathrm{id}_N\) is compact, and \(N\) is finite-dimensional Mathlib/Analysis/Normed/Operator/Compact/FiniteDimensionFiniteDimensional.of_isCompactOperator_id Chapter1/FredholmPerturbationfiniteDimensional_ker_one_add.

The range is closed. Take a closed complement \(G\) of \(N\) (which exists since \(N\) is finite-dimensional). \(1 + c\) is bounded below on \(G\): otherwise there are unit vectors \(g_n \in G\) with \((1 + c)g_n \to 0\); the \(c g_n\) lie in a compact set Mathlib/Analysis/Normed/Operator/Compact/BasicIsCompactOperator.image_closedBall_subset_compact, so along a subsequence \(c g_n \to y\) Mathlib/Topology/SequencesIsCompact.tendsto_subseq, hence \(g_n = (1+c)g_n - cg_n \to -y\); then \(-y \in G\) (closed), \(\|-y\| = 1\), and \((1+c)(-y) = 0\), so \(-y \in G \cap N = 0\), a contradiction Chapter1/FredholmPerturbationexists_bound_below_on_compl. A bounded-below operator from a Banach space has closed range (it is antilipschitz and uniformly continuous), and \((1+c)(G) = (1+c)(E)\) since \(1 + c\) kills \(N\) Chapter1/FredholmPerturbationisClosed_range_one_add.

The range has finite codimension. Suppose \(R := \operatorname{range}(1 + c)\) has infinite codimension. Pick, for every proper subspace, a vector outside it Chapter1/FredholmPerturbationpick Chapter1/FredholmPerturbationpick_notMem, and build the chain \(M_0 = R\), \(M_{j+1} = M_j + \mathbb R\,\mathrm{pick}(M_j)\) Chapter1/FredholmPerturbationchain. Each \(M_j\) is \(R\) plus a finite-dimensional subspace Chapter1/FredholmPerturbationchain_eq_sup, hence closed Mathlib/Topology/Algebra/Module/FiniteDimensionSubmodule.isClosed_sup_finiteDimensional Chapter1/FredholmPerturbationchain_isClosed, and proper, since \(R\) has infinite codimension Mathlib/RingTheory/Finiteness/CofiniteFG.cofg_of_codisjoint Chapter1/FredholmPerturbationchain_ne_top; the chain is increasing Chapter1/FredholmPerturbationchain_mono. Riesz’s lemma inside a subspace: for closed \(M \subsetneq M'\) there is a unit vector of \(M'\) at distance \(\ge 1/2\) from \(M\) (take \(x \in M' \setminus M\), a point \(y \in M\) with \(\|x - y\| < 2\,\mathrm{dist}(x, M)\) Mathlib/Topology/MetricSpace/HausdorffDistanceinfDist_lt_iff, and normalize \(x - y\)) Chapter1/FredholmPerturbationexists_unit_far. This gives unit vectors \(u_j \in M_{j+1}\) at distance \(\ge 1/2\) from \(M_j\). For \(j < l\), \(u_j + (1+c)u_l - (1+c)u_j \in M_l\), and \(u_l - [u_j + (1+c)u_l - (1+c)u_j] = -(cu_l - cu_j)\), so \(\|cu_l - cu_j\| \ge 1/2\). But the \(cu_j\) lie in a compact set and so have a convergent subsequence, two of whose terms are within \(1/2\) of each other: a contradiction Chapter1/FredholmPerturbationcoFG_range_one_add. Hence \(1 + c\) is Fredholm Chapter1/FredholmPerturbationisFredholm_one_add.

Compact perturbations. Let \(u : E \to F\) be Fredholm and \(k\) compact. Mathlib gives a quasi-inverse \(v : F \to E\) of \(u\), with \(vu - 1\) and \(uv - 1\) of finite rank Mathlib/Analysis/Normed/Operator/Fredholm/BasicisFredholm_iff_exists_isQuasiInverse; a finite-rank difference from the identity is compact Chapter1/FredholmPerturbationisCompactOperator_sub_one_of_equiv. Then \(v(u + k) = 1 + c_1\) and \((u + k)v = 1 + c_2\) with \(c_1 = (vu - 1) + vk\) and \(c_2 = (uv - 1) + kv\) compact. The kernel of \(u + k\) lies in the finite-dimensional kernel of \(1 + c_1\); the range of \(u + k\) contains the range of \(1 + c_2\), which is closed and of finite codimension, so \(\operatorname{range}(u + k)\) has finite codimension Mathlib/RingTheory/Finiteness/CofiniteCoFG.of_le and is closed, as a subspace containing a closed subspace of finite codimension Mathlib/Topology/Algebra/Module/FiniteDimensionSubmodule.isClosed_mono_of_finiteDimensional_quotient. By the criterion, \(u + k\) is Fredholm Chapter1/FredholmPerturbationisFredholm_add_isCompactOperator.

The index. Mathlib has no index; it is built here, first for linear maps over a field. For \(u : E \to F\) put \(\operatorname{ind}(u) := \dim\ker u - \dim(F/\operatorname{range}u) \in \mathbb Z\) Chapter1/FredholmIndexlinIndex, meaningful when \(u\) has finite index, i.e. finite-dimensional kernel and cokernel Chapter1/FredholmIndexHasFiniteIndex. Additivity. If \(u : E \to F\) and \(v : F \to G\) have finite index, so has \(vu\), and \(\operatorname{ind}(vu) = \operatorname{ind}(u) + \operatorname{ind}(v)\) Chapter1/FredholmIndexHasFiniteIndex.comp_and_linIndex Chapter1/FredholmIndexHasFiniteIndex.comp Chapter1/FredholmIndexlinIndex_comp. The proof is the dimension count along the exact sequence \(0 \to \ker u \to \ker vu \to \operatorname{range}u \cap \ker v \to F/\operatorname{range}u \to G/\operatorname{range}vu \to G/\operatorname{range}v \to 0\), done as four applications of rank–nullity Mathlib/LinearAlgebra/FiniteDimensional/LemmasLinearMap.finrank_range_add_finrank_ker and two of the third isomorphism theorem Mathlib/LinearAlgebra/IsomorphismsSubmodule.quotientQuotientEquivQuotient: to \(u\) restricted to \(\ker vu\) (kernel \(\ker u\), range \(\operatorname{range}u \cap \ker v\)), to the quotient map \(F \to F/\operatorname{range}u\) restricted to \(\ker v\), and to \(v\) followed by \(G \to G/\operatorname{range}vu\) (kernel \(\operatorname{range}u + \ker v\)); finiteness of the new kernel and cokernel comes out of the same maps Chapter1/FredholmIndexfinite_of_finite_ker_range Chapter1/FredholmIndexfinite_of_finite_quotient. Conversely, if \(vu\) and \(uv\) have finite index then so has \(u\), since \(\ker u \subseteq \ker vu\) and \(\operatorname{range}uv \subseteq \operatorname{range}u\) Chapter1/FredholmIndexfiniteDimensional_ker_of_comp Chapter1/FredholmIndexfiniteDimensional_coker_of_comp Chapter1/FredholmIndexHasFiniteIndex.of_comp_of_comp. Index zero. A linear equivalence has index \(0\) Chapter1/FredholmIndexHasFiniteIndex.equiv Chapter1/FredholmIndexlinIndex_equiv. If \(w - 1\) has finite-dimensional range \(R\), then \(\ker w \subseteq R\), \(\operatorname{range}w + R = E\) and \(R \cap \operatorname{range}w = w(R)\), so \(\dim\ker w\) and \(\dim(E/\operatorname{range}w)\) both equal \(\dim R - \dim w(R)\) and \(\operatorname{ind}(w) = 0\) Chapter1/FredholmIndexHasFiniteIndex.of_finiteRange_sub_id_and_linIndex Chapter1/FredholmIndexlinIndex_eq_zero_of_finiteRange_sub_id. If \(a\) is bijective and \(r\) has finite rank, \(a + r = a(1 + a^{-1}r)\) has index \(0 + 0\) by additivity Chapter1/FredholmIndexHasFiniteIndex.of_bijective_add_and_linIndex.

Banach spaces. For \(u : E \to F\) continuous linear, the Fredholm index is \(\operatorname{ind}(u)\) Chapter1/FredholmIndexfredholmIndex; a Fredholm operator has finite index Chapter1/FredholmIndexIsFredholm.hasFiniteIndex. Small perturbations. Let \(v\) be a quasi-inverse of \(u\) and \(\|v\|\,\|s\| < 1\). Then \(\|vs\|, \|sv\| < 1\) Mathlib/Analysis/Normed/Operator/BasicContinuousLinearMap.opNorm_comp_le, so \(1 + vs\) and \(1 + sv\) are invertible by the Neumann series Mathlib/Analysis/SpecificLimits/NormedisUnit_one_sub_of_norm_lt_one Chapter1/FredholmIndexbijective_one_add_of_norm_lt. Since \(vu - 1\) and \(uv - 1\) have finite rank Chapter1/FredholmIndexfiniteDimensional_range_sub_id_of_equiv, \(v(u + s) = (1 + vs) + (vu - 1)\) and \((u + s)v = (1 + sv) + (uv - 1)\) are bijections plus finite-rank maps, hence of index \(0\) Chapter1/FredholmIndexhasFiniteIndex_comp_add_of_norm_lt; the same with \(s = 0\) for \(vu\) and \(uv\). By the converse above, \(u + s\), \(u\) and \(v\) have finite index, and additivity gives \(\operatorname{ind}(u + s) + \operatorname{ind}(v) = 0 = \operatorname{ind}(u) + \operatorname{ind}(v)\), so \(\operatorname{ind}(u + s) = \operatorname{ind}(u)\) Chapter1/FredholmIndexfredholmIndex_add_of_norm_lt. Compact perturbations. Let \(u\) be Fredholm and \(k\) compact, and \(\varphi(t) := \operatorname{ind}(u + tk)\) for \(t \in \mathbb R\). At each \(t_0\), \(u + t_0k\) is Fredholm (the previous paragraph, \(t_0k\) being compact Mathlib/Analysis/Normed/Operator/Compact/BasicIsCompactOperator.smul), with a quasi-inverse \(v_0\); for \(t\) so close to \(t_0\) that \(\|v_0\|\,\|(t - t_0)k\| < 1\), \(\varphi(t) = \operatorname{ind}((u + t_0k) + (t - t_0)k) = \varphi(t_0)\). So \(\varphi\) is locally constant Mathlib/Topology/LocallyConstant/BasicIsLocallyConstant.iff_eventually_eq on the connected \(\mathbb R\), hence constant Mathlib/Topology/LocallyConstant/BasicIsLocallyConstant.apply_eq_of_preconnectedSpace, and \(\operatorname{ind}(u + k) = \varphi(1) = \varphi(0) = \operatorname{ind}(u)\) Chapter1/FredholmIndexfredholmIndex_add_isCompactOperator. This replaces the citation of Kato IV.5.26 in the exposition’s (F2).

I.8 Proposition 1.9: sc-Fredholm operators are regularizing

Statement. Let \(T\) have an sc-Fredholm splitting, \(e \in E_0\), and \(T_0 e \in \operatorname{range}\iota_m\). Then \(e \in \operatorname{range}\iota_m\) Chapter1/ScFredholmproposition_1_9.

Proof (the text’s). Write \(T_0 e = \iota_m y\). Since \(F_m = C_m \oplus Y_m\), \(y = c + y'\) with \(c \in C_m\) and \(y' \in Y_m\), and \(y' = T_m x'\) for some \(x' \in X_m\) by the bijectivity of \(T_m : X_m \to Y_m\). Then \(T_0(e - \iota_m x') = \iota_m c\), so \(\iota_m c\) lies in \(C\) and in \(Y = \operatorname{range} T_0\); these are complementary on level \(0\), so \(\iota_m c = 0\). Hence \(e - \iota_m x' \in \ker T_0 = K \le E_\infty\) (§I.6), so it lifts to some \(z \in E_m\), and \(e = \iota_m(z + x')\). The step “\(c = 0\)” is where \(C \cap Y = 0\) enters, as the exposition notes.

I.9 Proposition 1.10: compact perturbations of sc-Fredholm operators

Statement. If \(T : E \to F\) is sc-Fredholm and \(S : E \to F\) is an \(\mathrm{sc}^+\)-operator, then \(T + S\) is sc-Fredholm Chapter1/ScFredholmproposition_1_10. Here \(S\) is read as the sc-operator \(E \to F\) underlying it (§I.2), and \(T + S\) is the sum of sc-operators.

The bootstrap. The text says: if \(y = (T + S)e \in Y_m\) then, since \(T\) is regularizing, \(e \in E_m\). But \(Te = y - Se\) with \(Se\) only one level up. The formal proof iterates: if \((T + S)_0 e \in \operatorname{range}\iota_{m+1}\), then a fortiori \((T+S)_0 e \in \operatorname{range}\iota_m\) Chapter1/ScFredholmScBanach.range_toBase_succ_le, so \(e \in \operatorname{range}\iota_m\) by induction, so \(S_0 e \in \operatorname{range}\iota_{m+1}\) (§I.2), so \(T_0 e = (T+S)_0 e - S_0 e \in \operatorname{range}\iota_{m+1}\), and Proposition 1.9 gives \(e \in \operatorname{range}\iota_{m+1}\) Chapter1/ScFredholmScPlus.regularizing_add. So \(T + S\) is regularizing.

The kernel. Each \((T + S)_m = T_m + S_m\) is Fredholm, as a compact perturbation (§I.7) of the Fredholm operator \(T_m\) (§I.6) Chapter1/FredholmPerturbationisFredholm_add_isCompactOperator. Let \(K' := \ker (T+S)_0\), finite-dimensional. Every \(x \in K'\) is smooth: \((T+S)_0 x = 0 \in \operatorname{range}\iota_m\) for every \(m\), so \(x \in \operatorname{range}\iota_m\) by the bootstrap. By Proposition 1.6 there is an sc-splitting \(E = K' \oplus X'\) Chapter1/ScBanachScBanach.proposition_1_6. (The text’s \(K_m = K_{m+1}\) is the same bootstrap.)

The range. Let \(Y' := \operatorname{range}(T + S)_0\), closed since \((T+S)_0\) is Fredholm. The range of \((T+S)_m\) is exactly \(Y'_m\): one inclusion from §I.6; conversely if \(\iota_m y = (T+S)_0 e\) then \(e\) lifts to level \(m\) by the bootstrap, and \(y = (T+S)_m e'\) by injectivity of \(\iota_m\). \(Y'\) is an sc-subspace: for \(y = (T+S)_m e \in Y'_m\), approximate \(e\) by smooth points \(e_n \in E_m\); then \((T+S)_m e_n \to y\) and the \((T+S)_m e_n\) are smooth points of \(Y'_m\) (sc-operators preserve smooth points, §I.2). This is the text’s argument “\(y_n = (T+S)e_n \in Y_\infty\), \(y_n \to y\)”.

The complement. \(F_0/Y'\) is finite-dimensional. Let \(p : F_0 \to F_0/Y'\) be the quotient map. The image \(p(F_\infty)\) is a subspace of the finite-dimensional \(F_0/Y'\), dense because \(F_\infty\) is dense in \(F_0\) and \(p\) is a continuous surjection, hence closed, hence everything. Instead of lifting a basis, take a linear right inverse \(g\) of \(p|_{F_\infty}\) and let \(\sigma := F_\infty \hookrightarrow F_0\) composed with \(g\), so \(p \circ \sigma = \mathrm{id}\); put \(C' := \operatorname{range}\sigma\), a finite-dimensional subspace of \(F_\infty\). On every level \(Y'_m\) and \(C'_m\) are complementary: disjoint because an element of \(C'_m \cap Y'_m\) is \(\sigma(q)\) with \(p\sigma(q) = q = 0\); spanning because for \(z \in F_m\) the point \(c := \sigma(p(\iota_m z))\) is smooth, so it lifts to level \(m\), and \(z - c \in Y'_m\). So \(F = C' \oplus Y'\) is an sc-splitting (\(C'\) is an sc-subspace by Proposition 1.6 Chapter1/ScBanachScBanach.proposition_1_6_iff).

The bijections. \((T+S)_m\) maps \(X'_m\) into \(Y'_m\); it is injective on \(X'_m\) because its kernel on level \(m\) is \(K'_m\), which meets \(X'_m\) in \(0\); and it is onto \(Y'_m\) because every \(e \in E_m\) splits as \(k + x\) with \(k \in K'_m\), \(x \in X'_m\) and \((T+S)_m e = (T+S)_m x\). This is condition (3) of Definition 1.8, which the text does not verify; the exposition supplies it with the open mapping theorem, the formalization needs only the bijections (§I.6). Hence \(T + S\) is sc-Fredholm Chapter1/ScFredholmproposition_1_10.

The index. The text does not say that the index is preserved; the exposition does. The index of \(T + S\) is the Fredholm index of \((T + S)_0 = T_0 + S_0\) (§I.6); \(T_0\) is Fredholm and \(S_0\) compact, so by the invariance under compact perturbations (§I.7) \(\operatorname{ind}(T + S) = \operatorname{ind}(T)\) Chapter1/FredholmIndexproposition_1_10_index. On every level, \(T + S\) being sc-Fredholm, its level map \((T + S)_m\) is Fredholm of index \(\operatorname{ind}(T + S) = \operatorname{ind}(T)\) by the index on every level (§I.6) Chapter1/FredholmIndexproposition_1_10_index_lvl.

I.10 Partial quadrants, tuples and sc-domains (Definition 1.11)

The quadrant. In \(\mathbb R^n \oplus W\), with \(\mathbb R^n\) carrying its constant structure, the quadrant on level \(m\) is the set of \((a, w)\) with \(a_i \ge 0\) for all \(i\) Chapter1/ScSmoothquadrant; it is convex Chapter1/ScSmoothquadrant_convex, closed Chapter1/ScSmoothquadrant_isClosed, has non-empty interior (the point \((1, \dots, 1, 0)\)) Chapter1/ScSmoothquadrant_interior_nonempty, and the level sets of the level-\(0\) quadrant are the level quadrants Chapter1/ScSmoothlvlSet_quadrant.

Partial quadrants. \(C \subseteq E_0\) is a partial quadrant if \(C = T_0^{-1}(\text{quadrant})\) for some \(n\), some sc-Banach space \(W\) and some sc-isomorphism \(T : E \to \mathbb R^n \oplus W\) Chapter1/ScSmoothIsPartialQuadrant. The text asks in addition that \(C\) be closed and convex; both follow. Indeed the level set \(C_m\) is \(T_m^{-1}\) of the level-\(m\) quadrant Chapter1/ScSmoothIsPartialQuadrant.lvlSet_eq, hence convex Chapter1/ScSmoothIsPartialQuadrant.convex_lvlSet, closed Chapter1/ScSmoothIsPartialQuadrant.isClosed_lvlSet and with non-empty interior Chapter1/ScSmoothIsPartialQuadrant.interior_lvlSet_nonempty; for \(m = 0\) this is the text’s “closed convex” Chapter1/ScSmoothIsPartialQuadrant.convex Chapter1/ScSmoothIsPartialQuadrant.isClosed. A convex set with non-empty interior has unique differentiability at every point of its closure Mathlib/Analysis/Calculus/TangentCone/RealuniqueDiffWithinAt_convex, so \(C_m\) has unique differentiability at each of its points Chapter1/ScSmoothIsPartialQuadrant.uniqueDiffWithinAt_lvlSet; this is the exposition’s Lemma 3.D, that derivatives on a quadrant are unique, in Mathlib’s language. The whole space is a partial quadrant with \(n = 0\) Chapter1/ScSmoothisPartialQuadrant_univ.

Tuples. \((U, C, E)\) is a tuple, \(U\) a relatively open subset of the partial quadrant \(C\), if \(C\) is a partial quadrant and \(U = O \cap C\) for an open \(O \subseteq E_0\) Chapter1/ScSmoothIsRelOpenInQuadrant.

Sc-domains. \(U \subseteq E_0\) is an sc-domain if for every \(m\) the level set \(U_m\) is the intersection of an open and a convex subset of \(E_m\), and \(U_m\) has unique differentiability at each of its points Chapter1/ScSmoothIsScDomain. A relatively open subset of a partial quadrant is an sc-domain: \(U_m = O_m \cap C_m\) with \(O_m\) open and \(C_m\) convex, and unique differentiability of \(C_m\) at a point survives intersection with a neighbourhood Chapter1/ScSmoothIsRelOpenInQuadrant.isScDomain. The property passes to the tangent: \((TU)_m = U_{m+1} \times E_m\) (§I.11) is \((O \times E_m) \cap (C \times E_m)\), and unique differentiability of a product is the product of the two Chapter1/ScSmoothIsScDomain.tangentSet; and to the level shift, since the level sets of \(U_1\) in \(E^1\) are the \(U_{m+1}\) Chapter1/LevelsIsScDomain.shift. This is what the proofs of §§1.2–1.3 use in place of the text’s claim that \(T(U, C, E)\) is again a tuple (Definition 1.13). Every theorem of §§1.2–1.3 below is stated for sc-domains; the tuples are a special case.

The shift and the tangent of a tuple (Lemmas 3.A(2) and 3.B of the exposition). The text’s claim is nevertheless true, and is proved with Chapter 2, where retracts need it. If \(T : E \to \mathbb R^n \oplus W\) presents \(C\), its levels \(T_{m+1}\) form an sc-isomorphism \(T^1 : E^1 \to \mathbb R^n \oplus W^1\) Chapter2/LevelPolyfoldScIso.shift, and \(C_1 = T_1^{-1}(\text{quadrant})\) by the level description of a partial quadrant above, so \(C_1\) is a partial quadrant in \(E^1\) Chapter2/LevelPolyfoldIsPartialQuadrant.shift; with \(U = O \cap C\), \(U_1 = O_1 \cap C_1\) is relatively open in it Chapter2/LevelPolyfoldIsRelOpenInQuadrant.shift. For the tangent, \(T_{m+1} \times T_m\) maps \((TE)_m = E_{m+1} \times E_m\) onto \((\mathbb R^n \times W_{m+1}) \times (\mathbb R^n \times W_m)\), and the reassociation \(((a, w), q) \mapsto (a, (w, q))\) is an sc-isomorphism onto \(\mathbb R^n \oplus (W^1 \oplus (\mathbb R^n \oplus W))\) Chapter2/TangentBundletangentQuadrantIso; the composite presents \(TC = \{(x, h) : x \in C_1\}\), since the quadrant condition only looks at the \(\mathbb R^n\)-coordinates of \(T_1x\) Chapter2/TangentBundleIsPartialQuadrant.tangentSet. And \(TU = (O_1 \times E_0) \cap TC\) is relatively open in \(TC\) Chapter2/TangentBundleIsRelOpenInQuadrant.tangentSet. The identity \(T(U^1) = (TU)^1\) is §I.11’s Chapter1/LevelsScBanach.shift_tangentSet.

I.11 Sc⁰ maps, the tangent, sc¹ maps, sc^k (Definitions 1.12–1.15)

Level maps. For \(f : E_0 \to F_0\) and \(x \in E_m\), the level map \(f_m(x)\) is the inverse image under \(\iota_m\) of \(f(\iota_m x)\), when \(f(\iota_m x) \in \operatorname{range}\iota_m\), and a junk value otherwise Chapter1/ScSmoothlevelMap; so \(\iota_m f_m(x) = f(\iota_m x)\) whenever the right side lifts Chapter1/ScSmoothtoBase_levelMap, \(f_0 = f\) Chapter1/ScSmoothlevelMap_zero, and \(f_m(x)\) is characterized by \(\iota_m y = f(\iota_m x)\) Chapter1/ScSmoothlevelMap_eq_of_toBase_eq. Maps are total functions on \(E_0\); only the values on the domain \(U\) will matter.

Sc⁰. \(f\) is \(\mathrm{sc}^0\) on \(U\) if for every \(m\) and \(x \in U_m\) the point \(f(\iota_m x)\) lifts to \(F_m\), and \(f_m\) is continuous on \(U_m\) Chapter1/ScSmoothIsSc0 Chapter1/ScSmoothIsSc0.toBase_levelMap. Then \(f\) is continuous on \(U\) Chapter1/ScSmoothIsSc0.continuousOn_base, \(f_m\) maps \(U_m\) into \(V_m\) when \(f\) maps \(U\) into \(V\) Chapter1/ScSmoothIsSc0.levelMap_mapsTo, the property passes to subsets Chapter1/ScSmoothIsSc0.mono and depends only on the values on \(U\) Chapter1/ScSmoothIsSc0.congr. Level maps compose: \((g \circ f)_m = g_m \circ f_m\) on \(U_m\) Chapter1/ScSmoothIsSc0.levelMap_comp, so compositions of \(\mathrm{sc}^0\) maps are \(\mathrm{sc}^0\) Chapter1/ScSmoothIsSc0.comp. The identity is \(\mathrm{sc}^0\) Chapter1/ScSmoothisSc0_id, and an sc-operator is \(\mathrm{sc}^0\) on all of \(E_0\) with level maps \(T_m\) Chapter1/ScSmoothScOperator.isSc0 Chapter1/ScSmoothScOperator.levelMap_eq. The text’s definition says “\(f(U_m) \subset V_m\)” with \(V\) undefined; \(V\) is \(U'\), and the target tuple enters only as \(f(U) \subseteq U'\).

The tangent. \(TE := E^1 \oplus E\), with levels \(E_{m+1} \times E_m\) Chapter1/ScSmoothScBanach.tangent Chapter1/ScSmoothScBanach.tangent_toBase; \(TU \subseteq (TE)_0 = E_1 \times E_0\) is the set of \((x, h)\) with \(x \in U_1\) Chapter1/ScSmoothScBanach.tangentSet, with level-\(m\) part \(U_{m+1} \times E_m\) Chapter1/ScSmoothScBanach.mem_lvlSet_tangentSet Chapter1/ScSmoothScBanach.lvlSet_tangentSet, monotone in \(U\) Chapter1/ScSmoothScBanach.tangentSet_mono. The level-\(1\) part of \(TU\) is \(T(U_1)\) in \(T(E^1) = (TE)^1\), the identity \(T(U^1) = (TU)^1\) that the inductions of §1.2 use Chapter1/LevelsScBanach.shift_tangentSet.

Sc¹. Given a family \(D : E_1 \to \mathcal L(E_0, F_0)\), the tangent map is \(T_D f(x, h) = (f_1(x), D(x)h)\) Chapter1/ScSmoothtangentMapWith. \(f\) is \(\mathrm{sc}^1\) on \(U\) with derivatives \(D\) if (1) \(f\) is \(\mathrm{sc}^0\) on \(U\); (2) for every \(x \in U_1\) the map \(f \circ \iota_1 : E_1 \to F_0\) has derivative \(D(x) \circ \iota_1\) at \(x\) within \(U_1\) Mathlib/Analysis/Calculus/FDeriv/DefsHasFDerivWithinAt; (3) \(T_Df\) is \(\mathrm{sc}^0\) on \(TU\) Chapter1/ScSmoothIsSc1With. Condition (2) is the text’s limit \(|f(x+h) - f(x) - Df(x)h|_0/|h|_1 \to 0\) over \(h \in E_1\) with \(x + h \in U_1\), in Mathlib’s words. \(f\) is \(\mathrm{sc}^1\) on \(U\) if some \(D\) works Chapter1/ScSmoothIsSc1; scDeriv is a chosen such \(D\) Chapter1/ScSmoothscDeriv Chapter1/ScSmoothIsSc1.isSc1With_scDeriv and tangentMap the tangent map built from it Chapter1/ScSmoothtangentMap Chapter1/ScSmoothIsSc1.tangentMap_isSc0. If \(f\) maps \(U\) into \(V\) then \(T_Df\) maps \(TU\) into \(TV\) Chapter1/ScSmoothIsSc1With.tangentMapWith_mapsTo Chapter1/ScSmoothIsSc1.tangentMap_mapsTo; level \(0\) of (3) says \((x, h) \mapsto D(x)h\) is continuous on \(U_1 \times E_0\) Chapter1/ScSmoothIsSc1With.continuousOn_deriv; and both notions depend only on the values of \(f\) on \(U\) Chapter1/ScSmoothIsSc1With.congr Chapter1/ScSmoothIsSc1.congr.

Uniqueness of \(Df(x)\). The text writes “the” operator \(Df(x)\) and “the” tangent map. If \(D\) and \(D'\) both satisfy (2) at \(x \in U_1\) and \(U_1\) has unique differentiability at \(x\), then \(D(x) \circ \iota_1 = D'(x) \circ \iota_1\) Mathlib/Analysis/Calculus/FDeriv/BasicUniqueDiffWithinAt.eq; since \(\iota_1\) has dense range (§I.1) and both operators are continuous, \(D(x) = D'(x)\) Mathlib/Topology/Algebra/Module/ContinuousLinearMap/Basicext_on Chapter1/ScSmoothIsSc1With.eq_of_uniqueDiffWithinAt. Hence on a set \(U\) whose \(U_1\) has unique differentiability everywhere (an sc-domain), the chosen derivative agrees on \(U_1\) with any admissible family Chapter1/ScSmoothIsSc1.scDeriv_eqOn and the chosen tangent map agrees on \(TU\) with any \(T_Df\) Chapter1/ScSmoothIsSc1.tangentMap_eqOn. This is the exposition’s Lemma 3.E, and the formal proofs invoke it wherever the text says “the tangent map”. The uniform version of (3) at level \(0\): for \(x \in U_1\), a compact \(K \subseteq E_0\) and \(c > 0\) there is \(\delta > 0\) such that \(\|D(x')w - D(x)w\| \le c\) for all \(x' \in U_1\) within \(\delta\) of \(x\) and all \(w \in K\); this is the continuity of \((x', w) \mapsto D(x')w - D(x)w\) on \(U_1 \times E_0\) turned uniform over the compact \(K\) Mathlib/Topology/Compactness/CompactIsCompact.eventually_forall_of_forall_eventually Chapter1/PropertiesIsSc1With.exists_delta_deriv, and it is the text’s remark that \(x \mapsto Df(x)\) is continuous for the compact-open topology.

Compact-open continuity as an equivalence (Lemma 3.F of the exposition). For a metric space \(X\), \(s \subseteq X\) and \(A : X \to \mathcal L(Y, Z)\): \((x, h) \mapsto A(x)h\) is continuous on \(s \times Y\) if and only if for every \(x \in s\), compact \(K \subseteq Y\) and \(\varepsilon > 0\), eventually for \(x'\) near \(x\) in \(s\), \(\|A(x')w - A(x)w\| < \varepsilon\) for all \(w \in K\) Chapter1/ExpositionLemmascontinuousOn_apply_iff_uniformOnCompact. (⇒) As above, on the subtype \(s\): for each \(w \in K\), \((x', w') \mapsto A(x')w' - A(x)w'\) is continuous with value \(0\) at \((x, w)\), so it is small near \((x, w)\), and compactness of \(K\) makes the neighbourhood of \(x\) uniform in \(w\) Mathlib/Topology/Compactness/CompactIsCompact.eventually_forall_of_forall_eventually; neighbourhoods in the subtype are neighbourhoods within \(s\) Mathlib/Topology/NhdsWithineventually_nhds_subtype_iff. (⇐) Continuity within \(s \times Y\) at \((x, w)\) is tested on sequences Mathlib/Order/Filter/AtTopBot/CountablyGeneratedtendsto_iff_seq_tendsto: let \((x_n, w_n) \to (x, w)\) with \(x_n \in s\). The set \(K = \{w\} \cup \{w_n\}\) is compact Mathlib/Topology/Compactness/CompactFilter.Tendsto.isCompact_insert_range, so \(\|A(x_n)w_n - A(x)w_n\| \to 0\) by the hypothesis, and \(A(x)w_n \to A(x)w\) by continuity of \(A(x)\); adding, \(A(x_n)w_n \to A(x)w\). For an \(\mathrm{sc}^1\) map, level \(0\) of condition (3) is the left side for \(Df\) on \(U_1\), so \(x \mapsto Df(x)\) is compact-open continuous on \(U_1\) Chapter1/ExpositionLemmasIsSc1With.deriv_uniformOnCompact. The text’s other half, that norm continuity can fail, needs the shift map of the exposition’s §6 and is not formalized.

Sc^k and sc-smooth. By recursion on \(k\): \(\mathrm{sc}^0\) is \(\mathrm{sc}^0\), and \(f\) is \(\mathrm{sc}^{k+1}\) on \(U\) if it is \(\mathrm{sc}^1\) on \(U\) and the chosen tangent map is \(\mathrm{sc}^k\) on \(TU\) Chapter1/ScSmoothIsSck; \(f\) is sc-smooth on \(U\) if it is \(\mathrm{sc}^k\) for every \(k\) Chapter1/ScSmoothIsScSmooth. An \(\mathrm{sc}^k\) map is \(\mathrm{sc}^0\) Chapter1/ScSmoothIsSck.isSc0, \(\mathrm{sc}^{k+1}\) implies \(\mathrm{sc}^k\) Chapter1/ScSmoothIsSck.of_succ Chapter1/ScSmoothIsSck.of_le, and \(f\) is sc-smooth iff it is \(\mathrm{sc}^1\) with sc-smooth tangent map Chapter1/ScSmoothisScSmooth_iff. On an sc-domain the notion depends only on the values on \(U\), by induction with the uniqueness of the tangent map Chapter1/ChainRuleIsSc1.tangentMap_congr Chapter1/ChainRuleIsSck.congr. Finite dimensions. The text’s remark that \(\mathrm{sc}^1\) maps between finite-dimensional spaces are the \(C^1\) maps holds on every sc-domain, in particular on relatively open subsets of quadrants, with boundary. Let \(V\), \(W\) carry their constant structures and \(U \subseteq V\) be an sc-domain. All level sets of \(U\) are \(U\) itself Chapter1/ExpositionLemmasScBanach.lvlSet_const and all \(f \circ \iota_m\) are \(f\). If \(f\) is \(\mathrm{sc}^1\), then \(f \circ \iota_1 = f\) is \(C^1\) within \(U_1 = U\) by Proposition 1.16 (§I.14, Chapter1/PropertiesIsSc1With.contDiffOn_base); if \(f\) is \(C^1\) within \(U\), it is \(C^1\) on every level, so \(\mathrm{sc}^1\) by Corollary 1.20 at \(k = 0\) (§I.17, Chapter1/Propertiescorollary_1_20_zero) Chapter1/ExpositionLemmasisSc1_iff_contDiffOn_const. Mathlib’s “\(C^1\) within \(U\)” means, on a set with unique derivatives, differentiable within \(U\) at every point with \(x \mapsto \mathrm{fderivWithin}\,f\,U\,x\) continuous on \(U\) Mathlib/Analysis/Calculus/ContDiff/DefscontDiffOn_succ_iff_fderivWithin Chapter1/ExpositionLemmasisSc1_iff_fderivWithin_const: at a boundary point of a quadrant this is the one-sided derivative along \(U\), unique because the quadrant has interior (§I.10). Likewise sc-smooth is \(C^\infty\) within \(U\), by Proposition 1.18 at \(m = 0\) (§I.16) and the sc-smooth case of Corollary 1.20 Chapter1/ExpositionLemmasisScSmooth_iff_contDiffOn_const. For the text’s tuples: Chapter1/ExpositionLemmasisSc1_iff_contDiffOn_of_isRelOpenInQuadrant Chapter1/ExpositionLemmasisScSmooth_iff_contDiffOn_of_isRelOpenInQuadrant. The open case is also checked in the test file TestisSc1_iff_contDiffOn_of_finiteDimensional TestisScSmooth_iff_contDiffOn_of_finiteDimensional. By §I.1 every sc-structure on a finite-dimensional space is the constant one up to sc-isomorphism.

I.12 Theorem 1.21: the chain rule

Statement. Let \(U \subseteq C \subseteq E\) and \(V \subseteq D \subseteq F\) be relatively open subsets of partial quadrants, \(f\) \(\mathrm{sc}^1\) on \(U\) with \(f(U) \subseteq V\), and \(g\) \(\mathrm{sc}^1\) on \(V\). Then \(g \circ f\) is \(\mathrm{sc}^1\) on \(U\) and \(T(g \circ f) = Tg \circ Tf\) on \(TU\) Chapter1/ChainRuletheorem_1_21. The same holds for sc-domains Chapter1/ChainRuletheorem_1_21', and the existence part needs still less: if \(g\) is \(\mathrm{sc}^1\) on \(V\) with derivatives \(Dg\), \(f\) is \(\mathrm{sc}^1\) on \(U\) with derivatives \(Df\), \(f(U) \subseteq V\), and \(V_1\) is open-in-convex, then \(g \circ f\) is \(\mathrm{sc}^1\) on \(U\) with derivatives \(x \mapsto Dg(f_1(x)) \circ Df(x)\), with no hypothesis on \(U\) Chapter1/ChainRuleIsSc1With.comp. The text’s third tuple \(W \subset Q \subset G\) plays no role.

The derivative. Fix \(x \in U_1\), let \(y_0 := f_1(x) \in V_1\) and \(K\) a compact set containing \(Df(x)(\iota_1 \bar B_1)\), which exists because \(\iota_1\) is compact Mathlib/Analysis/Normed/Operator/Compact/BasicIsCompactOperator.image_closedBall_subset_compact. Write \(V_1 = O \cap C\) with \(O\) open and \(C\) convex, and choose \(\rho > 0\) with the \(\rho\)-ball around \(y_0\) inside \(O\). Given \(c > 0\), two tolerances are fixed. First, by the uniform smallness of \([Dg(y) - Dg(y_0)](w + b)\) for \(y \in V_1\) near \(y_0\), \(w \in K\) and \(b\) small, which is the continuity of \((y, b, w) \mapsto [Dg(y) - Dg(y_0)](w + b)\) on \(V_1 \times F_0 \times K\) made uniform over \(K\) Mathlib/Topology/Compactness/CompactIsCompact.eventually_forall_of_forall_eventually Chapter1/ChainRuleIsSc1With.exists_delta, there is \(\delta\) with this expression of norm \(\le c/2\). Second, \(\varepsilon := \min(\delta/2, (c/2)/(\|Dg(y_0)\| + 1))\). For \(z \in U_1\) close to \(x\) three things hold eventually: \(\|f_1(z) - y_0\|_1 < \min(\rho, \delta)\) (continuity of \(f_1\) on \(U_1\)), and \(r := f(\iota z) - f(\iota x) - Df(x)\iota(z - x)\) has \(\|r\| \le \varepsilon\|z - x\|_1\) (condition (2) for \(f\) Mathlib/Analysis/Calculus/FDeriv/DefshasFDerivWithinAt_iff_isLittleO). Let \(k := f_1(z) - y_0 \in F_1\). The segment \(y_0 + tk\), \(t \in [0, 1]\), lies in \(V_1\): inside the \(\rho\)-ball, hence in \(O\), and in \(C\) by convexity, since both endpoints are in \(C\). The text states this inclusion without comment; it is the one place where the structure of \(V\) enters.

The mean value inequality. The text’s second integral is replaced by: for \(\varphi(t) := g(\iota(y_0 + tk)) - t\,Dg(y_0)(\iota k)\) on \([0, 1]\), the derivative within \([0,1]\) is \([Dg(y_0 + tk) - Dg(y_0)](\iota k)\) (condition (2) for \(g\) along the segment, composed with the affine curve), and if its norm is \(\le C\) on \([0, 1]\) then \(\|\varphi(1) - \varphi(0)\| \le C\) Mathlib/Analysis/Calculus/MeanValueConvex.norm_image_sub_le_of_norm_hasDerivWithin_le Chapter1/ChainRuleIsSc1With.norm_sub_le_of_segment. Now write \(\iota k = f(\iota z) - f(\iota x) = s(w_1 + b)\) with \(s := \|z - x\|_1\), \(w_1 := Df(x)\iota(u)\) for the unit vector \(u := s^{-1}(z - x)\), so \(w_1 \in K\), and \(b := s^{-1} r\), so \(\|b\| \le \varepsilon \le \delta/2 < \delta\). For every \(t\), \(y_0 + tk\) is within \(\delta\) of \(y_0\), so \(\|[Dg(y_0 + tk) - Dg(y_0)](\iota k)\| \le (c/2)\,s\), and the mean value inequality gives \[\|g(f(\iota z)) - g(f(\iota x)) - Dg(y_0)(\iota k)\| \le \tfrac c2 \|z - x\|_1 .\] (When \(z = x\) both sides vanish.) The text’s first integral is not needed: \(\|Dg(y_0) r\| \le \|Dg(y_0)\|\,\varepsilon\|z - x\|_1 \le \tfrac c2\|z - x\|_1\) directly, because \(Dg(y_0)\) is bounded on \(F_0\). Adding the two estimates, since \(\iota k = Df(x)\iota(z - x) + r\), \[\|g(f(\iota z)) - g(f(\iota x)) - Dg(y_0)Df(x)\iota(z - x)\| \le c\|z - x\|_1\] eventually, which is condition (2) for \(g \circ f\) at \(x\) with the operator \(Dg(y_0) \circ Df(x)\) Chapter1/ChainRuleIsSc1With.hasFDerivWithinAt_comp. The text’s subsequence argument for the uniform convergence of the second integrand is the compactness step above; the text’s appeal to Proposition 1.18 to make \(g : V_1 \to G_0\) of class \(C^1\) is not used.

The tangent map. \(g \circ f\) is \(\mathrm{sc}^0\) as a composite. The tangent map of \(g \circ f\) with the composed derivatives equals \(T_{Dg}g \circ T_Df\) on \(TU\), since \((g \circ f)_1 = g_1 \circ f_1\) on \(U_1\) Chapter1/ChainRuleIsSc1With.tangentMapWith_comp; the right side is a composite of \(\mathrm{sc}^0\) maps (\(T_Df\) maps \(TU\) into \(TV\)), hence \(\mathrm{sc}^0\): condition (3) Chapter1/ChainRuleIsSc1With.comp. For the chosen derivatives, \(T(g \circ f) = Tg \circ Tf\) on \(TU\) follows from the uniqueness of the derivative on \(U_1\) (§I.11), which is where the quadrant structure of \(U\) enters Chapter1/ChainRuletheorem_1_21' Chapter1/ChainRuletheorem_1_21.

Iterating. If \(U\), \(V\) are sc-domains, \(f\) is \(\mathrm{sc}^k\) on \(U\) with \(f(U) \subseteq V\) and \(g\) is \(\mathrm{sc}^k\) on \(V\), then \(g \circ f\) is \(\mathrm{sc}^k\) on \(U\): induction on \(k\), the step being the theorem for the \(\mathrm{sc}^1\) parts, the induction hypothesis for \(Tg \circ Tf\) on the sc-domains \(TU\), \(TV\), and the identity \(T(g \circ f) = Tg \circ Tf\) with the independence of \(\mathrm{sc}^k\) from the values off \(TU\) Chapter1/ChainRuleIsSck.comp Chapter1/ChainRuleIsSck.comp_of_isRelOpenInQuadrant. Sc-smooth maps compose to sc-smooth maps Chapter1/ChainRuleIsScSmooth.comp. This is the exposition’s Corollary 4.A.

I.13 The compact-open lemma and the level operators \(Df(x) : E_m \to F_m\)

The proofs of Propositions 1.16–1.18 in the 2010 paper all rest on one mechanism, which the formal proof isolates.

The lemma, \(k = 0\). Let \(A : X \to \mathcal L(Y, Z)\) with \((x, y) \mapsto A(x)y\) continuous on \(s \times Y\), and \(\iota : Y' \to Y\) a compact operator. Then \(x \mapsto A(x) \circ \iota\) is continuous on \(s\) into \(\mathcal L(Y', Z)\) with the operator norm Chapter1/LevelscontinuousOn_clm_comp_of_isCompactOperator. Proof: the image of the unit ball of \(Y'\) under \(\iota\) lies in a compact \(K\); by uniform continuity on compact sets Chapter1/Levelsexists_delta_of_continuousOn, for \(x' \in s\) near \(x\) and all \(w \in K\), \(\|A(x')w - A(x)w\| \le \varepsilon/2\), so \(\|(A(x') - A(x)) \circ \iota\| \le \varepsilon/2\) on unit vectors. This is the 2010 paper’s subsequence argument (unit vectors \(h_n \in E_{m+1}\) have a subsequence converging in \(E_m\)) in uniform form.

The lemma, \(C^k\). Let \(s\) be open-in-convex with unique differentiability at every point, and \((x, y) \mapsto A(x)y\) of class \(C^k\) on \(s \times Y\). Then \(x \mapsto A(x) \circ \iota\) is \(C^k\) on \(s\) Chapter1/LevelscontDiffOn_clm_comp_of_isCompactOperator. Induction on \(k\) over all \(Z\) and \(A\). For \(k + 1\): the partial derivative in \(x\), \(B(x)y := D_x(A(x)y)\), is \(C^k\) in \((x, y)\) Mathlib/Analysis/Calculus/ContDiff/DefsContDiffOn, linear and continuous in \(y\) for \(x \in s\) (differentiate the linearity identities and use uniqueness of derivatives), so \(B : s \to \mathcal L(Y, \mathcal L(X, Z))\); by the induction hypothesis \(x \mapsto B(x) \circ \iota\) is \(C^k\), and so is its flip \(G'(x) \in \mathcal L(X, \mathcal L(Y', Z))\). \(G'\) is the derivative of \(x \mapsto A(x) \circ \iota\): for \(z \in s\) near \(x\) the segment from \(x\) to \(z\) lies in \(s\) (open-in-convex), and for a unit vector \(v \in Y'\) the mean value inequality applied to \(\tau \mapsto A(x + \tau(z - x))(\iota v) - \tau B(x)(\iota v)(z - x)\) Mathlib/Analysis/Calculus/MeanValueConvex.norm_image_sub_le_of_norm_hasDerivWithin_le, with the uniform continuity of \(B\) on \(\{x\} \times \iota(\bar B_1)\), bounds \(\|A(z)\iota v - A(x)\iota v - B(x)(\iota v)(z - x)\| \le c\|z - x\|\) uniformly in \(v\). So \(x \mapsto A(x)\circ\iota\) is differentiable within \(s\) with a \(C^k\) derivative, hence \(C^{k+1}\) Mathlib/Analysis/Calculus/ContDiff/DefscontDiffOn_succ_iff_hasFDerivWithinAt_of_uniqueDiffOn. The 2010 paper’s Proposition 2.3 carries the same information in the multilinear maps \(\Gamma(x)(h_1, \dots, h_k, h)\) and a differentiation under the integral sign; the lemma replaces both.

The level operators. Let \(f\) be \(\mathrm{sc}^1\) on \(U\) with derivatives \(D\), and \(x \in E_{m+1}\). The level-\(m\) operator \(Df(x) : E_m \to F_m\) is the continuous linear \(T\) with \(\iota_m \circ T = D(\iota x) \circ \iota_m\), when such \(T\) exists (it is unique by injectivity), and \(0\) otherwise Chapter1/LevelslevelDeriv Chapter1/LevelstoBase_levelDeriv; on level \(0\) it is \(D(x)\) itself Chapter1/LevelslevelDeriv_zero. For \(x \in U_{m+1}\) it exists: the level-\(m\) tangent map sends \((x, v) \in U_{m+1} \times E_m\) to a pair whose second component \(T_m(v)\) satisfies \(\iota_m T_m(v) = D(\iota x)\iota_m v\); \(T_m\) is linear (by injectivity of \(\iota_m\)) and continuous (condition (3) on level \(m\)) Chapter1/LevelsIsSc1With.exists_levelDeriv Chapter1/LevelsIsSc1With.toBase_levelDeriv. So the level-\(m\) tangent map is \((x, h) \mapsto (f_{m+1}(x), Df(x)h)\) on \(U_{m+1} \times E_m\) Chapter1/LevelsIsSc1With.levelMap_tangentMapWith, and condition (3) says exactly that \((x, h) \mapsto Df(x)h\) is continuous on \(U_{m+1} \times E_m\) Chapter1/LevelsIsSc1With.continuousOn_levelDeriv: this is condition (2) of Proposition 1.16. By the compact-open lemma with \(\iota = \mathrm{incl}_m : E_{m+1} \to E_m\), the map \(x \mapsto Df(x) \circ \mathrm{incl}_m\) is continuous \(U_{m+1} \to \mathcal L(E_{m+1}, F_m)\) in the operator norm Chapter1/LevelsIsSc1With.continuousOn_levelDeriv_clm: the continuity of \(df\) in condition (1) of Proposition 1.16. The base case, \(x \mapsto D(x) \circ \iota_1\) continuous \(U_1 \to \mathcal L(E_1, F_0)\), is also proved directly Chapter1/PropertiesIsSc1With.continuousOn_deriv_clm, and with it \(f \circ \iota_1 : U_1 \to F_0\) is \(C^1\) Chapter1/PropertiesIsSc1With.contDiffOn_base.

Level-raising: differentiability of \(f : U_{m+1} \to F_m\). Let \(U\) be an sc-domain. For \(x \in U_{m+1}\), the map \(f_m \circ \mathrm{incl}_m : U_{m+1} \to F_m\) has derivative \(Df(x) \circ \mathrm{incl}_m\) at \(x\) within \(U_{m+1}\) Chapter1/LevelsIsSc1With.hasFDerivWithinAt_level. This is the 2010 paper’s integral representation \(f(x+k) - f(x) = \int_0^1 Df(x + \tau k)k\,d\tau\). For \(z \in U_{m+1}\) near \(x\) and \(k := z - x\), the segment \(x + \tau k\) lies in \(U_{m+1}\) (open-in-convex). The integrand \(g(\tau) := Df(x + \tau k)(\mathrm{incl}_m k)\) is continuous into \(F_m\) by condition (3) on level \(m\), so its Bochner integral over \([0, 1]\) exists in \(F_m\). Its image under \(\iota_m\) is the integral of \(D(\iota(x + \tau k))\iota_{m+1}k\) in \(F_0\), which by the fundamental theorem of calculus for the \(C^1\) curve \(\tau \mapsto f(\iota(x + \tau k))\) (condition (2) for \(f\), composed with the affine curve) Mathlib/MeasureTheory/Integral/IntervalIntegral/FundThmCalculusintegral_eq_sub_of_hasDerivAt_of_le equals \(f(\iota z) - f(\iota x) = \iota_m(f_m(\mathrm{incl}_m z) - f_m(\mathrm{incl}_m x))\). By injectivity, \(f_m(\mathrm{incl}_m z) - f_m(\mathrm{incl}_m x) = \int_0^1 g\) in \(F_m\). Then \[\Big\|f_m(\mathrm{incl}_m z) - f_m(\mathrm{incl}_m x) - Df(x)\mathrm{incl}_m k\Big\|_m \le \sup_{\tau} \|(Df(x + \tau k) - Df(x)) \circ \mathrm{incl}_m\|\,\|k\|_{m+1},\] and the supremum tends to \(0\) by the norm continuity just proved. The 2010 paper forms the integral in \(F_0\) and remarks that the integrand is continuous into \(F_m\); here it is formed in \(F_m\) and pushed down. Consequently \(f_m \circ \mathrm{incl}_m : U_{m+1} \to F_m\) is \(C^1\) within \(U_{m+1}\) Chapter1/LevelsIsSc1With.contDiffOn_level, which is condition (1) of Proposition 1.16 in full.

The level operator is the derivative of \(f_m\). If \(f_m : U_m \to F_m\) happens to be differentiable at \(\mathrm{incl}_m x\) within \(U_m\) with derivative \(L\), then \(L = Df(x)\): both \(\iota_m \circ L \circ \mathrm{incl}_m\) and \(D(\iota x) \circ \iota_{m+1}\) are derivatives of \(f \circ \iota_{m+1}\) at \(x\) within \(U_{m+1}\), hence equal by uniqueness; and since \(\mathrm{incl}_m\) has dense range, \(\iota_m \circ L = D(\iota x) \circ \iota_m\) on all of \(E_m\) Mathlib/Topology/Algebra/Module/ContinuousLinearMap/Basicext_on Chapter1/LevelsIsSc1With.levelDeriv_eq. This is the exposition’s Lemma 3.H and the key to Proposition 1.19.

I.14 Proposition 1.16: sc¹ in terms of the levels

The level conditions. For a family \(D_m(x) \in \mathcal L(E_m, F_m)\), \(x \in E_{m+1}\), the level conditions are: (a) for every \(m\) and \(x \in U_{m+1}\), \(f_m \circ \mathrm{incl}_m\) has derivative \(D_m(x) \circ \mathrm{incl}_m\) at \(x\) within \(U_{m+1}\); (b) for every \(m\), \((x, h) \mapsto D_m(x)h\) is continuous on \(U_{m+1} \times E_m\) Chapter1/LevelsIsSc1Levels. These are the text’s (1) and (2) with \(m - 1\) renamed \(m\) and the extensions \(Df(x)\) made an explicit family. From them, \(x \mapsto D_m(x) \circ \mathrm{incl}_m\) is norm continuous (compact-open lemma) Chapter1/LevelsIsSc1Levels.continuousOn_clm, so \(f : U_{m+1} \to F_m\) is \(C^1\) on an sc-domain Chapter1/LevelsIsSc1Levels.contDiffOn: the rest of the text’s (1).

Statement. For an sc-domain \(U\) and \(f\) \(\mathrm{sc}^0\) on \(U\): \(f\) is \(\mathrm{sc}^1\) on \(U\) iff some family \(D_m\) satisfies the level conditions Chapter1/Levelsproposition_1_16.

(⇒). The level operators of §I.13 satisfy (a) (level-raising) and (b) (condition (3)) Chapter1/LevelsIsSc1With.isSc1Levels.

(⇐), and what the text hides. The 2010 paper calls this direction clear. It is, once one knows that the operators \(D_m(x)\) for different \(m\) are restrictions of one operator, which the text’s notation \(Df(x)\) assumes. Proof: for \(x \in U_{m+1}\), both \(\iota_m \circ D_m(x) \circ \mathrm{incl}_m\) and \(D_0(\iota x) \circ \iota_{m+1}\) are derivatives of \(f \circ \iota_{m+1}\) at \(x\) within \(U_{m+1}\) (compose (a) at level \(m\) with \(\iota_m\), and (a) at level \(0\) with the inclusion \(E_{m+1} \to E_1\)), so they agree by uniqueness, and since \(\mathrm{incl}_m\) has dense range, \(\iota_m \circ D_m(x) = D_0(\iota x) \circ \iota_m\) Chapter1/LevelsIsSc1Levels.toBase_apply. Then \(f\) is \(\mathrm{sc}^1\) with derivatives \(D_0\): condition (2) is (a) at level \(0\); condition (3) at level \(m\) reads, after the compatibility, \((x, h) \mapsto (f_{m+1}(x), D_m(x)h)\) on \(U_{m+1} \times E_m\), which is continuous by (b) and the continuity of \(f_{m+1}\) Chapter1/LevelsIsSc1Levels.isSc1With.

The “in particular”. If \(f\) is \(\mathrm{sc}^1\) with derivatives \(D\) and \(x \in U_1\) is a smooth point, then \(D(x) : E_0 \to F_0\) is an sc-operator: lift \(x\) to \(y \in U_{m+1}\); the level-\(m\) tangent map at \((y, v)\) has second component \(T_m(v)\) with \(\iota_m T_m(v) = D(x)\iota_m v\), linear and continuous in \(v\), which is the level-\(m\) map required by IsScOperator Chapter1/PropertiesIsSc1With.scOperator_deriv.

I.15 Proposition 1.17: lifting the index

Statement. If \(U\) is an sc-domain in \(E\) and \(f\) is \(\mathrm{sc}^k\) on \(U\), then \(f_1 : E_1 \to F_1\) is \(\mathrm{sc}^k\) on \(U_1\), as a map between the shifted spaces \(E^1\) and \(F^1\) Chapter1/LevelsIsSck.shift; sc-smooth maps lift to sc-smooth maps Chapter1/LevelsIsScSmooth.shift. The target \(V\) of the text plays no role.

Proof. The level maps of \(f_1\), computed in the shifted spaces, are the level maps of \(f\) shifted by one Chapter1/LevelsIsSc0.levelMap_shift, so an \(\mathrm{sc}^0\) map lifts to an \(\mathrm{sc}^0\) map, with no hypothesis on \(U\) Chapter1/LevelsIsSc0.shift. For \(\mathrm{sc}^1\) with derivatives \(D\): the derivatives of \(f_1\) are the level-\(1\) operators \(Df(x) : E_1 \to F_1\), \(x \in U_2\); condition (2) for \(f_1\) is the level-raising statement of §I.13 at \(m = 1\), and condition (3) is the shift of condition (3) for \(f\), since \(T(U_1) = (TU)^1\) (§I.11) and the level tangent maps are \((x, h) \mapsto (f_{m+2}(x), Df(x)h)\) Chapter1/LevelsIsSc1With.shift. For \(\mathrm{sc}^{k+1}\): the tangent map of \(f_1\) agrees on \(T(U_1)\) with the level-\(1\) map of \(Tf\) (uniqueness of derivatives on the sc-domain \(U_1\)), which is \(\mathrm{sc}^k\) by the induction hypothesis applied to \(Tf\) on \(TU\) Chapter1/LevelsIsSck.shift. This is the 2010 paper’s argument, with the compatibility \(T(U^1) = (TU)^1\) and the restriction of \(Df\) proved rather than assumed.

I.16 Proposition 1.18: sc^k maps are \(C^k\) from \(U_{m+k}\) to \(F_m\)

Statement. Let \(U\) be an sc-domain and \(f\) \(\mathrm{sc}^k\) on \(U\). Then \(f_m \circ (E_{m+k} \to E_m) : U_{m+k} \to F_m\) is \(C^k\) within \(U_{m+k}\) for every \(m\) Chapter1/LevelsIsSck.contDiffOn_levels; \(f : U_{m+l} \to F_m\) is \(C^l\) for \(l \le k\) Chapter1/LevelsIsSck.contDiffOn_levels_of_le; in particular \(f \circ \iota_k : U_k \to F_0\) is \(C^k\) Chapter1/LevelsIsSck.contDiffOn_base; and an sc-smooth map is \(C^k\) from \(U_{m+k}\) to \(F_m\) for all \(m\), \(k\) Chapter1/LevelsIsScSmooth.contDiffOn_levels.

Proof. The 2010 paper proves the case \(m = 0\) and reduces to it with Proposition 1.17 applied \(m\) times.
