The formal proof handles all levels at once, by induction on \(k\) over all sc-domains, with a compatible level-lowering operator \(\rho : E_n \to E_m\), \(n = m + k\), \(\iota_m \rho = \iota_n\), as a parameter Chapter1/LevelsIsSck.contDiffOn_levels'; this avoids identifying \((E^m)_k\) with \(E_{m+k}\). For \(k = 0\), \(\rho\) is the identity and the claim is the continuity of \(f_m\). For \(k + 1\): write \(\rho = \mathrm{incl}_m \circ \rho'\) with \(\rho' : E_{m+k+1} \to E_{m+1}\) Chapter1/LevelsScBanach.incl_shift_inclK Chapter1/LevelsScBanach.shift_inclK_mem_lvlSet. By the level-raising statement of §I.13, \(f_m \circ \rho\) has derivative \(x \mapsto Df(\rho' x) \circ \rho\) on \(U_{m+k+1}\), where \(Df(\cdot)\) is the level-\(m\) operator. It remains to see that this derivative is \(C^k\) into \(\mathcal L(E_{m+k+1}, F_m)\). The induction hypothesis for the \(\mathrm{sc}^k\) map \(Tf\) on the sc-domain \(TU\), with the level-lowering operator of \(TE\) (which is the pair of those of \(E^1\) and \(E\) Chapter1/LevelsScBanach.tangent_inclK), says that the level-\(m\) tangent map composed with it, \((x, h) \mapsto (f_{m+1}(\rho' x), Df(\rho' x)(E_{m+k} \to E_m)h)\), is \(C^k\) on \(U_{m+k+1} \times E_{m+k}\); its second component is \((x, h) \mapsto A(x)h\) with \(A(x) := Df(\rho' x) \circ (E_{m+k} \to E_m)\). The compact-open lemma with \(\iota = \mathrm{incl}_{m+k} : E_{m+k+1} \to E_{m+k}\) makes \(x \mapsto A(x) \circ \mathrm{incl}_{m+k} = Df(\rho' x) \circ \rho\) of class \(C^k\) Chapter1/LevelscontDiffOn_clm_comp_of_isCompactOperator. A map that is differentiable within an sc-domain with a \(C^k\) derivative is \(C^{k+1}\) Mathlib/Analysis/Calculus/ContDiff/DefscontDiffOn_succ_iff_hasFDerivWithinAt_of_uniqueDiffOn.

I.17 Proposition 1.19 and Corollary 1.20: sc^{k+1} from classical smoothness on the levels

Statement. Let \(U\) be an sc-domain and \(f\) \(\mathrm{sc}^0\) on \(U\). If for every \(m \ge 0\) and \(0 \le l \le k\) the map \(f_m \circ (E_{m+l} \to E_m) : U_{m+l} \to F_m\) is \(C^{l+1}\) within \(U_{m+l}\), then \(f\) is \(\mathrm{sc}^{k+1}\) on \(U\) Chapter1/LevelsWeakproposition_1_19_text. This is the text’s statement; its “\(f\) induces a map \(f : U_{m+l} \to F_m\)” is the \(\mathrm{sc}^0\) hypothesis (values of level \(m\) on \(U_m\); the continuity is then the case \(l = 0\)). The proof is the 2010 paper’s (its Proposition 2.4) and lives in Chapter1/LevelsWeak; an earlier, shorter proof under a stronger hypothesis is kept and described at the end of this section.

Why the hypothesis does not induct. The obvious induction would show that \(f\) is \(\mathrm{sc}^1\) and that \(Tf\) satisfies the hypothesis with \(k - 1\). It does not. The map \(Tf : (TU)_{m+l} \to (TF)_m\) has the second component \((x, h) \mapsto Df(x)h\) on \(U_{m+l+1} \times E_{m+l} \to F_m\), and \(Df(x)\) on \(E_{m+l}\) is the derivative of \(f : U_{m+l} \to F_m\) (§I.13), a \(C^{l+1}\) map; so this component is only \(C^l\), one order short of the \(C^{l+1}\) that the hypothesis for \(Tf\) would ask. What survives the induction is a description of the components of the iterated tangent maps: they are built from the derivatives \(d^jf(x)\) of \(f\) itself, evaluated at points and vectors of various levels, and the regularity of \(f\) on the coarser levels supplies the missing order. The 2010 paper’s inductive statement \((\mathrm S_k)\) carries exactly this description. The formal proof organizes it in six steps: (1) the derivatives \(d^jf(x)\) on all level pairs, with their compatibility, form a derivative tower; (2) an elementary map is \(d^jf\) evaluated at sc-operators; (3) it is \(\mathrm{sc}^0\), and \(\mathrm{sc}^1\) with an explicit derivative, by the level criterion of Proposition 1.16; (4) its tangent map is the pair of an elementary map and a sum of elementary maps; (5) by induction on \(s\), every elementary map with \(j + s \le k + 1\) is \(\mathrm{sc}^s\); (6) \(f\) is the elementary map with \(j = 0\).

The derivative tower. A derivative tower of order \(k + 1\) for \(f\) on \(U\) Chapter1/LevelsWeakIsDerivTower consists of base-level maps \(\Phi_i(x)(h_1, \dots, h_i) \in F_0\) (\(x, h_a \in E_0\)) and, for \(x \in U_{m+l}\), continuous \(i\)-linear maps \(\Psi_{i,m,l}(x)\) on \(E_{m+l}\) with values in \(F_m\), given for \(i \le l + 1\) and \(i \le k + 1\), such that: \(\Phi_0 = f\); \(\iota_m \Psi_{i,m,l}(x)(h_1, \dots, h_i) = \Phi_i(\iota_{m+l}x)(\iota_{m+l}h_1, \dots, \iota_{m+l}h_i)\), i.e. all the \(\Psi\) are one map seen on different levels; \(\Psi_{i,m,l}\) is continuous on \(U_{m+l}\); and for \(i \le l\), \(i \le k\) it is differentiable within \(U_{m+l}\) at every point, with derivative \(\xi \mapsto \Psi_{i+1,m,l}(x)(\xi, \cdot)\). The ranges of \(i\) are exactly what “\(f : U_{m+l} \to F_m\) is \(C^{l+1}\)” provides; the compatibility is the text’s use of one symbol \(d^jf(x)\) on all levels. Two values with the same images in \(E_0\) agree, by injectivity of \(\iota_m\) Chapter1/LevelsWeakIsDerivTower.eq_of_toBase.

The tower of a map satisfying the hypothesis. \(\Psi_{i,m,l}\) is Mathlib’s \(i\)-th derivative within \(U_{m+l}\) of \(f_m \circ (E_{m+l} \to E_m)\) Chapter1/LevelsWeaklevelDerivTower Mathlib/Analysis/Calculus/ContDiff/FTaylorSeriesiteratedFDerivWithin, and \(\Phi_i\) is the \(i\)-th derivative of \(f : U_{i-1} \to F_0\) at the lifts of its arguments to \(E_{i-1}\) (arbitrary off the image of \(E_{i-1}\)) Chapter1/LevelsWeakbaseDerivTower. For \(l > k\) the hypothesis is used with order \(k + 1\): \(f : U_{m+l} \to F_m\) is the \(C^{k+1}\) map \(f : U_{m+k} \to F_m\) restricted along the inclusion \(E_{m+l} \to E_{m+k}\), and \(U_{m+l}\) is the preimage of \(U_{m+k}\) Chapter1/LevelsWeakScBanach.inclLE Chapter1/LevelsWeakScBanach.preimage_inclLE_lvlSet; so \(f : U_{m+l} \to F_m\) is \(C^{\min(l,k)+1}\) for all \(m\), \(l\) Chapter1/LevelsWeakcontDiffOn_levels_min. Continuity of \(\Psi_{i,m,l}\) for \(i \le \min(l, k) + 1\) is the continuity of the iterated derivatives of a \(C^{\min(l,k)+1}\) map Mathlib/Analysis/Calculus/ContDiff/DefsContDiffOn.continuousOn_iteratedFDerivWithin; for \(i \le \min(l, k)\) the \(i\)-th derivative is \(C^1\) Mathlib/Analysis/Calculus/ContDiff/CompContDiffWithinAt.iteratedFDerivWithin_right, and its derivative is the \((i+1)\)-st derivative with the new vector in front Mathlib/Analysis/Calculus/ContDiff/FTaylorSeriesiteratedFDerivWithin_succ_apply_left. Both use the uniqueness of derivatives on the level sets of the sc-domain. The compatibility Chapter1/LevelsWeaklevelDerivTower_toBase is proved in three steps, for \(i \le l + 1\) (so that \(i - 1 \le m + l\)): (i) composing on the left with the continuous linear \(\iota_m\) commutes with iterated derivatives within a set Mathlib/Analysis/Calculus/ContDiff/BasicContinuousLinearMap.iteratedFDerivWithin_comp_left; (ii) on \(U_{m+l}\), \(\iota_m \circ f_m \circ (E_{m+l} \to E_m)\) equals \((f : U_{i-1} \to F_0) \circ (E_{m+l} \to E_{i-1})\), since \(f\) is \(\mathrm{sc}^0\) Chapter1/ScSmoothIsSc0.toBase_levelMap, and a derivative within a set depends only on the values on the set Mathlib/Analysis/Calculus/ContDiff/FTaylorSeriesiteratedFDerivWithin_congr; (iii) composing on the right with the continuous linear inclusion \(E_{m+l} \to E_{i-1}\) commutes as well, the preimage of \(U_{i-1}\) being \(U_{m+l}\) Mathlib/Analysis/Calculus/ContDiff/BasicContinuousLinearMap.iteratedFDerivWithin_comp_right. With the lifts in the definition of \(\Phi_i\) Chapter1/LevelsWeakbaseDerivTower_toBase this gives the tower Chapter1/LevelsWeakisDerivTower_of_contDiffOn_levels.

Shifted spaces. \(E^p\) is the sc-Banach space with \((E^p)_l = E_{p+l}\) by definition Chapter1/LevelsWeakScBanach.shiftAdd (the \(p\)-fold iterate of the shift of §I.1 has these levels only up to rewriting \(p + l\)). The identifications \(E \cong E^0\) and \((E^p)^1 \cong E^{p+1}\) are sc-isomorphisms whose level maps are identities transported along \(l = 0 + l\), resp. \(p + (l + 1) = p + 1 + l\) Chapter1/LevelsWeakScBanach.castCLE Chapter1/LevelsWeakScBanach.shiftAddZeroIso Chapter1/LevelsWeakScBanach.shiftAddShiftIso; they are used only through their compatibility with the inclusions into the base level Chapter1/LevelsWeakScBanach.toBase_shiftAddShiftIso_symm. For \(b \le a\) the inclusion \(E_a \to E_b\) is compatible with the \(\iota\)’s Chapter1/LevelsWeakScBanach.toBase_inclLE.

Elementary maps. Elementary data on an sc-Banach space \(X\) Chapter1/LevelsWeakElemData are an sc-operator \(\pi_0 : X \to E^p\) (the base point), \(i\) sc-operators \(\pi_a : X \to E^{n_a}\) (the vectors) and a target shift \(m\). The elementary map is \[g(z) = d^if(\pi_0 z)(\pi_1 z, \dots, \pi_i z) := \Phi_i(\pi_0 z)(\pi_1 z, \dots, \pi_i z),\] lifted to \(F_m = (F^m)_0\) Chapter1/LevelsWeakElemData.map, on the domain \(W = \pi_0^{-1}(U_p)\) Chapter1/LevelsWeakElemData.dom, whose level-\(l\) set is \(\pi_0^{-1}(U_{p+l})\) Chapter1/LevelsWeakElemData.mem_lvlSet_dom. The exposition’s map of type \((p, l; n_1, \dots, n_j)\) on \(U^p \oplus E^{n_1} \oplus \cdots \oplus E^{n_j}\) is the case \(X = E^p \oplus E^{n_1} \oplus \cdots\) with the projections as slots. The conditions are Chapter1/LevelsWeakElemData.Good \[m + i \le p, \qquad m + i \le n_a + 1 \ (1 \le a \le i), \qquad i \le k .\] The second is the text’s \(j + l - 1 \le n_i\). The first is \(j + l \le k + 1\) for the base point \(x \in U_{k+1}\), which the text derives from \(j + l - 1 \le n_i \le k\) (and states separately, as \(l \le k + 1\), only for \(j = 0\) in the exposition). The third bounds the order of derivative that will be used. The text’s upper bound \(n_i \le k\) is not needed.

On level \(l\), the base point and the vectors pushed down to a common level \(q\) (\(q \le p + l\), \(q \le n_a + l\)) are \(\rho_0 = (E_{p+l} \to E_q) \circ \pi_0\) and \(\rho_a = (E_{n_a+l} \to E_q) \circ \pi_a\) Chapter1/LevelsWeakElemData.ρ₀ Chapter1/LevelsWeakElemData.ρ. Seen in \(F_0\), \(g\) at a point of level \(l\) is \(\Phi_i\) at the base-level images of \(\pi_0 z\) and \(\pi_a z\) Chapter1/LevelsWeakElemData.map_toBase, and its level-\(l\) map is \(z \mapsto \Psi_{i,m+l,\lambda}(\rho_0 z)(\rho_1 z, \dots, \rho_i z)\) for any \(\lambda\) with \(i \le \lambda + 1\), \(m + l + \lambda \le p + l\) and \(m + l + \lambda \le n_a + l\) Chapter1/LevelsWeakElemData.levelMap_eq. The first two conditions make \(\lambda = i - 1\) admissible, and \(i \le k\) gives \(i \le k + 1\), so the tower value exists. Hence \(g\) is \(\mathrm{sc}^0\): its values at level-\(l\) points lie in \(F_{m+l}\), and its level-\(l\) map is continuous on \(W_l\) as the evaluation of the continuous \(\Psi_{i,m+l,i-1} \circ \rho_0\) at the continuous \((\rho_1, \dots, \rho_i)\) Chapter1/LevelsWeakElemData.isSc0.

The sc¹ step. For \(z \in W_{l+1}\) the candidate derivative \(Dg(z) : X_l \to F_{m+l}\) is the derivative (3.5) of the exposition Chapter1/LevelsWeakElemData.deriv Chapter1/LevelsWeakElemData.deriv_apply: \[Dg(z)\zeta = \Psi_{i+1,m+l,i}(\rho_0 z)(\rho_0\zeta, \rho_1 z, \dots, \rho_i z) + \sum_{a=1}^i \Psi_{i,m+l,i-1}(\rho_0 z)(\rho_1 z, \dots, \rho_a\zeta, \dots, \rho_i z),\] the first term on the uniform level \(m + l + i\), the sum on \(m + l + i - 1\). The conditions put every argument where it belongs: \(\rho_0 z\) and \(\rho_a z\) (with \(z\) of level \(l + 1\)) in \(E_{m+l+i}\), because \(m + i \le p + 1\) and \(m + i \le n_a + 1\); \(\rho_0\zeta\) (with \(\zeta\) of level \(l\)) in \(E_{m+l+i}\), because \(m + i \le p\); \(\rho_a\zeta\) in \(E_{m+l+i-1}\), because \(m + i - 1 \le n_a\); and \(\Psi_{i+1,m+l,i}\) exists because \(i + 1 \le k + 1\), which is where \(i \le k\) enters. On the base level, \(Dg(z)\zeta\) is \(\Phi_{i+1}(\pi_0 z)(\pi_0\zeta, \pi z) + \sum_a \Phi_i(\pi_0 z)(\pi z \text{ with } \pi_a z := \pi_a\zeta)\) Chapter1/LevelsWeakElemData.deriv_toBase. The level criterion of Proposition 1.16 (§I.14) asks two things.

Differentiability of \(g : W_{l+1} \to F_{m+l}\) with derivative \(Dg(z)\) restricted to \(X_{l+1}\). On \(W_{l+1}\), the level-\(l\) map of \(g\) is \(z' \mapsto \Psi_{i,m+l,i}(\rho_0 z')(\rho_1 z', \dots, \rho_i z')\) with the slots taken at level \(l + 1\) (the formula above with \(\lambda = i\)) Chapter1/LevelsWeakElemData.levelMap_incl_eq. In the tower, \(\Psi_{i,m+l,i}\) is differentiable with derivative \(\Psi_{i+1,m+l,i}\) (\(i \le i\) and \(i \le k\)); the slots are continuous linear; and the evaluation \((A, h) \mapsto A(h_1, \dots, h_i)\) of continuous multilinear maps is differentiable with derivative \((B, \eta) \mapsto B(h) + \sum_a A(h \text{ with } h_a := \eta_a)\) Chapter1/LevelsWeakhasFDerivAt_cmm_eval, proved from Mathlib’s derivative of a multilinear map in its arguments Mathlib/Analysis/Calculus/FDeriv/AnalyticContinuousMultilinearMap.hasFDerivAt and the linearity in \(A\) (the evaluation written as a flipped multilinear map Chapter1/LevelsWeakcmm_eval_eq). The chain rule gives a derivative whose first term is that of \(Dg\) (the base point restricted from level \(l+1\) to level \(l\) is the same vector Chapter1/LevelsWeakElemData.ρ₀_incl) and whose sum terms are values of \(\Psi_{i,m+l,i}\); these equal the \(\Psi_{i,m+l,i-1}\) terms of \(Dg\) because they have the same images in \(E_0\) (the tower’s compatibility) Chapter1/LevelsWeakElemData.hasFDerivWithinAt_level.

Continuity of \((z, \zeta) \mapsto Dg(z)\zeta\) on \(W_{l+1} \times X_l\): \(\Psi_{i+1,m+l,i}\) and \(\Psi_{i,m+l,i-1}\) are continuous on their level sets, and the slots, the insertion of \(\rho_a\zeta\) and the evaluation are continuous Chapter1/LevelsWeakElemData.continuousOn_deriv.

So \(g\) satisfies the level conditions Chapter1/LevelsWeakElemData.isSc1Levels Chapter1/LevelsIsSc1Levels, and when \(W\) is an sc-domain it is \(\mathrm{sc}^1\) with derivative \(Dg\) at level \(0\) Chapter1/LevelsIsSc1Levels.isSc1With Chapter1/LevelsWeakElemData.isSc1With. This is the text’s “\(\Gamma\) is \(\mathrm{sc}^1\)”, with the level criterion in place of the direct check of Definition 1.14 that the exposition carries out.

The tangent map of an elementary map. On \(TX = X^1 \oplus X\) a slot \(\pi : X \to E^n\) gives two slots: \(\pi\) on the first factor, \(TX \to E^{n+1}\) through \((E^n)^1 \cong E^{n+1}\) Chapter1/LevelsWeakScOperator.tangentX, and \(\pi\) on the second factor, \(TX \to E^n\) Chapter1/LevelsWeakScOperator.tangentH. Three kinds of elementary data on \(TX\) arise from \(g\). The first, \(g'\), has all slots on the first factor, with levels \(p + 1\), \(n_a + 1\) and target shift \(m + 1\) Chapter1/LevelsWeakElemData.shiftData: it is \(g\) one level up. The second, \(g_0\), has the base point \(\pi_0\) on the first factor (level \(p + 1\)), \(i + 1\) vectors, namely \(\pi_0\) on the second factor (level \(p\)) followed by the \(\pi_a\) on the first (levels \(n_a + 1\)), and target shift \(m\) Chapter1/LevelsWeakElemData.derivData: it is the term \(d^{i+1}f(x)(\delta x, h)\). The third, \(g_a\) for \(1 \le a \le i\), is like \(g'\) but with \(\pi_a\) moved to the second factor (level \(n_a\)) and target shift \(m\) Chapter1/LevelsWeakElemData.slotData: it is the term \(d^if(x)(h \text{ with } h_a := \delta h_a)\). All satisfy the conditions, which is the text’s “one checks that the new indices satisfy the required inequalities”: for \(g'\), \(m + 1 + i \le p + 1\) and \(m + 1 + i \le n_a + 2\) Chapter1/LevelsWeakElemData.Good.shiftData; for \(g_0\), \(m + i + 1 \le p + 1\) (for the base point and for the new first vector, of level \(p\)) and \(m + i + 1 \le n_a + 2\), and \(i + 1 \le k\), which has to be assumed Chapter1/LevelsWeakElemData.Good.derivData; for \(g_a\), \(m + i \le p + 1\), \(m + i \le n_a + 1\) for the moved slot and \(m + i \le n_b + 2\) for the others Chapter1/LevelsWeakElemData.Good.slotData. The domain of all three (they share the base point \(\pi_0\) on the first factor) is \(TW\) Chapter1/LevelsWeakElemData.tangentSet_dom.

If \(W\) is an sc-domain and \(i + 1 \le k\), the tangent map of \(g\) agrees on \(TW\) with the pair (\(g'\) carried along \((F^m)^1 \cong F^{m+1}\), \(g_0 + \sum_a g_a\)) Chapter1/LevelsWeakElemData.tangentMap_eqOn. Proof: by the uniqueness of the derivative on the sc-domain \(W\), the tangent map is \((g\) on level \(1\), \(Dg)\) Chapter1/ScSmoothIsSc1.tangentMap_eqOn; the first components agree in \(F_0\), both being \(\Phi_i\) at the base-level images of the level-\(1\) slots Chapter1/LevelsWeakElemData.map_toBase Chapter1/LevelsWeakScBanach.toBase_shiftAddShiftIso_symm; the second components agree in \(F_0\) term by term, by the base-level formula for \(Dg\) Chapter1/LevelsWeakElemData.deriv_toBase.

Sums. The constant map \(0\) is \(\mathrm{sc}^k\), being the zero sc-operator Chapter1/LevelsWeakScOperator.zeroOp Chapter1/LevelsWeakIsSck.zero. If \(g_1\), \(g_2\) are \(\mathrm{sc}^k\) on an sc-domain, \(g_1 + g_2\) is the addition \(Y \oplus Y \to Y\) Chapter1/LevelsWeakScOperator.addOp, an sc-operator and hence sc-smooth Chapter2/TangentBundleScOperator.isScSmooth, composed with the pairing \((g_1, g_2)\), which is \(\mathrm{sc}^k\) Chapter2/StrongBundleIsSck.scPair; so it is \(\mathrm{sc}^k\) by the chain rule (§I.12, Chapter1/ChainRuleIsSck.comp) Chapter1/LevelsWeakIsSck.add. Finite sums follow by induction over the index set Chapter1/LevelsWeakIsSck.sum. Scalar multiples are not needed: the text’s “linear combinations” are sums.

The induction \((\mathrm S_k)\). Claim: for every \(s\), every sc-Banach space \(X\) and all elementary data on \(X\) satisfying the conditions, with sc-domain \(W\) and \(i + s \le k + 1\), the elementary map is \(\mathrm{sc}^s\) on \(W\) Chapter1/LevelsWeakElemData.isSck. The induction is on \(s\), for all \(X\), \(i\) and data at once. For \(s = 0\) this is the \(\mathrm{sc}^0\) statement. For \(s + 1\): \(g\) is \(\mathrm{sc}^1\) by the sc¹ step, and it remains to show that its tangent map is \(\mathrm{sc}^s\). If \(s = 0\), the tangent map of an \(\mathrm{sc}^1\) map is \(\mathrm{sc}^0\) Chapter1/ScSmoothIsSc1.tangentMap_isSc0. If \(s \ge 1\), then \(i + 1 \le k\) (from \(i + s + 1 \le k + 1\)), so the tangent map agrees on \(TW\) with (\(g'\) carried along \((F^m)^1 \cong F^{m+1}\), \(g_0 + \sum_a g_a\)); \(TW\) is an sc-domain Chapter1/ScSmoothIsScDomain.tangentSet, equal to the domain of the three new data Chapter1/LevelsWeakIsScDomain.of_eq Chapter1/LevelsWeakIsSck.of_eq_set, and \(\mathrm{sc}^s\) passes to maps that agree on the domain Chapter1/ChainRuleIsSck.congr. The pair is \(\mathrm{sc}^s\) if its two components are Chapter2/StrongBundleIsSck.scPair. Now \(g'\) and the \(g_a\) have \(i\) vectors and \(i + s \le k + 1\), and \(g_0\) has \(i + 1\) vectors and \((i + 1) + s \le k + 1\), so all are \(\mathrm{sc}^s\) by the induction hypothesis (applied on \(X' = TX\)); \(g'\) composed with the sc-isomorphism \((F^m)^1 \cong F^{m+1}\), an sc-operator Chapter1/ScBanachScIso.toScOperator, is \(\mathrm{sc}^s\) by the chain rule; and \(g_0 + \sum_a g_a\) by the sum rule.

This is the text’s induction, run on \(s\) over all elementary maps rather than on the description of \(T^{k+1}f\). The 2010 paper proves that every term of \(\pi \circ T^{k+1}f\) is \(\mathrm{sc}^1\), hence \(T^{k+1}f\) is, and that the terms of \(T^{k+2}f\) are again elementary with admissible indices; the formal proof shows that an elementary map is \(\mathrm{sc}^{s+1}\) because its tangent map is made of elementary maps that are \(\mathrm{sc}^s\). The computations are the same — the derivative (3.5), the three kinds of new terms and their indices — and the formal version never names \(T^{k+1}f\) or its \(2^{k+1}\) components.

Proposition 1.19. \(f\) is the elementary map on \(X = E\) with no vectors, \(p = m = 0\) and \(\pi_0 : E \cong E^0\) Chapter1/LevelsWeakElemData.base; its domain is \(U\) Chapter1/LevelsWeakElemData.base_dom and the conditions hold trivially Chapter1/LevelsWeakElemData.base_good. With the tower of \(f\) (step 1) and \(s = k + 1\), \(0 + (k + 1) \le k + 1\), this elementary map is \(\mathrm{sc}^{k+1}\); composed with the sc-isomorphism \(F^0 \cong F\) it agrees with \(f\) on \(U\), since \(\Phi_0 = f\); so \(f\) is \(\mathrm{sc}^{k+1}\) Chapter1/LevelsWeakproposition_1_19_text. If the hypothesis holds for every \(l\), then \(f\) is \(\mathrm{sc}^{k+1}\) for every \(k\), i.e. sc-smooth Chapter1/LevelsWeakIsScSmooth.of_contDiffOn_levels_text.

Corollary 1.20. For a finite-dimensional target \(V\) with its constant structure, the level maps of \(f : E_0 \to V\) are \(f \circ \iota_m\) Chapter1/ScSmoothlevelMap_eq_of_toBase_eq Chapter1/ScBanachScBanach.const_toBase. Suppose \(f \circ \iota_l\) is \(C^{l+1}\) within \(U_l\) for \(0 \le l \le k\). Then \(f\) is \(\mathrm{sc}^0\) with no further hypothesis: \(f\) is continuous on \(U = U_0\) (the case \(l = 0\)), so each \(f \circ \iota_m\) is continuous on \(U_m\). And the hypothesis of Proposition 1.19 holds: \(f_m \circ (E_{m+l} \to E_m) = (f \circ \iota_l) \circ (E_{m+l} \to E_l)\), a \(C^{l+1}\) map composed with a continuous linear one, on \(U_{m+l}\), the preimage of \(U_l\) Chapter1/LevelsWeakScBanach.preimage_inclLE_lvlSet. So \(f\) is \(\mathrm{sc}^{k+1}\) Chapter1/LevelsWeakcorollary_1_20_text. If \(f \circ \iota_l\) is \(C^{l+1}\) within \(U_l\) for every \(l\), then \(f\) is sc-smooth (for \(k = 0\) the corollary gives \(\mathrm{sc}^1\), hence \(\mathrm{sc}^0\)) Chapter1/LevelsWeakIsScSmooth.of_contDiffOn_levels_finiteDimensional_text; and if \(f\) is \(C^\infty\) on \(U\), it is sc-smooth Chapter1/LevelsIsScSmooth.of_contDiffOn_finiteDimensional (proved with the stronger version below, since \(C^\infty\) on \(U\) restricts to \(C^{k+1}\) on every \(U_m\)). The two sc-smooth statements are the exposition’s; the second is what the theory uses (bump functions, Chapter 5).

The earlier version, under a stronger hypothesis. Chapter1/Levels proves Proposition 1.19 under the hypothesis that every level map \(f_m : U_m \to F_m\) is \(C^{k+1}\) within \(U_m\) Chapter1/Levelsproposition_1_19. For \(k \ge 1\) this asks more than the text (\(C^{k+1}\) instead of \(C^1\) on \(U_m \to F_m\) itself), and in exchange the induction needs no \((\mathrm S_k)\); for \(k = 0\) the hypotheses coincide.

\(k = 0\). Suppose every \(f_m\) is \(C^1\) within \(U_m\). Put \(Df(x) :=\) the derivative of \(f = f_0\) within \(U\) at \(\iota_1 x\), for \(x \in E_1\) Mathlib/Analysis/Calculus/FDeriv/DefsfderivWithin. Condition (2) holds because \(f \circ \iota_1\) is the restriction of the differentiable \(f\) along the continuous linear \(\iota_1\). For condition (3) at level \(m\): the derivative \(d f_m(x)\) of \(f_m\) within \(U_m\) at \(x \in U_m\) is compatible with \(Df\), \(\iota_m \circ df_m(x) = Df(\iota_m x) \circ \iota_m\), because \(\iota_m \circ f_m = f \circ \iota_m\) on \(U_m\) and derivatives within \(U_m\) are unique Mathlib/Analysis/Calculus/FDeriv/BasicUniqueDiffWithinAt.eq; so the level-\(m\) tangent map is \((x, h) \mapsto (f_{m+1}(x), df_m(\mathrm{incl}_m x)h)\), continuous on \(U_{m+1} \times E_m\) because \(f_m\) is \(C^1\) (its derivative is continuous into \(\mathcal L(E_m, F_m)\), and evaluation is continuous) Chapter1/Propertiesproposition_1_19_zero. This is the text’s proof of \((\mathrm S_0)\).

\(k + 1\) from \(k\). Suppose every \(f_m\) is \(C^{k+2}\). Then \(f\) is \(\mathrm{sc}^1\) by the case \(k = 0\), with the derivative \(Df\) above, and we must show \(Tf\) is \(\mathrm{sc}^{k+1}\) on \(TU\). By the induction hypothesis (for the sc-domain \(TU\) and the \(\mathrm{sc}^0\) map \(Tf\)) it suffices that the level maps of \(Tf\) are \(C^{k+1}\). The level-\(m\) map of \(Tf\) is \((x, h) \mapsto (f_{m+1}(x), Df(x)h)\) with the level operator (§I.13), and the level operator at \(x \in U_{m+1}\) is the derivative of \(f_m\) at \(\mathrm{incl}_m x\) (Lemma 3.H, Chapter1/LevelsIsSc1With.levelDeriv_eq). So the level-\(m\) map of \(Tf\) is \((x, h) \mapsto (f_{m+1}(x), df_m(\mathrm{incl}_m x)h)\) on \(U_{m+1} \times E_m\), whose components are \(C^{k+1}\): the first as \(f_{m+1}\) is, the second as the derivative of a \(C^{k+2}\) map is \(C^{k+1}\) and evaluation is bilinear Chapter1/Levelsproposition_1_19. This is where the stronger hypothesis is used, and where the text’s hypothesis would fail (see “Why the hypothesis does not induct”).

Sc-smooth, and the corollary. If \(f\) maps each \(U_m\) into \(F_m\) and every \(f_m\) is \(C^\infty\), then \(f\) is sc-smooth Chapter1/LevelsIsScSmooth.of_contDiffOn_levels. For a finite-dimensional target: \(C^1\) on every \(U_m\) gives \(\mathrm{sc}^1\) Chapter1/Propertiescorollary_1_20_zero, \(C^{k+1}\) on every \(U_m\) gives \(\mathrm{sc}^{k+1}\) Chapter1/Levelscorollary_1_20, in particular \(C^{k+1}\) on \(U = U_0\) does, since restricting along \(\iota_m\) preserves \(C^{k+1}\) Chapter1/Levelscorollary_1_20_base.

I.18 Definition 1.23 and Lemma 1.24: the degeneracy index

Definitions. For \(p = (a, w) \in \mathbb R^n \oplus W\) let \(\#(p)\) be the number of indices \(i\) with \(a_i = 0\) Chapter1/DegeneracyquadrantDeg. For an sc-isomorphism \(T : E \to \mathbb R^n \oplus W\) presenting a partial quadrant \(C\) and \(x \in E_0\), let \(d_T(x) := \#(T_0 x)\) Chapter1/DegeneracydegIndexWith. The degeneracy index \(d_C(x)\) is \(d_T(x)\) for a presentation \(T\) of \(C\) chosen once and for all, and \(0\) if \(C\) is not a partial quadrant Chapter1/DegeneracydegIndex; by Lemma 1.24 below it equals \(d_T(x)\) for every presentation and every \(x \in C\) Chapter1/DegeneracydegIndex_eq, and on the quadrant itself it is \(\#\) Chapter1/DegeneracydegIndex_quadrant. The text’s interior points, boundary points and corners are the points with \(d_C = 0\), \(1\), \(\ge 2\); Chapter 2 makes the boundary a definition.

Lemma 1.24, core form. Let \(S : \mathbb R^n \times W_0 \to \mathbb R^{n'} \times W'_0\) be a continuous linear equivalence with \(q \in Q \iff Sq \in Q'\) for the two quadrants. Then \(\#(p) = \#(Sp)\) for every \(p \in Q\) Chapter1/DegeneracyquadrantDeg_eq_of_equiv. Only level \(0\) and linear algebra are used; the sc-structure plays no role. Proof. For \(p \in Q\) let \(E_p := \{(b, v) : b_i = 0 \text{ whenever } p_i = 0\}\), the kernel of the surjection \((b, v) \mapsto (b_i)_{i \in I(p)}\) Chapter1/DegeneracycoordMap Chapter1/DegeneracycoordMap_surjective Chapter1/Degeneracymem_ker_coordMap, so that \(\dim(V/E_p) = \#(p)\) Chapter1/Degeneracyfinrank_quotient_ker_coordMap: this makes the text’s “codimension of \(E_x\)” precise. For \(u \in E_p\), \(p + tu \in Q\) for all \(t\) near \(0\): coordinate by coordinate, if \(p_i = 0\) then \(u_i = 0\) and the coordinate stays \(0\); if \(p_i > 0\) it stays positive for small \(t\) by continuity Chapter1/Degeneracyeventually_add_smul_mem_quadrant. Hence \(Sp + tSu \in Q'\) for \(t\) near \(0\), so for each \(i\) with \((Sp)_i = 0\) we have \(0 \le t(Su)_i\) for all \(t\) near \(0\), of both signs, which forces \((Su)_i = 0\) Chapter1/Degeneracyeq_zero_of_eventually_nonneg_mul; so \(S(E_p) \subseteq E'_{Sp}\) Chapter1/Degeneracymap_ker_coordMap_le. The same argument for \(S^{-1}\) gives the reverse inclusion (the text concludes equality from one inclusion “since \(S\) is an isomorphism”, which for infinite-dimensional \(W\) needs this second step), so \(S(E_p) = E'_{Sp}\) and \(S\) induces a linear isomorphism \(V/E_p \cong V'/E'_{Sp}\); comparing dimensions, \(\#(p) = \#(Sp)\).

Lemma 1.24. If \(T\) and \(T'\) both present \(C\), then \(S := T'_0 \circ T_0^{-1}\) carries the quadrant onto the quadrant (both are the image of \(C\)), and the core form at \(p = T_0 x\) gives \(d_T(x) = d_{T'}(x)\) for \(x \in C\) Chapter1/Degeneracylemma_1_24. The text proves first that \(k = k'\); here this is a consequence: \(T_0^{-1}(0) \in C\) and \(\#(0) = n\) in \(\mathbb R^n \oplus W\) Chapter1/DegeneracyquadrantDeg_zero, so the lemma at this point gives \(n = n'\) Chapter1/Degeneracylemma_1_24_dim.

I.19 Theorem 1.25: boundary recognition

Statement. Let \(U \subseteq C \subseteq E\) and \(U' \subseteq C' \subseteq E'\) be relatively open subsets of partial quadrants, \(f\) \(\mathrm{sc}^1\) on \(U\) with \(f(U) \subseteq U'\), \(g\) \(\mathrm{sc}^1\) on \(U'\) with \(g(U') \subseteq U\), \(g \circ f = \mathrm{id}\) on \(U\) and \(f \circ g = \mathrm{id}\) on \(U'\). Then \(d_C(x) = d_{C'}(f(x))\) for every \(x \in U\) Chapter2/DegeneracyIndextheorem_1_25. The text’s “germ of a local sc-diffeomorphism” is undefined in Chapter 1 and is read this way, with \(U\), \(U'\) as small as one likes; the text has sc-smooth where \(\mathrm{sc}^1\) suffices, so the formal statement is stronger. The text gives no proof, referring to “[20], Theorem 1.19”; the formal proof is the argument of §2.3 (Lemma 2.29, Theorem 2.31, Corollary 2.32) specialized to the identity retraction, and lives in the Chapter 2 file because it uses the retraction vocabulary. Smooth points are not needed; level-\(1\) points suffice.

The subspaces \(E_x\). For a presentation \(T\) of \(C\) and \(x \in E_0\), let \(E_x := \{v \in E_0 : (T_0 v)_i = 0 \text{ whenever } (T_0 x)_i = 0\}\), the kernel of a continuous linear map to a finite-dimensional space Chapter2/DegeneracyIndexminimalSubspaceWith; its codimension is \(d_T(x)\) Chapter2/DegeneracyIndexfinrank_quotient_minimalSubspaceWith. Two facts about the index: it is upper semicontinuous, \(d_T(y) \le d_T(x)\) for \(y\) near \(x\) (a nonzero coordinate stays nonzero) Chapter2/DegeneracyIndexeventually_degIndexWith_le; and every \(x \in C\) is the limit of points of \(C\) on level \(1\) with the same index, namely \(T_0^{-1}(a, w_n)\) with \(w_n \in W_1\) converging to \(w\) in \(W_0\), which exist by density Chapter2/DegeneracyIndexexists_tendsto_lvl1_degIndexWith. These are the exposition’s Lemma 5.A, with level \(1\) in place of smooth.

The sign argument. Let \(f\) be \(\mathrm{sc}^1\) on \(U \subseteq C\) with values in \(C'\), \(x \in U_1\), and \(v \in E_1\) with \(\iota_1 v \in E_x\). Then \(x + tv \in U_1\) for \(t\) near \(0\) (the quadrant coordinates as in §I.18, and the openness of \(U_1\)) Chapter2/DegeneracyIndexeventually_add_smul_mem_lvlSet, so \(f(\iota(x + tv)) \in C'\) and, for each \(j\) with \((T'_0 f(x))_j = 0\), the function \(t \mapsto (T'_0 f(\iota(x + tv)))_j\) is \(\ge 0\) with a zero at \(t = 0\): a local minimum, so its derivative at \(0\), which is \((T'_0 Df(x)\iota_1 v)_j\) by condition (2), vanishes Mathlib/Analysis/Calculus/LocalExtr/BasicIsLocalMin.hasDerivAt_eq_zero Chapter2/DegeneracyIndexIsSc1With.deriv_mem_minimalSubspace_of_lvl1. So \(Df(x)\) maps \(E_x \cap \iota_1(E_1)\) into \(E'_{f(x)}\). Since \(f\) is differentiable only along \(E_1\), the density of \(E_x \cap \iota_1(E_1)\) in \(E_x\) is needed to conclude \(Df(x)(E_x) \subseteq E'_{f(x)}\); it holds because \(E_x\) is the kernel of a continuous linear map to a finite-dimensional space and \(\iota_1(E_1)\) is dense Chapter2/DegeneracyIndexScBanach.subset_closure_ker_inter_range_toBase Chapter2/DegeneracyIndexIsSc1With.mapsTo_minimalSubspace. The text asserts the corresponding density (“the closure of \((T^R_xO)_\infty\) is \(T^R_xO\)”) without proof.

One inequality at level-\(1\) points. With \(g\) the inverse, the chain rule gives \(Dg(f_1(x)) \circ Df(x) = \mathrm{id}\) on \(E_0\) at \(x \in U_1\) Chapter2/DegeneracyIndexscDeriv_comp_eq_self, so \(Df(x)\) is injective and \(E_x \cong Df(x)(E_x) \le E'_{f(x)}\) sits inside a subspace of codimension \(d_{C'}(f(x))\), while \(Dg(f_1(x))\) maps \(E'_{f(x)}\) into \(E_x\) by the sign argument for \(g\); comparing codimensions, \(d_C(x) \le d_{C'}(f(x))\) Chapter2/DegeneracyIndexdegIndexWith_le_of_germ. Applying this to \(g\) at \(f_1(x)\) gives the reverse inequality, so \(d_C(x) = d_{C'}(f(x))\) for \(x \in U_1\) Chapter2/DegeneracyIndextheorem_1_25_lvl1.

General points. For \(x \in U\), approximate \(x\) by level-\(1\) points \(x_n \in U\) of \(C\) with \(d_C(x_n) = d_C(x)\); then \(f(x_n) \to f(x)\) (continuity of \(f\) on \(U\)), so \(d_{C'}(f(x_n)) \le d_{C'}(f(x))\) eventually by semicontinuity, and \(d_{C'}(f(x_n)) = d_C(x_n) = d_C(x)\) by the level-\(1\) case; hence \(d_C(x) \le d_{C'}(f(x))\). The symmetric argument for \(g\) at \(f(x)\) gives equality Chapter2/DegeneracyIndextheorem_1_25.

I.20 What the formalization taught us

  • The chain rule needs one integral less than the text writes, and one hypothesis more than it states. The term \(Dg(f(x))[f(x+h) - f(x) - Df(x)h]\) is \(o(|h|_1)\) because \(Dg(f(x))\) is bounded, with no integral Chapter1/ChainRuleIsSc1With.hasFDerivWithinAt_comp; the segment from \(f(x)\) to \(f(x+h)\) lies in \(V_1\) only because \(V_1\) is open-in-convex and \(f : U_1 \to F_1\) is continuous, which the text does not say. The whole proof uses, of the quadrant structure of \(U\), only the uniqueness of derivatives, and that only for \(T(g \circ f) = Tg \circ Tf\) Chapter1/ChainRuletheorem_1_21'.
  • “The” derivative \(Df(x)\) is a theorem, not a notation. It is unique because \(E_1\) is dense in \(E_0\) and \(U_1\) has unique differentiability Chapter1/ScSmoothIsSc1With.eq_of_uniqueDiffWithinAt; without it the tangent map, hence \(\mathrm{sc}^2\), is undefined. The same density argument shows that the extensions \(Df(x) : E_{m-1} \to F_{m-1}\) of Proposition 1.16, written with one symbol in the text, are restrictions of one operator Chapter1/LevelsIsSc1Levels.toBase_apply, which is what makes the “clear” direction of that proposition work.
  • One compactness argument carries §1.2. The compact-open lemma Chapter1/LevelscontDiffOn_clm_comp_of_isCompactOperator turns joint continuity (or \(C^k\)-ness) of \((x, h) \mapsto Df(x)h\) into norm continuity (or \(C^k\)-ness) of \(x \mapsto Df(x)|_{E_{m+1}}\); Propositions 1.16, 1.17 and 1.18 are this lemma plus bookkeeping of levels.
  • Proposition 1.19 does not induct on its own hypothesis. If \(f\) satisfies it with \(k\), then \(Tf\) in general does not satisfy it with \(k - 1\): the second component \((x, h) \mapsto Df(x)h : U_{m+l+1} \times E_{m+l} \to F_m\) is one order short. The stronger hypothesis “\(C^{k+1}\) on every level” makes the induction two lines Chapter1/Levelsproposition_1_19; the text’s needs the 2010 paper’s \((\mathrm S_k)\), which remembers \(f\) through the elementary maps \(d^jf\) on mixed levels Chapter1/LevelsWeakElemData.isSck Chapter1/LevelsWeakproposition_1_19_text. Written out, \((\mathrm S_k)\) needs three things the text leaves implicit: one \(d^jf(x)\) on all levels Chapter1/LevelsWeakisDerivTower_of_contDiffOn_levels, the base-point condition \(j + l \le k + 1\) in place of the bound \(n_i \le k\) (which is not needed) Chapter1/LevelsWeakElemData.Good, and the derivative of the multilinear evaluation Chapter1/LevelsWeakhasFDerivAt_cmm_eval.
  • Regularizing is a bootstrap. In §1.4.1 the step “\(e \in E_m\) by Proposition 1.9” needs \(m\) applications, since \(Se\) is only one level above \(e\) Chapter1/ScFredholmScPlus.regularizing_add.
  • The index is an addition, and an easy one once additivity is there. Neither Proposition 1.10 nor the remark after Definition 1.8 mentions the index of \(T + S\) or of the level operators; with the additivity of the index Chapter1/FredholmIndexlinIndex_comp and a quasi-inverse, the index is locally constant along \(u + tk\), hence invariant Chapter1/FredholmIndexfredholmIndex_add_isCompactOperator, and the sc-statements follow on every level Chapter1/FredholmIndexproposition_1_10_index_lvl.
  • The text’s quick remarks are all true, and some need real arguments. “Precisely one sc-structure” in finite dimensions Chapter1/ExpositionLemmasScBanach.isoConstOfFiniteDimensional; “\((E/A)_\infty\) consists of the classes of \(E_\infty\)”, a Mittag-Leffler series Chapter1/ExpositionLemmasScBanach.exists_smooth_mem_coset; “it is a sc-projection” Chapter1/ExpositionLemmasScBanach.isScSplitting_iff_exists_scProj; “sc¹ is \(C^1\) in finite dimensions”, which at the boundary of a quadrant means derivatives within \(U\) Chapter1/ExpositionLemmasisSc1_iff_fderivWithin_const.
  • Mathlib had Fredholm operators but not Riesz–Schauder. The theorem that \(1 + \text{compact}\) is Fredholm, and the stability under compact perturbations, had to be proved Chapter1/FredholmPerturbationisFredholm_one_add Chapter1/FredholmPerturbationisFredholm_add_isCompactOperator; the finite codimension of the range comes from a chain of closed subspaces and Riesz’s lemma Chapter1/FredholmPerturbationcoFG_range_one_add.
  • The degeneracy index knows nothing of the sc-structure. Lemma 1.24 holds for any linear equivalence of the base levels carrying one quadrant onto the other Chapter1/DegeneracyquadrantDeg_eq_of_equiv, and \(k = k'\) is its value at the origin Chapter1/Degeneracylemma_1_24_dim. Boundary recognition needs only \(\mathrm{sc}^1\) and only level-\(1\) points, not smooth ones Chapter2/DegeneracyIndextheorem_1_25.
Part II. Differential geometry based on retracts (HWZ Chapter 2, §§2.1–2.6) →

Part II. Differential geometry based on retracts (HWZ Chapter 2, §§2.1–2.6)

Chapter 2 builds a differential geometry whose local models are not open sets of Banach spaces but images of sc-smooth retractions, sets whose “dimension” may jump. The formal proof establishes the chapter in its order: retractions and retracts and the independence of their tangent from the retraction (§§II.2–II.4), M-polyfolds with their filtration, metrizability and tangent bundle (§§II.5–II.9), sub-M-polyfolds (§II.10), the degeneracy index with the boundary recognition argument (§§II.11–II.13), tame retracts and the faces of tame M-polyfolds (§§II.14–II.16), products and fibred products (§II.17), and strong bundles with their pull-backs (§§II.18–II.20). What is not formalized is the classical Proposition 2.2 (motivation only), Lemma 2.29 in its formulation by sc-smooth paths (its content, the sign arguments, is formalized and used instead), the second statement of Theorem 2.31 in general (for tame retracts its conclusion, Proposition 2.36’s partial quadrant, is proved directly), the openness of \(p : TX \to X_1\), and the categories \(\mathcal R\), \(\mathcal{BR}\), \(\mathcal{SBR}\).

Three choices shape the formal route. First, a retraction is a total map \(r : E_0 \to E_0\) with an explicit domain \(U\), and the tangent \(TO\) of a retract is described as the fixed-point set of \(Tr\) in \(TU\) (§II.2); this description, which the text’s proofs use without stating it, makes Propositions 2.4 and 2.6 one-line consequences of the chain rule. Second, an M-polyfold is a space with one atlas, and every notion is defined through the maximal atlas of all charts compatible with it (§II.5); this needs the fact, not in the text, that compatibility is a local property, proved from the chain rule and the locality of sc-smoothness (§II.1). Third, where the text computes in the model \(C = [0, \infty)^k \oplus W\), the formal statements carry a presentation \(T : E \cong \mathbb R^n \oplus W\) of the partial quadrant and its coordinate functionals \(\lambda_i = (T\,\cdot)_i\); the subspaces \(E_x\) and cones \(C_x\) are defined through \(T\), and are shown not to depend on it (§II.14).

Six proofs take a different road from the text’s (or the exposition’s). Theorem 2.16 (metrizability of the levels) is proved without Lemma 2.56 and Proposition 2.57, which need a regularity of \(X_m\) the text does not check: a partition of unity of \(X\) pulled back to \(X_m\) gives an explicit metric, and the same argument proves Smirnov’s theorem, which Mathlib lacks (§II.7). Proposition 2.30 is proved from the sign arguments at points on level \(1\), not from Lemma 2.29 at smooth points (§II.13). Theorem 2.31 is proved for every chart of every M-polyfold by a direct isomorphism of quotients, without reducing to a chart that realizes the index (§II.13). Proposition 2.35 uses only the second condition of tameness (§II.14). Proposition 2.36’s partial quadrant is proved for tame retracts without the equality case of Theorem 2.31, the smooth vectors of its proof being written down explicitly (§II.14). The second sentence of Proposition 2.44 is proved by removing all coordinates of \(\sigma\) at once rather than by the exposition’s induction on \(\#\sigma\) (§II.16).

Map.

  • Chapter2/Retracts: restriction and locality of sc^k maps; retractions, retracts, Proposition 2.4, Definitions 2.5, 2.7, Propositions 2.6, 2.10, Theorem 2.8; local models.
  • Chapter2/TangentBundle: the tangent of a retract as a retract, the tangent functor, locality of \(Tf\); the tangent bundle \(TX\), Proposition 2.19 (1)–(2), \(TX\) as an M-polyfold.
  • Chapter2/MPolyfold: charts, atlases, M-polyfolds, Definition 2.14, the levels \(X_m\), Lemma 2.15, sub-M-polyfolds (Definition 2.20), a retract as an M-polyfold.
  • Chapter2/LevelPolyfold: \(X^1\) as an M-polyfold; the locality of Definition 2.14.
  • Chapter2/Metrizable: Smirnov’s theorem, Theorem 2.16, Proposition 2.19 (3), Proposition 2.21 (3)–(4).
  • Chapter2/TangentMap: the tangent map \(Tf : TX \to TY\) and the chain rule.
  • Chapter2/SubMPolyfold: Proposition 2.21 (1)–(2), Lemma 2.26.
  • Chapter2/DegeneracyIndex: \(E_x\), the two-sided sign argument, the core of Theorem 2.31, Theorem 1.25, Definition 2.22, Lemma 2.23, Proposition 2.24, Corollary 2.32.
  • Chapter2/Boundary: the boundary, the one-sided sign argument, Proposition 2.30, Theorem 2.31.
  • Chapter2/Tame: the definitions of §2.4 and of §2.5’s local objects.
  • Chapter2/TameRetracts: Propositions 2.35, 2.36, the local geometry of faces, Lemma 2.40, Corollary 2.41, Propositions 2.42, 2.43 (the retraction onto a face).
  • Chapter2/TameFaces: independence of the presentation; Proposition 2.43 (faces are tame), Proposition 2.44 (first sentence), Theorem 2.45.
  • Chapter2/PartialCone: Proposition 2.36, \(T^R_xO\) an sc-subspace and \(C_xO\) a partial quadrant.
  • Chapter2/CornerGerms: Proposition 2.44 (second sentence), the corners \(f_\sigma\).
  • Chapter2/FibredProduct: products of M-polyfolds (the exposition’s Lemma 4.D), Proposition 2.46.
  • Chapter2/StrongBundle, Chapter2/StrongBundlePullback: §2.5.
  • Chapter2/StrongBundleOne: the M-polyfold \(Y[1]\), \(P[1]\), the chart independence of \(Y_{m,k}\), sc⁺-sections into \(Y[1]\).

II.1 Restriction and locality of sc^k maps

The text restricts sc-smooth maps to smaller sets (“\(r : U \to U \cap U'\) is sc-smooth”) and glues local sc-smoothness without comment. Both need an argument, because the tangent map of an \(\mathrm{sc}^1\) map is built from a chosen derivative family (Part I, §I.11), and a chosen derivative on \(U\) and one on \(U' \subseteq U\) need not be the same objects.

Restriction. If \(f\) is \(\mathrm{sc}^1\) on \(U\) with derivative family \(D\) and \(U' \subseteq U\), the same \(D\) works on \(U'\) Chapter2/RetractsIsSc1With.of_subset Chapter2/RetractsIsSc1.of_subset. When \(U'\) is an sc-domain (unique differentiability on every level, Part I, §I.10), derivatives at points of \(U'_1\) are unique, so the tangent maps built on \(U'\) and on \(U\) agree on \(TU'\) Chapter2/RetractsIsSc1.tangentMap_eqOn_of_subset. By induction on \(k\), using that \(TU'\) is again an sc-domain and that the tangent maps agree there, an \(\mathrm{sc}^k\) map restricts to \(\mathrm{sc}^k\) on every smaller sc-domain Chapter2/RetractsIsSck.of_subset, and so does an sc-smooth map Chapter2/RetractsIsScSmooth.of_subset; sc-smoothness depends only on the values on \(U\) Chapter2/RetractsIsScSmooth.congr. Relatively open subsets of quadrants, and their intersections with open sets, are sc-domains Chapter2/RetractsIsRelOpenInQuadrant.inter_isOpen Chapter2/RetractsIsScDomain.inter_isOpen, and \(T(U \cap W) = TU \cap (W_1 \times E_0)\) Chapter2/RetractsScBanach.tangentSet_inter_isOpen.

Locality. \(\mathrm{sc}^0\) is local: continuity on each level is a local property Chapter2/RetractsIsSc0.of_locally. For \(\mathrm{sc}^1\), suppose every \(x \in U\) has an open \(W_x \ni x\) with \(f\) \(\mathrm{sc}^1\) on \(U \cap W_x\). Two such local structures give the same derivative at a common point, by uniqueness on the sc-domain Chapter2/RetractsIsSc1With.eq_of_eq_near. Glue: at a point \(x \in U_1\) take the derivative of the structure on \(U \cap W_{\iota_1 x}\). This family \(D\) agrees near every point with a local derivative family; the three conditions of Definition 1.14 (the \(\mathrm{sc}^0\) property, differentiability on \(U_1\), and the \(\mathrm{sc}^0\) property of the tangent map on \(TU\)) are local and hold Chapter2/RetractsIsSc1.of_locally. The induction on \(k\) applies the same argument to the tangent maps on \(TU\) Chapter2/RetractsIsSck.of_locally, and gives the sc-smooth case Chapter2/RetractsIsScSmooth.of_locally. The identity is \(\mathrm{sc}^1\) with derivative the identity Chapter2/RetractsisSc1With_id, its tangent map is the identity on \(TU\) Chapter2/RetractstangentMap_id_eqOn, and it is sc-smooth on every sc-domain Chapter2/RetractsisSck_id Chapter2/RetractsisScSmooth_id.

II.2 Retractions, retracts and their tangent (Definitions 2.1, 2.3, 2.5; Proposition 2.4)

Definition 2.1. An sc-smooth retraction on a partial quadrant \(C \subseteq E_0\) is a set \(U\) relatively open in \(C\) and a map \(r : E_0 \to E_0\) with \(r(U) \subseteq U\), \(r\) sc-smooth on \(U\) and \(r(r(x)) = r(x)\) for \(x \in U\) Chapter2/RetractsScRetraction. Since \(U\) is relatively open, it is an sc-domain and \(r\) is \(\mathrm{sc}^1\) Chapter2/RetractsScRetraction.isScDomain Chapter2/RetractsScRetraction.isSc1. The retract is \(O = r(U)\) Chapter2/RetractsScRetraction.retract. It is contained in \(U\) and is exactly the fixed-point set of \(r\) in \(U\): if \(x = r(y)\) then \(r(x) = r(r(y)) = x\) Chapter2/RetractsScRetraction.retract_subset Chapter2/RetractsScRetraction.apply_eq_self_of_mem_retract Chapter2/RetractsScRetraction.mem_retract_iff. On level \(1\), \(r_1\) fixes the points of \(O_1\) Chapter2/RetractsScRetraction.levelMap_one_eq_self, and \(O_m \subseteq U_m\) Chapter2/RetractsScRetraction.lvlSet_retract_subset.

Definition 2.3. \((O, C, E)\) is an sc-smooth retract if \(O\) is the retract of some sc-smooth retraction on \(C\) Chapter2/RetractsIsScRetract Chapter2/RetractsScRetraction.isScRetract. Every relatively open \(U \subseteq C\) is one, with \(r = \mathrm{id}\) Chapter2/RetractsScRetraction.id Chapter2/RetractsIsRelOpenInQuadrant.isScRetract. A local model is a triple \((E, C, O)\) with \(C\) a partial quadrant and \(O\) a retract in \(C\) Chapter2/RetractsLocalModel; these are the models of M-polyfold charts.

The tangent of a retraction. Put \(Tr(TU) := \{Tr(p) : p \in TU\} \subseteq E_1 \times E_0\) Chapter2/RetractsScRetraction.tangent. The chain rule applied to \(r \circ r = r\) (Part I, Theorem 1.21) gives \(Tr \circ Tr = Tr\) on \(TU\) Chapter2/RetractsScRetraction.tangentMap_tangentMap Chapter1/ChainRuletheorem_1_21, since \(Tr\) maps \(TU\) into \(TU\) Chapter2/RetractsScRetraction.tangentMap_mapsTo. Hence the fixed-point description: \(p \in Tr(TU)\) iff \(p \in TU\) and \(Tr(p) = p\) Chapter2/RetractsScRetraction.mem_tangent_iff. Base points of \(Tr(TU)\) lie in \(O_1\) Chapter2/RetractsScRetraction.fst_mem_of_mem_tangent. For \(x \in O_1\) the fixed-point condition reads \(Dr(x)h = h\) Chapter2/RetractsScRetraction.mem_tangent_iff_of_mem, and the second component of \(Tr \circ Tr = Tr\) at \((x, h)\) gives \(Dr(x) \circ Dr(x) = Dr(x)\) Chapter2/RetractsScRetraction.scDeriv_comp_self — the remark after Definition 2.3 that \(Dr(x)\) is a projection. So for \(x \in O_1\), \((x, h) \in Tr(TU)\) iff \(h\) is in the range of \(Dr(x)\) Chapter2/RetractsScRetraction.mem_tangent_iff_mem_range, and \(Tr(TU) = \{(r(x), Dr(x)h) : x \in U_1, h \in E_0\}\) Chapter2/RetractsScRetraction.mem_tangent_iff_exists.

Proposition 2.4. If \(r(U) \subseteq r'(U')\) then \(r' \circ r = r\) on \(U\): for \(y \in U\), \(r(y) \in r'(U')\) is a fixed point of \(r'\) Chapter2/RetractsScRetraction.comp_eq_self_of_retract_subset. And then \(Tr(TU) \subseteq Tr'(TU')\): let \(p \in Tr(TU)\), so \(p \in TU\) and \(Tr(p) = p\). Its base point lies in \(O_1 \subseteq U'_1\), so \(p \in TU'\). The map \(r\) sends \(U\) into \(U'\) (into \(O \subseteq U'\)), so the chain rule applies to \(r' \circ r\) on \(U\): \(T(r' \circ r)(p) = Tr'(Tr(p)) = Tr'(p)\); and \(T(r' \circ r) = Tr\) on \(TU\) because \(r' \circ r = r\) on \(U\) (tangent maps depend only on the values on \(U\)). So \(Tr'(p) = Tr(p) = p\), which is the fixed-point condition for \(r'\) Chapter2/RetractsScRetraction.tangent_subset_of_retract_subset. Applied in both directions, two retractions with the same retract have the same tangent image Chapter2/Retractsproposition_2_4. This is the text’s proof, with its step “\(Tr'(x, h) = (x, h)\)” made the definition of membership.

Definition 2.5. \(TO\) is \(Tr(TU)\) for a retraction chosen (by choice) among those onto \(O\), and the empty set if \(O\) is not a retract Chapter2/RetractsretractTangent; by Proposition 2.4 it equals \(Tr(TU)\) for every retraction onto \(O\) Chapter2/RetractsretractTangent_eq. The tangent space at \(x \in O_1\) is the fibre \(T_xO = \{h : (x, h) \in TO\}\) Chapter2/RetractstangentSpace, the range of \(Dr(x)\) Chapter2/RetractstangentSpace_eq_range, a linear subspace Chapter2/RetractstangentSpace_eq_coe_submodule (closed, as the range of a continuous projection).

II.3 Sc-smooth maps between retracts (Proposition 2.6, Definition 2.7, Theorem 2.8, Proposition 2.10)

Proposition 2.6. Let \(r\) on \(U\) and \(s\) on \(V\) be retractions onto the same \(O\). Since \(s\) takes values in \(O\), which \(r\) fixes, \((f \circ r) \circ s = f \circ s\) on \(V\) Chapter2/RetractsScRetraction.comp_comp_eqOn. (1) If \(f \circ r\) is sc-smooth on \(U\), then \(f \circ r \circ s\) is sc-smooth on \(V\) by the chain rule (\(s\) maps \(V\) into \(O \subseteq U\)), hence so is \(f \circ s\) Chapter2/Retractsproposition_2_6_1 Chapter1/ChainRuleIsScSmooth.comp. (2) For \(p \in TO\): \(p \in TV\) and \(Ts(p) = p\) (fixed-point description for \(s\), after Proposition 2.4); so \(T(f \circ r)(p) = T(f \circ r)(Ts(p)) = T((f \circ r) \circ s)(p) = T(f \circ s)(p)\) Chapter2/Retractsproposition_2_6_2. (3) If \(f\) maps \(O\) into \(O' = r'(U')\), then \(r' \circ f \circ r = f \circ r\) on \(U\); the chain rule gives \(Tr'(T(f \circ r)(p)) = T(f \circ r)(p)\) for \(p \in TU\), and \(T(f \circ r)(p) \in TU'\), so \(T(f \circ r)(p) \in TO'\) by the fixed-point description Chapter2/Retractsproposition_2_6_3.

Definition 2.7. \(f\) is sc-smooth from \((O, C, E)\) to \((O', C', E')\) if \(f(O) \subseteq O'\) and \(f \circ r\) is sc-smooth on \(U\) for every retraction \(r\) onto \(O\) Chapter2/RetractsIsScSmoothRetractMap. For a retract \(O\) this is equivalent to “\(f(O) \subseteq O'\) and \(f \circ r\) sc-smooth for one \(r\)”, by Proposition 2.6 (1) Chapter2/RetractsisScSmoothRetractMap_iff_exists. Quantifying over all retractions makes the definition independent of choices without further argument; the target triple enters only through \(f(O) \subseteq O'\). The tangent map \(Tf\) is \(T(f \circ r)\) for the chosen retraction Chapter2/RetractsretractTangentMap; on \(TO\) it equals \(T(f \circ r)\) for every \(r\) onto \(O\), by Proposition 2.6 (2) Chapter2/RetractsretractTangentMap_eqOn, it maps \(TO\) into \(TO'\) by (3) Chapter2/RetractsIsScSmoothRetractMap.tangentMap_mapsTo, and \(Tf(x, h) = (f(x), D(f \circ r)(x)h)\) Chapter2/RetractsretractTangentMap_apply. An sc-smooth map between retracts is continuous on \(O\) (level \(0\) of the \(\mathrm{sc}^0\) property of \(f \circ r\), and \(f = f \circ r\) on \(O\)) Chapter2/RetractsIsScSmoothRetractMap.continuousOn and maps points of \(O\) on level \(m\) to points on level \(m\) Chapter2/RetractsIsScSmoothRetractMap.mem_range_toBase.

Theorem 2.8. Let \(O = r(U)\), \(O' = r'(U')\) be retracts, \(f\) sc-smooth from \(O\) to \(O'\) and \(g\) from \(O'\) to \(O''\). Since \(f \circ r\) takes values in \(O'\), which \(r'\) fixes, \((g \circ r') \circ (f \circ r) = (g \circ f) \circ r\) on \(U\) Chapter2/RetractsScRetraction.comp_comp_comp_eqOn. The left side is sc-smooth by the chain rule (\(f \circ r\) maps \(U\) into \(O' \subseteq U'\), and \(g \circ r'\) is sc-smooth on \(U'\)), so \(g \circ f\) is sc-smooth from \(O\) to \(O''\) Chapter2/RetractsIsScSmoothRetractMap.comp. For the tangent maps, at \(p \in TO\): \(T(g \circ f)(p) = T((g \circ f) \circ r)(p) = T(g \circ r')(T(f \circ r)(p)) = Tg(Tf(p))\), the last step because \(Tf(p) \in TO'\) Chapter2/RetractsretractTangentMap_comp. Together Chapter2/Retractstheorem_2_8. The text gives no proof (“follows from Theorem 1.21”); this is the one it has in mind, with \(r' \circ f \circ r = f \circ r\) made explicit. Further: the identity is sc-smooth Chapter2/RetractsisScSmoothRetractMap_id, a retraction is sc-smooth as a map \((U, C, E) \to (O, C, E)\) and the inclusion \(O \to U\) as a map \((O, C, E) \to (U, C, E)\) Chapter2/RetractsScRetraction.isScSmoothRetractMap Chapter2/RetractsScRetraction.isScSmoothRetractMap_inclusion, and sc-smoothness depends only on \(f|_O\) Chapter2/RetractsIsScSmoothRetractMap.congr.

Proposition 2.10. (1) For \(W \subseteq E_0\) open, \(U \cap r^{-1}(W)\) is relatively open in \(C\) because \(r\) is continuous on \(U\) Chapter2/RetractsScRetraction.relOpen_inter_preimage; the restriction of \(r\) to it is a retraction Chapter2/RetractsScRetraction.restrict (sc-smooth by §II.1) with retract \(O \cap W\) Chapter2/RetractsScRetraction.restrict_retract. So \((O \cap W, C, E)\) is a retract Chapter2/Retractsproposition_2_10_1 Chapter2/RetractsLocalModel.restrict; “an open subset \(O'\) of \(O\)” is \(O \cap W\) in the subspace topology. (2) If \(V = r(U)\) and \(s\) is sc-smooth from \((V, C, E)\) to itself with \(s \circ s = s\) on \(V\), then \(\rho = s \circ r\) is sc-smooth on \(U\) (that is what sc-smoothness of \(s\) on the retract \(V\) means), maps \(U\) into \(s(V) \subseteq V \subseteq U\), and is idempotent: \(\rho(\rho(x)) = s(r(s(r(x)))) = s(s(r(x))) = s(r(x))\) because \(r\) fixes \(s(r(x)) \in V\). Its retract is \(s(V)\) Chapter2/Retractsproposition_2_10_2. As the text’s proof.

Restriction and locality between retracts. An sc-smooth map between retracts restricts to \(O \cap W\): a retraction onto \(O \cap W\) composed with \(r\) is handled by the chain rule Chapter2/RetractsIsScSmoothRetractMap.restrict; the target may be shrunk to any set containing the image Chapter2/RetractsIsScSmoothRetractMap.mono_target. Conversely, if every point of \(O\) has an open \(W\) with \(f\) sc-smooth on \((O \cap W, C, E)\), then \(f\) is sc-smooth on \((O, C, E)\): for a retraction \(r\) onto \(O\) and \(y \in U\), the set \(W\) around \(r(y)\) pulls back under the continuous \(r\) to an open \(u \ni y\); on \(U \cap u\) the map \(f \circ r\) equals \((f \circ r') \circ r\) with \(r'\) the restriction of \(r\) onto \(O \cap W\), which is sc-smooth, and the locality of §II.1 concludes Chapter2/RetractsIsScSmoothRetractMap.of_locally. The text uses this silently every time it says “the definition does not depend on the choice of charts”.

II.4 The tangent functor on retracts

The tangent of a partial quadrant. If \(C = T_0^{-1}(\text{quadrant})\) for \(T : E \cong \mathbb R^n \oplus W\), then \(TC = C_1 \times E_0\) is a partial quadrant in \(TE = E^1 \oplus E\): compose the tangent of \(T\), an sc-isomorphism \(TE \cong T(\mathbb R^n \oplus W)\), with the re-association \(((a, w), (b, v)) \mapsto (a, (w, (b, v)))\) onto \(\mathbb R^n \oplus (W^1 \oplus (\mathbb R^n \oplus W))\) Chapter2/TangentBundletangentQuadrantIso Chapter2/TangentBundleIsPartialQuadrant.tangentSet. \(TU\) is relatively open in \(TC\) Chapter2/TangentBundleIsRelOpenInQuadrant.tangentSet (this is Lemma 3.B of the exposition of Chapter 1; Part I, V1.36). Sc-operators are sc-smooth on every sc-domain Chapter2/TangentBundleScOperator.isScSmooth.

\(Tr\) is a retraction. \(Tr\) is sc-smooth on \(TU\) (Part I: the tangent map of an sc-smooth map is sc-smooth) Chapter2/RetractsLocalModel.tangent_isScSmooth, maps \(TU\) into itself and is idempotent; so it is an sc-smooth retraction on \(TC\) Chapter2/TangentBundleScRetraction.tangentRetraction with retract \(TO\) Chapter2/TangentBundleScRetraction.tangentRetraction_retract. Hence \((TO, TC, TE)\) is a retract Chapter2/TangentBundleIsScRetract.tangentSet Chapter2/TangentBundleLocalModel.tangent, base points of \(TO\) lie in \(O_1\) and \((x, 0) \in TO\) for \(x \in O_1\) Chapter2/TangentBundleretractTangent_fst_mem Chapter2/TangentBundlemk_zero_mem_retractTangent.

\(Tf\) is sc-smooth. If \(f\) is sc-smooth from \(O\) to \(O'\) then \(Tf\) is sc-smooth from \((TO, TC, TE)\) to \((TO', TC', TE')\): with the retraction \(Tr\) onto \(TO\), \(Tf \circ Tr = T(f \circ r) \circ Tr = T(f \circ r \circ r) = T(f \circ r)\) on \(TU\), which is sc-smooth Chapter2/TangentBundleIsScSmoothRetractMap.tangent. \(Tf\) depends only on \(f|_O\) Chapter2/TangentBundleretractTangentMap_congr, and a map equal to the identity on \(O\) has tangent map the identity on \(TO\) Chapter2/TangentBundleretractTangentMap_id. With Theorem 2.8 this is the tangent functor \(T : \mathcal R \to \mathcal R\) of the text; the bundle structure (\(\mathcal{BR}\), Definition 2.9) is not formalized.

Locality of the tangent. For \(W\) open, \(T(O \cap W) = TO \cap (W_1 \times E_0)\): with the restricted retraction, a fixed point of \(Tr\) over a base point in \(W_1\) is a fixed point of the restricted \(Tr\), the two tangent maps agreeing on the smaller domain (§II.1) Chapter2/TangentBundleretractTangent_inter_isOpen Chapter2/TangentBundleretractTangent_mono_inter. And \(Tf\) computed on \((O \cap W, C, E)\) agrees with \(Tf\) computed on \((O, C, E)\) on \(T(O \cap W)\) Chapter2/TangentBundleretractTangentMap_inter_isOpen. These two facts are what Definitions 2.17–2.18 use silently when the chain rule is applied on a triple overlap.

II.5 Charts, atlases and M-polyfolds (Definitions 2.11–2.14)

Definition 2.11. A chart on \(X\) is a local model \((O, C, E)\) and a partial equivalence \(\varphi\) between \(X\) and \(E_0\) with open source \(V\) and target \(O\), continuous on \(V\), with inverse continuous on \(O\) Chapter2/MPolyfoldMChart. Images of open subsets of \(V\) are open subsets \(O \cap W\) of \(O\) Chapter2/MPolyfoldMChart.exists_isOpen_image_eq, hence retracts (Proposition 2.10 (1)) Chapter2/MPolyfoldMChart.isScRetract_image, and charts restrict to open subsets of their sources Chapter2/MPolyfoldMChart.restrict. The overlap \(\varphi(V \cap V')\) Chapter2/MPolyfoldMChart.overlap is a retract Chapter2/MPolyfoldMChart.isScRetract_overlap, the transition map is \(\psi \circ \varphi^{-1}\) Chapter2/MPolyfoldMChart.transition, mapping \(\varphi(V \cap V')\) into \(\psi(V \cap V')\) Chapter2/MPolyfoldMChart.transition_mapsTo, and two charts are compatible if both transition maps are sc-smooth between the overlap retracts Chapter2/MPolyfoldMChart.Compatible. Compatibility is symmetric, reflexive, and passes to restrictions Chapter2/MPolyfoldMChart.Compatible.symm Chapter2/MPolyfoldMChart.compatible_self Chapter2/MPolyfoldMChart.Compatible.restrict.

Compatibility is local. Let \(\varphi\), \(\psi\) be charts and \(S\) a family of charts each compatible with \(\varphi\) and with \(\psi\), whose sources cover \(V \cap V'\). Then \(\varphi\) and \(\psi\) are compatible Chapter2/MPolyfoldMChart.compatible_of_locally. By the locality between retracts (§II.3) it suffices to show that \(\psi \circ \varphi^{-1}\) is sc-smooth near every point \(\varphi(x)\) of the overlap. Take \(\chi \in S\) around \(x\) and the triple overlap \(s = V \cap V' \cap V''\), with \(\varphi(s) = \varphi(V \cap V') \cap W\) for an open \(W\). On \(\varphi(s)\), \(\psi \circ \varphi^{-1} = (\psi \circ \chi^{-1}) \circ (\chi \circ \varphi^{-1})\) Chapter2/MPolyfoldMChart.transition_eq_comp_on; the two factors are sc-smooth on the restricted retracts \(\varphi(s)\) and \(\chi(s)\), and Theorem 2.8 composes them. The reverse transition is the same argument with the roles exchanged. This is the step that makes “the equivalence class of atlases” a usable notion; the text does not discuss it.

Definition 2.12. An atlas is a set of pairwise compatible charts covering \(X\) Chapter2/MPolyfoldMAtlas; two atlases are equivalent if their union is an atlas Chapter2/MPolyfoldMAtlas.Equiv, i.e. if every chart of one is compatible with every chart of the other Chapter2/MPolyfoldMAtlas.equiv_iff. The relation is reflexive and symmetric Chapter2/MPolyfoldMAtlas.Equiv.refl Chapter2/MPolyfoldMAtlas.Equiv.symm.

Definition 2.13. An M-polyfold structure on a Hausdorff paracompact space is an atlas Chapter2/MPolyfoldMPolyfold. Its charts are all charts compatible with every chart of the atlas Chapter2/MPolyfoldMPolyfold.IsChart Chapter2/MPolyfoldMPolyfold.isChart_of_mem. By locality of compatibility (with \(S\) the atlas), any two of them are compatible Chapter2/MPolyfoldMPolyfold.IsChart.compatible; restrictions of charts are charts Chapter2/MPolyfoldMPolyfold.IsChart.restrict; every point lies in one Chapter2/MPolyfoldMPolyfold.exists_isChart_mem_source; and equivalent atlases have the same charts, again by locality Chapter2/MPolyfoldMPolyfold.isChart_congr. So the maximal atlas represents the equivalence class, and every later definition (levels, index, tangent bundle) quantifies over it.

Definition 2.14. \(f : X \to Y\) is sc-smooth on the open set \(U\) if it is continuous on \(U\) and for all charts \(\varphi\) of \(X\), \(\psi\) of \(Y\) and every open \(V \subseteq U \cap \operatorname{dom}\varphi\) with \(f(V) \subseteq \operatorname{dom}\psi\), the representation \(\psi \circ f \circ \varphi^{-1}\) is sc-smooth from \((\varphi(V), C, E)\) into \((O', C', E')\) Chapter2/MPolyfoldMPolyfold.IsScSmoothOn; sc-smooth means sc-smooth on \(X\) Chapter2/MPolyfoldMPolyfold.IsScSmoothMap. Continuity is a field: the text’s pairs of charts with \(f(V) \subseteq V'\) exist around every point only for continuous \(f\). The notion passes to open subsets and to maps agreeing on \(U\) Chapter2/MPolyfoldMPolyfold.IsScSmoothOn.mono Chapter2/MPolyfoldMPolyfold.IsScSmoothOn.congr. One pair of charts suffices: if every \(x \in U\) has charts \(\varphi\), \(\psi\) and an open \(V \ni x\) with \(\psi \circ f \circ \varphi^{-1}\) sc-smooth on \(\varphi(V)\), then \(f\) is sc-smooth on \(U\) Chapter2/LevelPolyfoldMPolyfold.IsScSmoothOn.of_exists_charts. For arbitrary charts \(\varphi'\), \(\psi'\) and \(V'\), locality reduces to a neighbourhood \(\varphi'(V \cap V')\) of each point, where \(\psi' \circ f \circ \varphi'^{-1} = (\psi' \circ \psi^{-1}) \circ (\psi \circ f \circ \varphi^{-1}) \circ (\varphi \circ \varphi'^{-1})\), three sc-smooth maps between retracts composed by Theorem 2.8. This is the text’s “the definition does not depend on the choice of charts”. The identity is sc-smooth Chapter2/MPolyfoldMPolyfold.isScSmoothMap_id, and compositions are sc-smooth by the same three-factor argument with a chart of the middle space Chapter2/MPolyfoldMPolyfold.IsScSmoothOn.comp Chapter2/MPolyfoldMPolyfold.IsScSmoothMap.comp.

II.6 The filtration \(X_m\) and the M-polyfold \(X^1\) (Lemma 2.15)

Levels. \(x\) is on level \(m\) if \(\varphi(x) \in \iota_m(E_m)\) for some chart \(\varphi\) around \(x\) Chapter2/MPolyfoldMPolyfold.levelSet. Independence of the chart: if \(\psi\) is another chart around \(x\), the transition map \(\varphi \circ \psi^{-1}\) is sc-smooth between the overlap retracts, hence maps points on level \(m\) to points on level \(m\) (§II.3), and \(\varphi(x) = (\varphi \circ \psi^{-1})(\psi(x))\) Chapter2/MPolyfoldMPolyfold.mem_levelSet_iff. \(X_0 = X\), \(X_{m+1} \subseteq X_m\), and \(X_\infty = \bigcap_m X_m\) Chapter2/MPolyfoldMPolyfold.levelSet_zero Chapter2/MPolyfoldMPolyfold.levelSet_succ_subset Chapter2/MPolyfoldMPolyfold.smoothSet. For \(x \in V_m\) the lift of \(\varphi(x)\) to \(E_m\) Chapter2/MPolyfoldMPolyfold.levelLift satisfies \(\iota_m(\text{lift}) = \varphi(x)\) and is compatible with the inclusions Chapter2/MPolyfoldMPolyfold.toBase_levelLift Chapter2/MPolyfoldMPolyfold.levelLift_eq_incl. \(X_m\) carries the topology generated by the sets \(\{x \in V : \text{lift}(x) \in W\}\), \(W\) open in \(E_m\) Chapter2/MPolyfoldMPolyfold.levelBasis Chapter2/MPolyfoldMPolyfold.levelTopology; that this family is a basis is not needed.

Lemma 2.15. The preimage under \(X_{m+1} \to X_m\) Chapter2/MPolyfoldMPolyfold.levelIncl of a generating set \(\{\text{lift}_m \in W\}\) is the generating set \(\{\text{lift}_{m+1} \in \mathrm{incl}_m^{-1}(W)\}\), by the compatibility of lifts with inclusions; so the inclusion is continuous Chapter2/MPolyfoldlemma_2_15. This is the text’s proof.

The space \(X_m\). As a type, \(X_m\) is the subtype of points on level \(m\) with this topology Chapter2/LevelPolyfoldMPolyfold.Level. The inclusion \(X_m \to X\) is continuous: for \(V\) open in \(X\) and \(x \in X_m\), a chart \(\varphi\) around \(x\) gives \(\varphi(V \cap \operatorname{dom}\varphi) = O \cap W\), and the generating set \(\{\text{lift}_m \in W_m\}\) is a neighbourhood of \(x\) inside the preimage of \(V\) Chapter2/LevelPolyfoldMPolyfold.continuous_levelVal Chapter2/LevelPolyfoldMPolyfold.isOpen_level_basic. Since this inclusion is injective and continuous into the Hausdorff \(X\), \(X_m\) is Hausdorff (an instance in LevelPolyfold, the text’s argument with disjoint neighbourhoods).

The level shift of the local data. An sc-isomorphism shifts to \(E^1 \to F^1\) Chapter2/LevelPolyfoldScIso.shift, so \(C_1\) is a partial quadrant in \(E^1\) and \(U_1\) relatively open in it Chapter2/LevelPolyfoldIsPartialQuadrant.shift Chapter2/LevelPolyfoldIsRelOpenInQuadrant.shift. A retraction \(r\) induces the retraction \(r_1\) on \(U_1\) — sc-smooth by Proposition 1.17 (Part I, §I.15), idempotent by the injectivity of \(\iota_1\) Chapter2/LevelPolyfoldScRetraction.shift — with retract \(O_1\) Chapter2/LevelPolyfoldScRetraction.shift_retract Chapter2/LevelPolyfoldIsScRetract.shift Chapter2/LevelPolyfoldLocalModel.shift. An sc-smooth map between retracts is \(\mathrm{sc}^0\) on \(O\), maps \(O_m\) into \(O'_m\) and is continuous there Chapter2/LevelPolyfoldIsScSmoothRetractMap.isSc0 Chapter2/LevelPolyfoldIsScSmoothRetractMap.mapsTo_levelMap Chapter2/LevelPolyfoldIsScSmoothRetractMap.continuousOn_levelMap, and its level-\(1\) map is sc-smooth from \(O_1\) to \(O'_1\): with the retraction \(r_1\), \(f_1 \circ r_1 = (f \circ r)_1\), sc-smooth by Proposition 1.17 Chapter2/LevelPolyfoldIsScSmoothRetractMap.shift.

The M-polyfold \(X^1\). For a chart \(\varphi\) of \(X\), \(x \mapsto \text{lift}_1(x)\) on \(V_1\) with model \((O_1, C_1, E^1)\) is a chart of \(X_1\) Chapter2/LevelPolyfoldMPolyfold.levelChart (with a junk value for the inverse off \(O_1\), since \(X_1\) might be empty Chapter2/LevelPolyfoldMPolyfold.levelChartInv); its overlap with another level chart is the level-\(1\) part of the overlap Chapter2/LevelPolyfoldMPolyfold.levelChart_overlap, its transition map the level-\(1\) map of the transition map Chapter2/LevelPolyfoldMPolyfold.levelChart_transition, and so any two level charts are compatible by the level shift of sc-smooth maps Chapter2/LevelPolyfoldMPolyfold.levelChart_compatible. They form an atlas Chapter2/LevelPolyfoldMPolyfold.levelAtlas, and \(X_1\) with it is the M-polyfold \(X^1\) Chapter2/LevelPolyfoldMPolyfold.shift Chapter2/LevelPolyfoldMPolyfold.shift_isChart. Its paracompactness, an instance argument, is supplied by Theorem 2.16 (§II.7). Only \(m = 1\) is constructed.

II.7 Metrizability: Smirnov’s theorem and Theorem 2.16 (Theorem 2.55)

The text proves Theorem 2.16 with Smirnov’s theorem (2.55), Michael’s characterization of paracompactness (Lemma 2.56) and Proposition 2.57 (a regular space with a locally finite closed cover by paracompact subspaces is paracompact). Proposition 2.57 needs \(X_m\) to be regular, which the text does not check. The formal proof needs neither 2.56 nor 2.57.

The metrization lemma. Let \(Y\) have open subspaces \(V_i\), each metrizable with a metric \(d_i\), and continuous \(\rho_i : Y \to [0, \infty)\) with \(\operatorname{supp}\rho_i \subseteq V_i\), the supports locally finite and \(\rho_i(y) > 0\) for some \(i\) at every \(y\) Chapter2/MetrizablemetrizableSpace_of_partition. Put \(\delta_i(x, y) := \min(d_i(x, y), 1)\) for \(x, y \in V_i\) and \(1\) otherwise Chapter2/MetrizabletruncDist — nonnegative, at most \(1\), symmetric, zero only on the diagonal, and satisfying the triangle inequality inside \(V_i\) Chapter2/MetrizabletruncDist_nonneg Chapter2/MetrizabletruncDist_le_one Chapter2/MetrizabletruncDist_triangle Chapter2/MetrizabletruncDist_eq_zero — and the cone metric \[e_i(x, y) := |\rho_i(x) - \rho_i(y)| + \min(\rho_i(x), \rho_i(y))\,\delta_i(x, y),\qquad D(x, y) := \sum_i e_i(x, y).\] The sum is finite (only the \(i\) with \(x\) or \(y\) in \(\operatorname{supp}\rho_i\) contribute). \(D(x, x) = 0\) and \(D\) is symmetric. Triangle inequality: termwise, by an elementary inequality for \(a, b, c \ge 0\) and \(\delta\)’s bounded by \(1\), which needs the triangle inequality for \(\delta_i\) only when \(\min(\rho_i(x), \rho_i(z)) > 0\) and \(\rho_i(y) > 0\), i.e. when all three points lie in \(V_i\) Chapter2/Metrizablecone_triangle. Separation: if \(D(x, y) = 0\), take \(i\) with \(\rho_i(x) > 0\); then \(\rho_i(y) = \rho_i(x)\) and \(\delta_i(x, y) = 0\), so \(x = y\). Topology: \(y \mapsto D(x, y)\) is continuous (locally a finite sum of continuous functions; the term \(\min(\rho_i(x), \rho_i(y))\delta_i(x, y)\) is continuous where \(y \in V_i\) and vanishes near points outside \(\operatorname{supp}\rho_i\)), so \(D\)-balls are open; conversely, if \(s\) is open and \(x \in s\), take \(i\) with \(\rho_i(x) > 0\) and a \(d_i\)-ball of radius \(r \le 1\) around \(x\) inside \(s\); then \(D(x, y) < \frac12\rho_i(x) r\) forces \(\rho_i(y) > \frac12\rho_i(x)\) (so \(y \in V_i\)) and \(\frac12\rho_i(x)\delta_i(x, y) < \frac12\rho_i(x) r\), so \(d_i(x, y) < r\) and \(y \in s\). Mathlib then builds a metric space structure with this distance and the given topology Mathlib/Topology/MetricSpace/DefsMetricSpace.ofDistTopology.

Pulled back, and Smirnov. If \(\pi : Y \to X\) is continuous into a paracompact Hausdorff \(X\) and every point of \(X\) has an open \(U\) with \(\pi^{-1}(U)\) metrizable, then \(Y\) is metrizable: a partition of unity of \(X\) subordinate to these \(U\) Mathlib/Topology/PartitionOfUnityPartitionOfUnity.exists_isSubordinate, composed with \(\pi\), satisfies the hypotheses of the lemma with \(V_i = \pi^{-1}(U_i)\) Chapter2/MetrizablemetrizableSpace_of_pullback. With \(\pi = \mathrm{id}\) this is Smirnov’s theorem (Theorem 2.55) Chapter2/MetrizablemetrizableSpace_of_locally. Metrizable spaces are paracompact (Stone; in Mathlib through the instance for pseudo-emetric spaces) Chapter2/MetrizableparacompactSpace_of_metrizableSpace.

Theorem 2.16. \(X\) is metrizable: chart domains are homeomorphic to subsets \(O\) of the Banach space \(E_0\) Chapter2/MetrizableMChart.sourceHomeomorph Chapter2/MetrizableMChart.metrizableSpace_source, and Smirnov applies Chapter2/MetrizableMPolyfold.metrizableSpace. \(V_m \cong O_m\): the lift \(x \mapsto \text{lift}_m(x)\) is a topological embedding of \(V \cap X_m\) into \(E_m\) Chapter2/MetrizableMPolyfold.isEmbedding_levelLift. Its injectivity is that of \(\varphi\); the induced topology is finer than that of \(X_m\) because generating sets of \(X_m\) inside \(V\) are preimages of open sets; it is coarser because a generating set \(\{\text{lift}^\psi_m \in W\}\) of another chart, intersected with \(V\), is the preimage under \(\text{lift}^\varphi_m\) of the open set \(\{z \in \varphi(V \cap V')_m : (\psi \circ \varphi^{-1})_m(z) \in W\}\), open since the level-\(m\) map of the transition is continuous on the level-\(m\) part of the overlap retract. \(X_m\) is metrizable: apply the pulled-back Smirnov to the continuous inclusion \(X_m \to X\) and the chart domains \(V\), whose preimages \(V \cap X_m\) embed in \(E_m\) Chapter2/MetrizableMPolyfold.metrizableSpace_level; hence paracompact Chapter2/MetrizableMPolyfold.paracompactSpace_level. \(X_\infty\): the text does not define its topology; it is taken to be the initial topology of the inclusions \(X_\infty \to X_m\) Chapter2/MetrizableMPolyfold.SmoothLevel Chapter2/MetrizableMPolyfold.smoothIncl Chapter2/MetrizableMPolyfold.smoothLevel_topology_eq. It embeds in the countable product \(\prod_m X_m\), which is metrizable Chapter2/MetrizablemetrizableSpace_pi_nat, so \(X_\infty\) is metrizable Chapter2/MetrizableMPolyfold.metrizableSpace_smoothLevel. Together Chapter2/Metrizabletheorem_2_16. No hypothesis is added. As a by-product every subset of an M-polyfold is metrizable, hence paracompact Chapter2/MetrizableMPolyfold.paracompactSpace_subtype, which discharges the paracompactness of sub-M-polyfolds (§II.10).

II.8 The tangent bundle \(TX\) (Definitions 2.17–2.18, Proposition 2.19)

Tuples and transport. A tangent tuple is \((x, \varphi, h)\) with \(x \in X_1\), \(\varphi\) a chart of the structure around \(x\) and \((\text{lift}_1 x, h) \in TO\) Chapter2/TangentBundleMPolyfold.TangentPre; its vector is \((\text{lift}_1 x, h)\) Chapter2/TangentBundleMPolyfold.TangentPre.vec Chapter2/TangentBundleMPolyfold.TangentPre.vec_mem. For a vector of \(TO\) over a point of an open \(\varphi(s)\), membership in \(TO\) and in \(T(\varphi(s))\) agree (locality of the tangent, §II.4) Chapter2/TangentBundleMPolyfold.TangentPre.mem_retractTangent_image_iff. The transport of the tuple to a chart \(\psi\) around \(x\) is \(T(\psi \circ \varphi^{-1})(\text{vec})\), the tangent map computed on the overlap retract Chapter2/TangentBundleMPolyfold.TangentPre.transport. Transport to \(\varphi\) itself does nothing, by \(T(\mathrm{id}) = \mathrm{id}\) on the overlap \(\varphi(V)\) Chapter2/TangentBundleMPolyfold.TangentPre.transport_self Chapter2/TangentBundleMChart.transition_self_eqOn; the transported vector lies in \(TO'\) Chapter2/TangentBundleMPolyfold.TangentPre.transport_mem and has base point \(\text{lift}^\psi_1(x)\) Chapter2/TangentBundleMPolyfold.TangentPre.transport_fst.

The chain rule for transports. Transporting to \(\psi\) and then by \(T(\chi \circ \psi^{-1})\) is transporting to \(\chi\) Chapter2/TangentBundleMPolyfold.TangentPre.transport_transport. On the triple overlap \(s = V \cap V' \cap V''\) the transition maps are sc-smooth from \(\varphi(s)\) to \(\psi(s)\) and from \(\psi(s)\) to \(\chi(s)\) Chapter2/TangentBundleMChart.Compatible.transition_image Chapter2/TangentBundleMChart.image_eq_overlap_inter, \(\chi \circ \varphi^{-1} = (\chi \circ \psi^{-1}) \circ (\psi \circ \varphi^{-1})\) there, and Theorem 2.8 gives \(T(\chi \circ \varphi^{-1}) = T(\chi \circ \psi^{-1}) \circ T(\psi \circ \varphi^{-1})\) on \(T(\varphi(s))\). The three tangent maps here are computed on \(\varphi(s)\) and \(\psi(s)\), the transports on the full overlaps; the locality of \(Tf\) (§II.4) identifies them. The text never checks this.

Definition 2.17. Two tuples are equivalent if their points agree and the transport of the first to the chart of the second is the second Chapter2/TangentBundleMPolyfold.TangentPre.Rel. Equivalent tuples transport to the same vector in every chart (chain rule for transports) Chapter2/TangentBundleMPolyfold.TangentPre.Rel.transport; hence the relation is reflexive, symmetric and transitive Chapter2/TangentBundleMPolyfold.TangentPre.Rel.refl Chapter2/TangentBundleMPolyfold.TangentPre.Rel.symm Chapter2/TangentBundleMPolyfold.TangentPre.Rel.trans, an equivalence relation Chapter2/TangentBundleMPolyfold.TangentPre.setoid.

For a chart \(\varphi\): \(TV = p^{-1}(V_1)\) Chapter2/TangentBundleMPolyfold.tangentChartSet and \(T\varphi : TV \to TO\) sends a class to the transport of a representative to \(\varphi\), well defined by the previous paragraph Chapter2/TangentBundleMPolyfold.tangentChartMap Chapter2/TangentBundleMPolyfold.tangentChartMap_mk; \(T\varphi[(x, \varphi, h)] = (\varphi(x), h)\) Chapter2/TangentBundleMPolyfold.tangentChartMap_mk_self, \(T\varphi\) lands in \(TO\) over the lift of the base point Chapter2/TangentBundleMPolyfold.tangentChartMap_mem Chapter2/TangentBundleMPolyfold.tangentChartMap_fst, and it is injective on \(TV\): equal images have equal base points (injectivity of \(\varphi\) and \(\iota_1\)) and then the representatives are equivalent Chapter2/TangentBundleMPolyfold.tangentChartMap_injOn. Its inverse on \(TO\) is \(a \mapsto [(\varphi^{-1}(\iota_1 a_1), \varphi, a_2)]\) Chapter2/TangentBundleMPolyfold.TangentPre.ofVec Chapter2/TangentBundleMPolyfold.tangentChartMap_mk_ofVec Chapter2/TangentBundleMPolyfold.mk_ofVec_tangentChartMap, and in another chart \(T\psi \circ (T\varphi)^{-1} = T(\psi \circ \varphi^{-1})\) on \(T(\varphi(V \cap V'))\) Chapter2/TangentBundleMPolyfold.tangentChartMap_mk_ofVec_of_mem Chapter2/TangentBundleMPolyfold.mk_ofVec_mem_tangentChartSet_iff. The topology is generated by the sets \(\{\alpha \in TV : T\varphi(\alpha) \in W\}\), \(W\) open Chapter2/TangentBundleMPolyfold.tangentBasis Chapter2/TangentBundleMPolyfold.isOpen_tangent_basic; \(TV\) itself is open Chapter2/TangentBundleMPolyfold.isOpen_tangentChartSet. Proposition 2.19. (2) \(p\) is continuous: the preimage of a generating set \(\{\text{lift}^\psi_1 \in W\}\) of \(X_1\) is the generating set of \(TX\) given by \(\psi\) and \(W \times E_0\) Chapter2/TangentBundleMPolyfold.continuous_tangentProj; so is \(TX \to X\) Chapter2/TangentBundleMPolyfold.continuous_levelVal_tangentProj. Openness of \(p\) is not proved. (1) \(TX\) is Hausdorff (the instance T2Space in TangentBundle): two classes over the same point lie in one \(TV\) and have distinct images under the injective \(T\varphi\), separated by open sets of \(E_1 \times E_0\) whose preimages are basic; classes over distinct points are separated by preimages of disjoint open sets of \(X\) under the continuous \(TX \to X\). (3) \(TX\) is metrizable: apply the pulled-back Smirnov theorem to \(TX \to X\) and the chart domains \(V\), whose preimages \(TV\) are homeomorphic to subsets of \(E_1 \times E_0\) through the charts of §II.8’s next paragraph Chapter2/MetrizableMPolyfold.metrizableSpace_tangentSpace Chapter2/MetrizableMChart.metrizableSpace_source; hence paracompact Chapter2/MetrizableMPolyfold.paracompactSpace_tangentSpace Chapter2/Metrizableproposition_2_19_3.

\(TX\) as an M-polyfold. The text uses \(Tf\) for maps between M-polyfolds from §2.3 on without defining it. Levels: an sc-smooth map maps \(X_m\) into \(Y_m\), because its coordinate representations do Chapter2/TangentMapMPolyfold.IsScSmoothOn.mapsTo_levelSet Chapter2/TangentMapMPolyfold.IsScSmoothMap.mapsTo_levelSet. The image vector: for a tuple \((x, \varphi, h)\) and a chart \(\psi\) around \(f(x)\), \(T(\psi \circ f \circ \varphi^{-1})(\text{vec})\), computed on \(\varphi(V \cap f^{-1}(V'))\) Chapter2/TangentMapMPolyfold.TangentPre.fdom Chapter2/TangentMapMPolyfold.TangentPre.ftransport, lies in \(TO'\) over \(\psi(f(x))\) Chapter2/TangentMapMPolyfold.TangentPre.ftransport_mem Chapter2/TangentMapMPolyfold.TangentPre.ftransport_fst; changing \(\psi\) changes it by \(T\) of the transition map Chapter2/TangentMapMPolyfold.TangentPre.ftransport_transport, changing \(\varphi\) by transport Chapter2/TangentMapMPolyfold.TangentPre.ftransport_eq_of_transport, and equivalent tuples give the same image Chapter2/TangentMapMPolyfold.TangentPre.Rel.ftransport — all by the chain rule with locality.
