IV.22 The fibre over a stratified regular point

Partial quadrants of the model. \(\{\ell_i \ge 0, i \in \sigma\}\) Chapter4/FamiliesLocalquadAt is, for \(\sigma = \sigma(v_0)\), the partial quadrant \(C_{v_0}\) of Definition 2.33. With a linear section \(s\) of \(\ell\), \(v \mapsto (\ell(v), v - s(\ell(v)))\) is a linear isomorphism \(V \cong \mathbb R^n \times \ker\ell\) Chapter4/FamiliesLocalsliceEquiv, which presents both as partial quadrants Chapter4/FamiliesLocalisPartialQuadrant_quadC Chapter4/FamiliesLocalisPartialQuadrant_quadAt; \(C\) is convex Chapter4/FamiliesLocalconvex_quadC with nonempty interior Chapter4/FamiliesLocalinterior_quadC_nonempty, so derivatives within \(O \cap C\) are unique Chapter4/FamiliesLocaluniqueDiffWithinAt_quadC.

The kernel at a stratified regular point is in good position Chapter4/FamiliesLocalexists_goodComplement_stratSub — the argument of Lemma 5.26, which the text needs here and does not give. Let \(K + \{\ell_i = 0, i \in \sigma\} = V\) (for \(K = \ker Df(v_0)\), \(\sigma = \sigma(v_0)\), this is stratified regularity). The stratum subspace is closed, so \(K\) has a closed complement \(Y\) inside it (§IV.16). Adding a vector of \(Y\) changes none of the coordinates \(\ell_i\), \(i \in \sigma\), so \(Y\) is a good complement with \(\varepsilon = 1\). For the interior points: choose \(x\) with \(\ell(x) = (1, \dots, 1)\) and write \(x = k + y\); then \(\ell_i(k) = 1\) for \(i \in \sigma\), and the open set \(\{k' \in K : \ell_i(k') > 0, i \in \sigma\}\) contains \(k\) and lies in \(K \cap \{\ell_i \ge 0, i \in \sigma\}\).

The fibre retraction Chapter4/FamiliesLocalexists_fibre_retraction. Let \(\ell\) be onto, \(f\) \(C^\infty\) on \(O \cap C\) and \(v_0 \in O \cap C\) not stratified-critical. There are an open \(O' \ni v_0\), \(O' \subseteq O\), and \(\rho\), \(C^\infty\) on \(O' \cap C\), mapping \(O' \cap C\) into itself and into \(f^{-1}(f(v_0))\), equal to the identity on the fibre there, with \(D\rho(v_0)\) of range \(\ker Df(v_0)\) and equal to the identity on it. Proof:

  1. Stratified regularity gives \(Df(v_0)\) onto (its restriction to the stratum already is) and \(K + \text{stratum} = V\) for \(K = \ker Df(v_0)\); so \(K\) is in good position to \(C_{v_0}\) with a closed good complement \(Y\) in the stratum subspace.
  2. Near \(0\), \(v_0 + C_{v_0}\) and \(C\) agree: on \(G_0 = \{w : \ell_j(v_0 + w) > 0, j \notin \sigma\}\), a point \(v_0 + w\) is in \(C\) iff \(w \in C_{v_0}\), since \(\ell_i(v_0) = 0\) for \(i \in \sigma\) — the re-centring of §IV.5 in the model. So \(U_1 = (O - v_0) \cap G_0 \cap C_{v_0}\) is relatively open in \(C_{v_0}\), contains \(0\), and \(w \mapsto v_0 + w\) maps it into \(U\).
  3. \(g(w) = f(v_0 + w) - f(v_0)\) is \(C^\infty\) on \(U_1\), \(g(0) = 0\), \(Dg(0) = Df(v_0)\) onto; Theorem 3.78 in \(C^\infty\) form gives the fibre near \(v_0\) as the graph \(\{v_0 + k + \tau(k)\}\) of a \(C^\infty\) map \(\tau : V' \to Y\), \(V' \subseteq K \cap C_{v_0}\), unique for small \(k\) and \(y\).
  4. With \(q(v)\) the projection of \(v - v_0\) onto \(K\) along \(Y\) Chapter4/LocalStructureexists_proj_of_isCompl, put \(\rho(v) = v_0 + q(v) + \tau(q(v))\) on \(O' \cap C\), \(O'\) a small ball around \(v_0\) chosen so that \(q\) maps it into the uniqueness region and \(\rho(O' \cap C) \subseteq O'\). The projection along \(Y\) keeps the coordinates in \(\sigma\), so \(q\) maps \(C\) near \(v_0\) into \(C_{v_0}\); \(\rho\) lands on the fibre; and on the fibre \(\rho(v) = v\) by uniqueness.
  5. \(D\tau(0) = 0\) gives \(D\rho(v_0) = q\), whose range is \(K\) and which is the identity on \(K\).

IV.23 Stratified regularity, the sc⁺-retraction onto \(A_\lambda\), and its general position

The family. For tame \(X\), \(\mathbb R^m \times X\) with the product charts is tame Chapter3/ParamPerturbationprod_rn_isTame (§III.40 for \(\mathbb R^m\) as an M-polyfold Chapter3/ParamPerturbationrnPolyfold with its translation charts Chapter3/ParamPerturbationrnChart). The fibre of \(A \subseteq \mathbb R^m \times X\) over \(\lambda\) is \(A_\lambda = \{x : (\lambda, x) \in A\}\) Chapter4/FamiliesfibreSet. \(\mathbb R^m\) is presented as a partial quadrant without half-line coordinates Chapter4/FamiliesrnPres Chapter4/FamiliesrnPres_eq, and the product chart \(\chi = (r \mapsto r - a) \times \varphi\) has the product presentation Chapter2/FibredProductprodPresentation, whose minimal subspace at \(z\) is \(E_z = \mathbb R^m \times (E_X)_{\varphi(z_2)}\).

Stratified regular points Chapter4/FamiliesIsStratRegularPoint. \(z \in A\) is a stratified regular point if, for some data of Definition 4.13 at \(z\), some \(a \in \mathbb R^m\), some chart \(\varphi\) of \(X\) at \(z_2\), some presentation of its partial quadrant and the level-\(1\) point \(y\) over \(\chi(z)\), every \(\mu \in \mathbb R^m\) is the first component of a tangent vector \(v\) of the chart model of \(A\) at \(y\) with \(v_2 \in E_{\varphi(z_2)}\): the projection maps \(T_zA \cap E_z\) — the tangent space of the stratum through \(z\) — onto \(\mathbb R^m\). \(\lambda\) is a stratified regular value if every point of \(A\) over \(\lambda\) is a stratified regular point Chapter4/FamiliesIsStratRegularValue. This is the text’s “regular value of every \(p_\sigma\)”. The chart independence is not formalized (§IV.25). The naive notion does not suffice: in \(\mathbb R \times [0, \infty)\), \(A = \{(x, x) : 0 \le x < 1\} \cup (-1, 1) \times \{5\}\) and \(\varepsilon = \frac12\) satisfy the hypotheses of Theorem 4.23 (at \((0, 0)\), \(T_zA = \mathbb R(1, 1)\) has the complement \(\mathbb R \times 0 = T^R_zZ\)), \(Dp\) is onto everywhere, but \(A_0 = \{0, 5\}\) is zero-dimensional and meets \(\partial X\), so it is not in general position (Remark 4.24); \((0, 0)\) is stratified-critical, \(T_zA \cap E_z = 0\).

The slice \(e \mapsto (c, e)\): the inclusion \(h \mapsto (0, h)\) Chapter4/FamiliesScBanach.prodInrOp followed by the translation by the smooth vector \((c, 0)\) Chapter4/Familiesmem_smooth_rn_zero is sc-smooth Chapter4/FamiliesisScSmooth_slice with derivative \(h \mapsto (0, h)\) Chapter4/FamiliesscDeriv_slice. On a finite-dimensional source the sc-derivative is the classical one Chapter4/FamilieshasFDerivWithinAt_scDeriv_const'.

The sc⁺-retraction onto \(A_\lambda\) Chapter4/Familiesexists_slice_retraction — Definition 4.13 requires it and the text does not construct it. In the model \(\mathbb R^m \oplus E\) of a product chart, let \(t\) be an sc⁺-retraction (the chart model of \(A\)), described near a point as the graph \(\Gamma : V \to t(U) \cap W\) with inverse \(p\) (Proposition 4.9), and \(\rho\) a \(C^\infty\) retraction of \(O' \cap (\mathbb R^m \times C) \subseteq V\) onto the points \(v\) with \(\Gamma(v)_1 = c\) (the fibre retraction of §IV.22 for \(f = (\Gamma)_1\)). Then \[\tau(e) = \big(\Gamma(\rho(p(t(c, e))))\big)_2\] is an sc⁺-retraction of \(E\) (partial quadrant \(C\)) onto \(\{e : (c, e) \in t(U) \cap W,\ p(c, e) \in O'\}\): it is sc⁺ because \(t\) is sc⁺ and the slice, \(p\), \(\rho\) (sc-smooth as a \(C^\infty\) map on a finite-dimensional set, Corollary 1.20), \(\Gamma\) and the second projection Chapter2/StrongBundleScBanach.prodSndOp are sc-smooth (§IV.2); and it is a retraction, because for \(e' = \tau(e)\), \(\Gamma(w) = (c, e')\) with \(w = \rho(\cdot)\) on the fibre, so \(t(c, e') = \Gamma(w)\), \(p\Gamma(w) = w = \rho(w)\) and \(\tau(e') = e'\). Its tangent space: if \(D\rho(v_0) = 1\) on the \(h\) with \((D\Gamma(v_0)h)_1 = 0\), then at the level-\(1\) point over \(\Gamma(v_0)_2\) the tangent space of the retract of \(\tau\) contains \((D\Gamma(v_0)h)_2\) for all such \(h\), by the chain rule \(D\tau(y)w = (D\Gamma(v_0)D\rho(v_0)p\,Dt(c, y)(0, w))_2\), \(Dt\) fixing \(T(t(U)) = D\Gamma(v_0)N\) and \(p \circ D\Gamma(v_0) = 1\).

General position of the fibre Chapter4/FamiliesisGeneralPositionRetractAt_slice. Let \(r_X\) be tame, the chart model of \(A\) in general position at \(z = (c, y)\) with respect to \(\mathrm{id} \times r_X\) and the product presentation, \(z\) regular on its stratum (every \(\mu\) is the first component of some \(a \in T_zA \cap E_z\)), and \(\tau\) an sc⁺-retraction onto \(Q \subseteq O\) whose tangent space at the smooth \(y\) contains the second components of the tangent vectors of \(A\) at \(z\) with first component \(0\). Then \(Q\) is in general position at \(y\). For \(w \in T_yO\) write \((0, w) = a + b\) with \(a \in T_zA\) and \(b \in T^R_zZ = \mathbb R^m \times T^R_yO\) (general position of \(A\) at \(z\)); correct \(a\) by \(a_2 \in T_zA \cap E_z\) with the same first component as \(a\) (regularity on the stratum); then \((a - a_2)_2 \in T_yQ\) and \((b + a_2)_2 \in T^R_yO\), \(a_2\) lying in \(E_z\), so \(w \in T_yQ + T^R_yO\). This is the text’s “\(T_{z'}(A \cap F_\sigma^\circ) = T_{z'}((\{\lambda\} \times A_\lambda) \cap F^\circ_\sigma) \oplus \xi_{z'}\) … in view of the assumption (2)”, made precise: regularity on the stratum is what puts \(a_2\) in \(E_z\).

IV.24 Theorem 4.23: families and Sard’s theorem

The conclusions at a point Chapter4/FamiliesFibreLocal: \(z = (\lambda, x)\) is a stratified regular point, \(A_\lambda\) is near \(x\) the image of an sc⁺-retraction on an open subset of \(X\), and \(A_\lambda\) is in general and in good position at \(x\).

The local step Chapter4/Familiesexists_local_family. For \(X\) tame and \(A \subseteq \mathbb R^m \times X\) a smooth finite-dimensional submanifold in general position at every point, every \(z_0 \in A\) has an open neighbourhood \(U\) and a Lebesgue-null \(\mathrm{CV} \subseteq \mathbb R^m\) such that the conclusions hold at every \(z \in A \cap U\) with \(z_1 \notin \mathrm{CV}\). Proof:

  1. The chart. \(z_{0,2}\) is smooth Chapter3/ParamPerturbationprod_rn_mem_smoothSet_iff, so there is a tame chart \(\varphi\) of \(X\) centred at it (§IV.5); the product chart \(\chi = (r \mapsto r - \lambda_0) \times \varphi\) is a chart of \(\mathbb R^m \times X\) Chapter3/ParamPerturbationisChart_rnChart Chapter2/FibredProductMPolyfold.IsChart.prod centred at \(z_0\), with the tame retraction \(\mathrm{id} \times r_X\) Chapter2/FibredProductScRetraction.prod Chapter2/FibredProductScRetraction.IsTameWith.prod and coordinates those of \(\varphi\) (\(\mathbb R^m\) has none).
  2. Theorem 4.22 in the chart. The chart retraction \(t\) of \(A\) in \(\chi\) is sc⁺ (§IV.11), and general position at \(z_0\) read in \(\chi\) is general position at \(0\); Theorem 4.22 in the chart (§IV.17) gives \(N = T_0(\chi A)\) with \(N + E^{\min}_0 = E_0\), so the coordinates \(\ell\) are onto on \(N\), a closed good complement \(Y \subseteq E^{\min}_0\), the projection \(p\), and \(\Gamma : V \to \chi(A)\) over \(V = O_V \cap \{\ell \ge 0\} \subseteq N\), with \(\ell \circ \Gamma = \ell\).
  3. Sard. \(f(v) = \Gamma(v)_1 + \lambda_0\), the projection \(P\) read in the chart, is sc-smooth on \(V\) as the first projection Chapter2/StrongBundleScBanach.prodFstOp composed with \(\Gamma\), hence \(C^\infty\) (§IV.1); \(\mathrm{CV} = f(\text{stratified critical points of } f)\) is null (§IV.21). \(U = W_A \cap \chi^{-1}(W)\), with \(W_A\) the open set of the submanifold chart (§IV.11) and \(W\) that of Proposition 4.9.
  4. A point \(z \in A \cap U\) with \(z_1 \notin \mathrm{CV}\). \(\chi(z) \in t(U) \cap W\), so \(v_0 = p(\chi z) \in V\) with \(\Gamma(v_0) = \chi(z)\) and \(f(v_0) = z_1\); hence \(v_0\) is not stratified-critical. Since \(\ell(D\Gamma(v)h) = \ell(h)\), \(D\Gamma(v_0)\) maps the stratum subspace of \(\sigma(v_0)\) onto \(T_yA \cap E_y\), \(y = \Gamma(v_0)\); so \(z\) is a stratified regular point, in the chart \(\chi\).
  5. The fibre. The fibre retraction \(\rho\) of \(f\) at \(v_0\) (§IV.22), the sc⁺-retraction \(\tau\) onto the chart image of \(A_{z_1}\) (§IV.23), the sc⁺-retraction \(\varphi^{-1} \circ \tau \circ \varphi\) on an open subset of \(X\) (§IV.18), whose image is \(A_{z_1}\) near \(z_2\); the tangent space of \(\tau\)’s retract contains the vertical tangent vectors of \(A\), since \(D\rho(v_0) = 1\) on \(\ker Df(v_0)\); general position of \(A_{z_1}\) at \(z_2\) (§IV.23); good position from general position (Lemma 7.B).

The cover Chapter4/Familiestheorem_4_23_of_subset. For \(X\) tame and \(A \subseteq \mathbb R^m \times X\) a smooth finite-dimensional submanifold with compact closure, in general position at every point, and any set \(S \subseteq \mathbb R^m\) of parameters, there is \(\Sigma \subseteq S\) with \(S \setminus \Sigma\) null, consisting of stratified regular values, with the conclusions at every point of every \(A_\lambda\), \(\lambda \in \Sigma\). The text covers \(\{z \in A : |p(z)| \le \varepsilon\}\) “with the finitely many such neighborhoods \(U(z_1), \dots, U(z_k)\)”. That set need not be compact: in \(\mathbb R \times \mathbb R\), \(A = (-2\varepsilon, 2\varepsilon) \times \{2\} \cup \{(\varepsilon(1 - x), x) : 0 < x < 1\}\) has compact closure and compact non-empty fibres over \(|\lambda| \le \varepsilon\), but \(\{|p| \le \varepsilon\}\) contains the open segment, which accumulates at \((\varepsilon, 0) \notin A\), and neighbourhoods of radius less than half the distance to \((\varepsilon, 0)\) have no finite subfamily covering it. A countable subcover suffices: \(\mathbb R^m \times X\) is metrizable (Theorem 2.16) Chapter2/MetrizableMPolyfold.metrizableSpace, so the compact \(\overline A\), and with it \(A\), is separable, hence second countable; countably many of the neighbourhoods of the local step cover \(A\), the countable union of their null sets is null, and \(\Sigma = S \setminus \bigcup_i\mathrm{CV}(z_i)\) (Findings, item 103). Some countability is necessary: an uncountable discrete \(A\) can have critical values of positive measure; here it comes from the compactness of \(\overline A\), which the text assumes.

Theorem 4.23 Chapter4/Familiestheorem_4_23. Statement. Let \(X\) be tame, \(A \subseteq \mathbb R^m \times X\) a smooth finite-dimensional submanifold with tame induced structure and compact closure, \(\varepsilon > 0\), and (1) for \(|\lambda| \le \varepsilon\) (\(|\lambda|^2 = \sum\lambda_i^2\)) the set \(A \cap \{z_1 = \lambda\}\) is compact and non-empty, (2) \(A\) is in general position at every point. Then there is \(\Sigma \subseteq \{|\lambda| < \varepsilon\}\) with null complement in \(\{|\lambda| < \varepsilon\}\), consisting of stratified regular values, such that for \(\lambda \in \Sigma\) the fibre \(A_\lambda\) is compact, a smooth finite-dimensional submanifold of \(X\), in general position at each of its points, with a corner structure (Definition 4.1), and tame. Proof. The cover for \(S = \{|\lambda| < \varepsilon\}\). \(A_\lambda\) is the image of the compact \(A \cap \{z_1 = \lambda\}\) under the projection to \(X\), hence compact. It is a smooth finite-dimensional submanifold and in general position by the conclusions at its points; it is in good position at every point (Lemma 7.B), so Theorem 4.18 gives the corner structure and tameness. Hypothesis (2), misprinted in the text (“there exists a sc-complement \(T_zA\) in \(T_zZ\) which is contained in \(T^R_zZ\)”), is Definition 4.21, as the proof uses it. Not used: the tameness of the induced structure of \(A\), the non-emptiness in (1), \(\varepsilon > 0\) (Findings, item 101). Every stratified regular value is a regular value — \(T_zA \cap E_z \subseteq T_zA\) — so \(\Sigma\) consists of regular values in the text’s sense; but the conclusion is not true at every ordinary regular value (§IV.23).

IV.25 What is not formalized

  • Lemma 4.10 (the section \(u \mapsto (1 - p)(u - t(u))\) of \(U \triangleleft Y\) is sc-Fredholm): no longer used, since Proposition 4.9 is proved directly. It would need \(U \triangleleft Y\) as a strong bundle, \(Y\) and \(Y \cap F\) as sc-subspaces, a complement \(B\) of \(Y \cap F\) in \(Y\) chosen inside \(Y_\infty\) (an arbitrary algebraic complement does not give an sc-splitting), and at each smooth point the re-centred strong bundle chart (§IV.5), the trivial filler, the sc⁺-section \(s(v) = \mathbf f(u) + (1 - p)[t(u) - t(u + v)]\) and the conjugation of \(g - s = (1 - p)v\) to a basic germ with contraction part \(0\). The text’s proof has a sign slip in \(D\mathbf f(u)\), calls \(D\mathbf f(u)\) the sc⁺-operator where \(Dt(u)\) is meant, argues “a perturbation of the identity” for an operator into \(Y\), writes \(L(T_0O)\) for \(L(Y)\), and omits the interior points of \((T_0O \oplus B) \cap C\) (Findings, item 57).
  • §4.4 (Definitions 4.25, 4.27, Proposition 4.26, the exterior derivative, the relative complex, Theorem 4.28): it needs \(\oplus^kTX\) as an M-polyfold and a linear \(T_xX\) (gap G.7), the M-polyfolds \(X^i\) for \(i \ge 2\) (gap G.6), and integration on manifolds with corners of varying dimension. The text’s \(d : \Omega^k(X^{i+1}) \to \Omega^{k+1}(X^i)\) should presumably run \(\Omega^k(X^i) \to \Omega^{k+1}(X^{i+1})\), the bracket of Proposition 4.26 living one level up; \(d^2 = 0\) and \(dj^* = j^*d\) are asserted; forms on \(\partial X\) are not defined; and Theorem 4.28 has no proof (Findings, items 120–124).
  • The open question after Proposition 4.15 (§IV.11). For Remark 4.3 the example is formalized (§IV.27); the argument that an example cannot come from a retraction whose level maps are \(C^1\) is not.
  • The chart independence of stratified regularity (§IV.23), true by the transport argument of §IV.13, since transition maps of product charts are \(\mathrm{id} \times \tau\) up to translation; Theorem 4.23 does not need it.
  • The local form of Remark 4.14 near \(\{d_X = 0\}\) (§IV.11), the identification of the local faces of a chart with global faces in Theorem 4.22 (1) (§IV.17), and the classical manifold structure behind Definition 4.1 beyond the \(C^\infty\) transitions (§IV.1).

IV.26 What the formalization taught us

  1. Centred charts are a construction. They exist only at smooth points and live in the partial quadrant \(C_{\varphi(x)}\), on the set where it agrees with \(C\); four theorems of the chapter and Lemma 5.11 rely on them, and the text never builds them (§IV.5).
  2. Proposition 4.9 is a statement about fixed sets, and its proof is not the implicit function theorem. The text’s route, as we read it, gives a germ over a different complement from the one needed. The direct proof uses only the sc⁺ property — a mean value estimate on every level and the level-\(1\) continuity of \(t\) — and its regularity argument rests on two observations: the estimate is applied at \(\Gamma(a)\) with the frame \(B_{\Gamma(a)}\), not at \(0\), and derivatives of \(t\) only meet the finite-dimensional smooth tangent space, so the loss of levels does not accumulate (§§IV.6–IV.9). The projection must be the one along the closed good complement, not \(Dt(0)\).
  3. Theorem 4.2 does not need tameness, and its compatibility claim needs charts composed with sc-diffeomorphisms between retracts (§IV.10).
  4. The sc⁺ condition has to be read in charts, in both directions: a submanifold’s chart retraction is sc⁺ (§IV.11), and an sc⁺-retraction in a chart is one on an open set (§IV.18). Every statement of §§4.2–4.3 passes through these two facts.
  5. One step of Lemma 4.19 is false, and the repair is the observation that the complement of \(T_0O\) lies in \(C \cap (-C)\) at the corner of a centred chart (§IV.14).
  6. General position implies good position (§IV.16), a step the text uses in Theorem 4.22 (4) and Theorem 4.23 without stating it.
  7. Theorem 4.23 needs stratified regular values and a countable cover, and the fibre’s manifold structure needs the implicit function theorem at corner points with the kernel in good position — the argument of Lemma 5.26 — and Theorem 3.78 in \(C^\infty\) form (§§IV.21–IV.24). Sard’s theorem had to be supplied in all dimensions (§IV.20).

IV.27 Remark 4.3’s example: a retraction that loses a level

Remark 4.3 says that “\(X^1 \ne X\)” is possible as M-polyfolds although the underlying sets agree, and gives no example. By Proposition 4.8 in charts (§IV.4) an example is an sc-retract \(O = r(U)\) with \(O = O_\infty\) that is not an sc⁺-retract. It cannot come from a retraction whose level maps \(U_m \to E_m\) are \(C^1\) — the maps that Proposition 1.19, Corollary 1.20 and their composites produce: then \(T_oO = Dr(o)E_0\) is finite-dimensional by a Baire category argument (\(O\) is a countable union of the compact sets \(\mathrm{cl}_0\{x \in O : |x|_1 \le n\}\)), and the topologies of \(O\) in \(E_0\) and \(E_1\) agree near \(o\) (Findings 141; an argument, not formalized). So the retraction must lose a level in its first derivative, as the splicings of HWZ do, and its sc-smoothness needs a criterion the project did not have (Findings 140–146).

A criterion with loss. Let \(V\) be finite-dimensional and \(L(p)_m : Z_m \to W_m\), \(p \in V\), be bounded operators compatible with the inclusions, such that \((p, z) \mapsto L(p)_mz\) is continuous on \(V \times Z_m\) — strong continuity, not continuity of \(p \mapsto L(p)_m\) in the operator norm — and \(p \mapsto A_m(p) = L(p)_m \circ \iota\) is \(C^\infty\) as a map into the operators \(Z_{m+1} \to W_m\): one level of loss buys all the \(p\)-derivatives Chapter4/RemarkFourThreeExampleIsLossFamily Chapter4/RemarkFourThreeExamplefamLoss Chapter4/RemarkFourThreeExamplefamDeriv. Then \((p, z) \mapsto L(p)z\) is sc-smooth on \(V \oplus Z\) Chapter4/RemarkFourThreeExamplelossFamMap Chapter4/RemarkFourThreeExampleIsLossFamily.isScSmooth. The map is sc⁰ by the strong continuity Chapter4/RemarkFourThreeExampleIsLossFamily.isSc0, and sc¹ with derivative \((\pi, \zeta) \mapsto \partial_pA_0(p)[\pi]z + L(p)\zeta\) at a level-\(1\) point \((p, z)\) Chapter4/RemarkFourThreeExampleIsLossFamily.differentiable_famLoss Chapter4/RemarkFourThreeExampleIsLossFamily.isSc1With: the increment in \(p\) is taken in the operator norm of \(A_0\), which needs \(z \in Z_1\), and the derivative family is continuous on the tangent levels by the \(C^\infty\) dependence of \(\partial_pA_m\) Chapter4/RemarkFourThreeExampleIsLossFamily.continuous_famDeriv. The tangent map is again a map of the same kind: after the sc-isomorphism that reorders \((p, z, \pi, \zeta)\) as \(((p, \pi), (z, \zeta))\) Chapter4/RemarkFourThreeExamplefamSwap it is the map of the tangent family \(\tilde L(p, \pi)(z, \zeta) = (L(p)z, \partial_pA(p)[\pi]z + L(p)\zeta)\) on \(V \times V\) Chapter4/RemarkFourThreeExamplefamTangent Chapter4/RemarkFourThreeExampletangentMapWith_lossFamMap_eq, and \(\tilde L\) is a loss family Chapter4/RemarkFourThreeExampleIsLossFamily.tangent. Induction on \(k\) gives sc\(^k\) for every \(k\) Chapter4/RemarkFourThreeExampleisSck_lossFamMap. Only one level of loss is allowed: maps whose \(j\)-th derivative costs \(j\) levels, such as the map \((t, x) \mapsto (\cos(kt)x_k)_k\) of the example after Definition 1.14, are not covered.

The reduction. For a loss family of projections (\(L(p)_0^2 = L(p)_0\)), \(r(p, z) = (p, L(p)z)\) is an sc-smooth retraction of \(V \oplus Z\) Chapter4/RemarkFourThreeExampleIsLossFamily.isScSmooth_famRetr Chapter4/RemarkFourThreeExampleIsLossFamily.retraction; if the ranges of the \(L(p)_0\) are smooth points, \(O = O_\infty\) Chapter4/RemarkFourThreeExampleIsLossFamily.retract_subset_smooth; and if the lift \(O \to E_1\) is discontinuous, Proposition 4.8 says that \(O\) is not an sc⁺-retract Chapter4/RemarkFourThreeExampleIsLossFamily.not_isScPlusRetract. These are the data of the example Chapter4/RemarkFourThreeExampleRemarkFourThreeData Chapter4/RemarkFourThreeExampleexists_retract_smooth_not_scPlus_of_data.

The family. On the weighted sequence space \(X\) of the example after Definition 1.14 (\(|x|_m = \sup_k(k+1)^m|x_k|\); Chapter1/ScOneNotNormContinuousScOneExample.X) the moving vector must pass between coordinates of comparable weight, or the level-\(m\) operators are unbounded, so the transitions must be fast and the gain per step geometric: the indices are \(n_k = 2^k\) Chapter4/RemarkFourThreeFamilyRemarkFourThree.nk. With nodes \(1/(k+1)\) Chapter4/RemarkFourThreeFamilyRemarkFourThree.node and angles \(\theta_k(t)\) turning from \(0\) (for \(t \ge 1/(k+1)\)) to \(\pi/2\) (for \(t \le 1/(k+2)\)) through Mathlib’s smooth transition, flat at both ends Mathlib/Analysis/SpecialFunctions/SmoothTransitionReal.smoothTransition, the coefficients \(b_k = \sin\theta_{k-1}\cos\theta_k\) Chapter4/RemarkFourThreeFamilyRemarkFourThree.bb vanish except \(b_k = \cos\theta_k\) and \(b_{k+1} = \sin\theta_k\) at the active block \(k = \lfloor 1/t\rfloor - 1\) Chapter4/RemarkFourThreeFamilyRemarkFourThree.bb_eq_zero_of_pos Chapter4/RemarkFourThreeFamilyRemarkFourThree.bb_kt Chapter4/RemarkFourThreeFamilyRemarkFourThree.bb_kt_succ, and all vanish for \(t \le 0\). \(L(t) = \sum_k\) (block \(k\)) Chapter4/RemarkFourThreeFamilyRemarkFourThree.blk Chapter4/RemarkFourThreeFamilyRemarkFourThree.fam is a sum with two non-zero terms, which on level \(0\) is the projection onto \(b_ke_{n_k} + b_{k+1}e_{n_{k+1}}\) Chapter4/RemarkFourThreeFamilyRemarkFourThree.fam_of_pos; on level \(m\) its entries carry the weight ratios \(((a+1)/(b+1))^m \le 2^m\) Chapter4/RemarkFourThreeFamilyRemarkFourThree.elemL. It is a loss family Chapter4/RemarkFourThreeFamilyRemarkFourThree.isLossFamily_fam: compatible with the inclusions Chapter4/RemarkFourThreeFamilyRemarkFourThree.toBase_fam; uniformly bounded, \(\|L(t)_m\| \le 3 + 2^m\) Chapter4/RemarkFourThreeFamilyRemarkFourThree.norm_fam_le; strongly continuous, from the bound and the norm continuity after the dense inclusion by an \(\varepsilon/3\) argument Chapter4/RemarkFourThreeFamilyRemarkFourThree.continuous_apply_of_bound; and \(t \mapsto L(t)_m \circ \iota\) is \(C^\infty\) in the operator norm, by Mathlib’s differentiation of series Mathlib/Analysis/Calculus/SmoothSeriescontDiff_tsum: \(j\) derivatives of block \(k\) are bounded by a polynomial in \(k\) of degree \(2j\) (Leibniz’s rule and the derivatives of the flat transition), while one level of loss gains a factor \((2 + 2^m)2^{-k}\) Chapter4/RemarkFourThreeFamilyRemarkFourThree.contDiff_fam_comp. Every \(L(t)_0\) is a projection Chapter4/RemarkFourThreeFamilyRemarkFourThree.fam_idem with finitely supported, hence smooth, range Chapter4/RemarkFourThreeFamilyRemarkFourThree.fam_mem_smooth. The lift is discontinuous: the points \(o_k = (1/(k+1), (1/(k+1))e_{n_k})\) lie in \(O\) Chapter4/RemarkFourThreeFamilyRemarkFourThree.fam_node_smul_δv and tend to \(0\) in \(E_0\), while their level-\(1\) coordinates \((2^k + 1)/(k + 1)\,e_{n_k}\) have norm at least \(1\) Chapter4/RemarkFourThreeFamilyRemarkFourThree.not_continuousOn_liftOne. So the data exist Chapter4/RemarkFourThreeFamilyRemarkFourThree.remarkFourThreeData, and there is an sc-retract \(O = O_\infty\) that is not an sc⁺-retract Chapter4/RemarkFourThreeFamilyremark_4_3_retract_example.

The M-polyfold. A retract with its single chart \(O \to O\) is an M-polyfold Chapter4/RemarkFourThreeFamilyretractChart Chapter4/RemarkFourThreeFamilyretractPolyfold; if \(O \subseteq E_\infty\) and \(O\) is not an sc⁺-retract, every point of it is smooth and \(1_0^1 : X \to X^1\) is not sc-smooth, for every junk value (Proposition 4.8 in charts, §IV.4) Chapter4/RemarkFourThreeFamilyretractPolyfold_smooth_not_toLevelOne. Remark 4.3’s example Chapter4/RemarkFourThreeFamilyremark_4_3_example: there is an M-polyfold with \(X_0 = X_\infty\) for which \(1_0^1\) is not sc-smooth, hence (by the remark’s first part, §IV.4) not an sc-diffeomorphism: \(X^1 \ne X\) as M-polyfolds. In this example \(X\) and \(X^1\) even carry different topologies on the same set, since \(o_k \to 0\) in \(X\) and not in \(X^1\). “\(X^1 \ne X\)” is read as “\(1_0^1\) is not sc-smooth”; the M-polyfold is a single retract, which is all the remark needs; its parameter space is \(\mathbb R\) and its partial quadrant all of \(\mathbb R \oplus X\), so there is no boundary.

← Part III. Sc-Fredholm theory and the implicit function theorem (HWZ Chapter 3, §§3.1–3.8)Part V. The Fredholm package for M-polyfolds (HWZ Chapter 5, §§5.1–5.4) →

Part V. The Fredholm package for M-polyfolds (HWZ Chapter 5, §§5.1–5.4)

Chapter 5 turns the implicit function theorems of Chapter 3 into the working tools of a Fredholm theory: a way to measure perturbations (auxiliary norms, §5.1), the compactness that keeps the solution sets of small perturbations under control (§5.2), a supply of perturbations built from sc-smooth bump functions (the start of §5.3), and the perturbation theorems themselves — transversality when there is no boundary (Theorem 5.13), general position (Theorem 5.18), good position relative to the boundary (Theorems 5.19, 5.25), and the lemmas of the Morse-type Theorem 5.22. Appendix 5.4.1 proves Theorem 5.5; Appendix 5.4.2 relates sc-smooth bump functions and partitions of unity to the geometry of Banach spaces. This Part retells §5.1 (§§V.1–V.3); §5.2 with Appendix 5.4.1 (§§V.4–V.7), the longest retelling being Theorem 5.5 (§§V.5–V.6); the start of §5.3 — bump functions, the calculus of sections, Lemma 5.11, allowable sections (§§V.8–V.10); Theorem 5.13 (§§V.11–V.15); general position, Lemma 5.26 and Theorem 5.18 (§§V.16–V.20); Theorems 5.25 and 5.19 (§§V.21–V.22); the homotopy lemmas (§V.23); Appendix 5.4.2 (§§V.24–V.26); what is not formalized (§V.27); and what the formalization taught us (§V.28). A fourth addendum adds Corollary 5.8 on the shifted strong bundle (§V.29), the metric space of the allowable sections (§V.30) and weak against pointwise bump functions (§V.31).

What is proved, and what is not. Theorems 5.5, 5.6, 5.7, 5.13, 5.18, 5.19, 5.25, 5.34 and 5.37 are proved, Theorems 5.5–5.7 without tameness; so are Lemmas 5.2, 5.11, 5.23, 5.24, 5.26, Propositions 5.3, 5.10, 5.30, 5.35, 5.38, 5.42, Remark 5.12 and Corollary 5.44, the last with Theorem 5.43 as an explicit hypothesis. Every definition of the chapter is formalized. Corollary 5.8 is proved on the shifted strong bundle \(P^1 : Y^1 \to X^1\), which the text uses without defining it, and by iteration for every fixed \(i\), with the filler condition on level \(1\) that its “it is a priori clear” hides (§V.29). The perturbation theorems take \(f\) with tame germ data (Definition 3.51), the reading of the tame strong bundle with which §5.3 opens and the hypothesis under which the §3.6 implicit function theorems are proved since their repair (Part III, Findings of Chapter 3, items 190–199); Theorem 5.18 also assumes \(X\) tame, which its proof uses through Theorems 4.22 and 4.23. The metric space \((\Gamma^{+,1}_U(P), \rho)\) is built, and the text’s “not complete” turns out to need a hypothesis (§V.30). Not formalized: Theorems 5.22, 5.27, Remarks 5.14, 5.16, 5.21, the cited Theorems 5.32, 5.40, 5.43, the Sobolev remark, a dense form of Theorem 5.19, and Corollary 5.8 as one statement for a family indexed by \(i\) (§V.27).

Four structural choices. (1) The linearization is read in charts. \(T_xX\) carries no linear structure in the formalization (gap G.7 of Chapter 2), so \(f'(x)\) is the operator \(\mathrm{Lin}(z) : T_zO \to K_z\) of a strong bundle chart (Part III), transversality is surjectivity of \(\mathrm{Lin}\) in a chart, and general position is stated in a tame chart; its chart independence is proved where it matters (§V.18). (2) “Generic” is “off a null set”. Every perturbation theorem is proved first in a generic form — for \(\lambda\) outside a Lebesgue null set of a small ball, \(s_0 + \sum\lambda_it_i\) does the job — and the text’s dense-set form is derived from it. (3) The parametrized solution set is not built as a manifold. The Sard step is local: at each zero of \(F(\lambda, y) = g(y) + \sum\lambda_it_i(y)\) in good position, Theorem 3.54 (2) gives a regular tangent germ chart, Sard’s theorem is applied on its finite-dimensional model, and finitely many null sets are collected (§V.14). Where Theorem 4.23 needs a submanifold, the bridge lemma supplies it (§V.17). (4) Density is pointwise. “Within \(\varepsilon\)” is \(N(s(x) - s'(x)) \le \varepsilon\) for all \(x\); this is \(\rho(s, s') \le \varepsilon\) for the metric \(\rho(s, s') = \sup_xN(s(x) - s'(x))\), which the perturbation theorems never needed and which was built afterwards (§V.30).

Map.

  • Chapter5/AuxNorm: the charts \(\Phi[1]\), the fibre \((Y_{0,1})_x\) and its chart norms, Definition 5.1, Lemma 5.2, Proposition 5.3.
  • Chapter5/Compactness: Definition 5.4, Theorems 5.5–5.7, Corollary 5.8 in a chart, Remark 5.12.
  • Chapter5/BumpFunctions: \(\mathbb R\) as an M-polyfold, Definitions 5.9, 5.29, 5.33, Propositions 5.10, 5.30, 5.35, Theorem 5.34, the calculus of sections, Lemma 5.11, \(\Gamma^{+,1}_U(P)\).
  • Chapter5/Transversality: Definitions 5.15, 5.17, Lemma 5.26, the parametrized section, the Sard step, Theorem 5.13.
  • Chapter5/GeneralPosition: the bridge lemma, \(T_yS = \ker f'(y)\), chart independence and openness of general position, properties (i)–(ii), Theorems 5.18, 5.19, 5.25.
  • Chapter5/Homotopy: Definition 5.20, Lemmas 5.23, 5.24.
  • Chapter5/PartitionsOfUnity: the algebra of sc-smooth functions, Definitions 5.28, 5.31, 5.36, 5.39, 5.41, Theorem 5.37, Propositions 5.38, 5.42, Corollary 5.44, the statements of Theorems 5.40, 5.43.
  • Added in the fourth addendum (§§V.29–V.31): Chapter5/StrongBundleShift (the shifted strong bundle \(P^1\), raising the index of sc-smooth maps and sections), Chapter5/Corollary58 (the filler condition on every level, Corollary 5.8), Chapter5/AllowableSectionsMetric (the metric \(\rho\), completeness and its failure), Chapter5/BumpWeakPointwise (bump points, an sc-Banach space as an M-polyfold).

Throughout, \(P : Y \to X\) is a strong bundle over an M-polyfold (both paracompact and Hausdorff), a section is a map \(s : X \to Y\) with \(P \circ s = \mathrm{id}\), \(0_x\) is the zero of the fibre over \(x\), and \(\operatorname{supp}s\) is the closure of \(\{s \ne 0\}\) Chapter5/BumpFunctionssectionSupport. A strong bundle chart \(\Phi\) has base chart \(\varphi : V \to O\), \(O = r(U)\) a retract, and local bundle \(K \to O\); the principal part of \(f\) is \(\hat f(u) = \Phi(f(\varphi^{-1}(u)))_2\), and \(\mathrm{Lin}(z)\) is its linearization at a level-\(1\) point \(z\) (Part III). \(|\lambda|\) is the maximum norm on \(\mathbb R^m\).

V.1 The fibre \(Y_{0,1}\) and the charts \(\Phi[1]\)

§5.1 works on the part \(Y_{0,1}\) of biregularity \((0, 1)\), the M-polyfold \(Y[1]\) of §2.5 (Part II), and assumes two things the project did not have: charts \(\Phi[1]\) for every strong bundle chart, and a Banach structure on the fibres of \(Y_{0,1}\).

\(Y_{0,1}\) in any chart. For a strong bundle chart \(\Phi\) compatible with the atlas — the text’s “strong bundle isomorphism \(\Phi : Y|V \to K\)” — a point \(y\) over \(\operatorname{dom}\varphi\) lies in \(Y_{0,1}\) iff \(\Phi(y)_2 \in F_1\): compare with a chart of the atlas through the transition map, which is a strong bundle map and so preserves biregularity Chapter5/AuxNormStrongBundle.mem_oneSet_iff_of_isChart. On \(P^{-1}(V) \cap Y_{0,1}\) the map \(w \mapsto \Phi(w)\) lifted to \(K[1]\) is then a partial homeomorphism Chapter5/AuxNormStrongBundle.oneChartOf, compatible with every chart \(\Phi'[1]\) of the atlas because the transition is the \([1]\)-transition of Definition 2.50 Chapter5/AuxNormStrongBundle.oneChartOf_transition Chapter5/AuxNormStrongBundle.oneChartOf_compatible, hence a chart of the M-polyfold \(Y[1]\) Chapter5/AuxNormStrongBundle.isChart_oneChartOf. For a chart of the atlas it is the chart of Part II Chapter5/AuxNormStrongBundle.oneChart_eq_oneChartOf.

The fibre. The fibres \(P^{-1}(x)\) carry linear structures; the points of \(P^{-1}(x)\) in \(Y_{0,1}\) form a linear subspace \((Y_{0,1})_x\), because the charts are linear on the fibres and \(F_1 \subseteq F_0\) is a subspace Chapter5/AuxNormStrongBundle.oneFiber. Its points are points of \(Y[1]\) and conversely Chapter5/AuxNormStrongBundle.toOne Chapter5/AuxNormStrongBundle.ofOne; its zero is the point \(0_x\) of \(Y[1]\) Chapter5/AuxNormStrongBundle.zeroOne Chapter5/AuxNormStrongBundle.fiberZero_mem_oneSet.

The chart norm \(|h|_1\). In a chart around \(x\), the fibre component of \(\Phi[1]\) is a linear map \((Y_{0,1})_x \to F_1\) Chapter5/AuxNormStrongBundle.liftOneFiber, injective because \(\Phi\) is injective on the fibre Chapter5/AuxNormStrongBundle.liftOneFiber_injective. Its image is the slice \(\{h \in F_1 \mid (\varphi(x), h) \in K[1]\}\) Chapter5/AuxNormStrongBundle.mem_range_liftOneFiber, the fixed point set of the continuous map \(h \mapsto R[1](\varphi(x), h)\), hence closed in \(F_1\) Chapter5/AuxNormStrongBundle.isClosed_slice. So a sequence of the fibre that is Cauchy for \(|\Phi[1](\cdot)_2|_1\) converges: its images converge in \(F_1\), the limit stays in the slice, and it is the image of a point of the fibre Chapter5/AuxNormStrongBundle.complete_liftOneFiber. This is the text’s “the fibers \(Y_x\) have the structure of Banach spaces”. The norm depends on the chart, but only up to equivalence, and locally uniformly: by Lemma 5.2’s upper bound (§V.2) applied to \(g = |\Phi_1[1](\cdot)_2|_1\), the norms of two charts are comparable with one constant on the fibres over a neighbourhood of \(x\) Chapter5/AuxNormStrongBundle.exists_norm_liftOne_le_mul, and so are finitely many charts and one more Chapter5/AuxNormStrongBundle.exists_uniform_comparison.

V.2 Auxiliary norms and Lemma 5.2

Definition 5.1. A function \(N : Y[1] \to \mathbb R\) is a complete norm on the fibre over \(x\) if \(N(v) = 0\) only for \(v = 0\), \(N(tv) = |t|N(v)\), \(N(v + w) \le N(v) + N(w)\), and every \(N\)-Cauchy sequence of \((Y_{0,1})_x\) converges Chapter5/AuxNormStrongBundle.IsCompleteFiberNorm. An auxiliary norm is a continuous such \(N\), complete on every fibre, with condition (2): if \(P(w_k) \to x\) and \(N(w_k) \to 0\), then \(w_k \to 0_x\) in \(Y[1]\) Chapter5/AuxNormStrongBundle.IsAuxNorm. It is non-negative Chapter5/AuxNormStrongBundle.IsAuxNorm.nonneg and homogeneous on the fibres Chapter5/AuxNormStrongBundle.IsAuxNorm.smul.

Lemma 5.2, the upper bound. Let \(g : Y[1] \to \mathbb R\) be continuous at \(0_x\) and positively homogeneous on the fibres near \(x\), and \(\Phi\) a chart around \(x\). By continuity at \(0_x\) — read through the chart \(\Phi[1]\), whose neighbourhoods of \((\varphi(x), 0)\) are the sets \(|p - \varphi(x)|_0 + |h|_1 < \varepsilon\) — \(g < 1\) where \(|p - \varphi(x)|_0 < \varepsilon/2\) and \(|h|_1 \le \varepsilon/2\); homogeneity scales every vector of a nearby fibre to \(|h|_1 = \varepsilon/2\), which gives \(g(w) \le (2/\varepsilon)|h|_1\) on the fibres over a neighbourhood \(V\) of \(x\) Chapter5/AuxNormStrongBundle.exists_le_mul_norm_liftOne. This is the text’s first half of “(i) ⇒ (ii)”.

Lemma 5.2, the lower bound. For an auxiliary norm, \(|h|_1 \le A\,N(w)\) near \(x\) Chapter5/AuxNormStrongBundle.IsAuxNorm.exists_norm_liftOne_le. Suppose not: then for every \(k\) there is \(w_k\) over \(\varphi^{-1}(B(\varphi(x), 1/(k + 1)))\) with \(|h_k|_1 > (k + 1)N(w_k)\); rescale to \(|h_k|_1 = 1\). Then \(N(w_k) \to 0\) and \(P(w_k) \to x\) — the points of the shrinking balls converge to \(x\) because \(\varphi^{-1}\) is continuous on \(O\), so no metrizability of \(X\) is needed — hence \(w_k \to 0_x\) by condition (2), and \(\Phi[1](w_k) \to (\varphi(x), 0)\) by the continuity of \(\Phi[1]\), contradicting \(|h_k|_1 = 1\). Together: in every chart around \(x\) there are a neighbourhood \(V\) and \(0 < a < A\) with \(aN(w) \le |h|_1 \le AN(w)\) over \(V\) Chapter5/AuxNormStrongBundle.IsAuxNorm.exists_bounds.

Lemma 5.2. For \(N\) continuous and a complete norm on every fibre, \(N\) is an auxiliary norm iff every \(x\) has a chart and such two-sided bounds near \(x\) Chapter5/AuxNormlemma_5_2. “(i) ⇒ (ii)” is the previous paragraph. “(ii) ⇒ (i)”, “obvious” in the text: if \(P(w_k) \to x\) and \(N(w_k) \to 0\), the bound gives \(|h_k|_1 \to 0\), so \(\Phi[1](w_k) \to (\varphi(x), 0)\), and \(w_k \to 0_x\) because \(\Phi[1]^{-1}\) is continuous on \(K[1]\) (§V.1). In the statement \(V\) is a neighbourhood of \(x\) on which the bounds hold; the text’s \(V\) is the domain of \(\Phi\), but its own proof gives them “for \(P(w)\) close to \(x\)”.

V.3 Proposition 5.3

Existence. For the charts \(\Phi_i\) of the atlas and a partition of unity \((\rho_i)\) subordinate to their domains — it exists since \(X\) is paracompact and Hausdorff, hence normal Mathlib/Topology/PartitionOfUnityPartitionOfUnity.exists_isSubordinate — the glued norm is \(N(w) = \sum_i\rho_i(P(w))\,|\Phi_i[1](w)_2|_1\) Chapter5/AuxNormStrongBundle.gluedNorm Chapter5/AuxNormStrongBundle.gluedNorm_eq_sum. It is continuous on \(Y[1]\): each term vanishes off the closed set \(P^{-1}(\operatorname{supp}\rho_i)\), which lies in the open domain of \(\Phi_i[1]\), where the term is continuous, and the sum is locally finite Chapter5/AuxNormStrongBundle.continuous_gluedNorm. Near a point \(x\) only finitely many \(\rho_i\) are non-zero, all with \(x\) in the domain of \(\Phi_i\) and summing to \(1\) Chapter5/AuxNormStrongBundle.sum_partition_eq_one; their chart norms are uniformly comparable with the norm of any one chart \(\Phi'\) around \(x\) (§V.1), so \(N\) is two-sided comparable with \(|\Phi'[1](\cdot)_2|_1\) near \(x\) Chapter5/AuxNormStrongBundle.gluedNorm_bounds. On each fibre \(N\) is a convex combination of norms, hence a norm, and comparable with a complete norm, hence complete Chapter5/AuxNormStrongBundle.complete_of_bounds Chapter5/AuxNormStrongBundle.isCompleteFiberNorm_gluedNorm. Lemma 5.2 “(ii) ⇒ (i)” concludes Chapter5/AuxNormproposition_5_3_exists. The text gives this as one sentence.

Comparison. For auxiliary norms \(N_0\), \(N_1\), Lemma 5.2 “(i) ⇒ (ii)” for both in the same chart around \(y\) — which is why “(i) ⇒ (ii)” was proved in every chart — gives \(r_y > 0\) with \(r_yN_0 \le N_1\) and \(r_yN_1 \le N_0\) over a neighbourhood of \(y\). At each point the admissible constants \(r\) form a convex set (\(r\) admissible and \(0 < r' \le r\) give \(r'\) admissible), so a partition of unity glues the local constants into a continuous \(f > 0\) with values in these sets Mathlib/Analysis/Convex/PartitionOfUnityexists_continuous_forall_mem_convex_of_local_const, and \(f(x)N_0 \le N_1 \le f(x)^{-1}N_0\) on the fibre over \(x\) Chapter5/AuxNormproposition_5_3_compare. Tameness plays no role in §5.1.

V.4 Definition 5.4 and proper sections

“\(N(y) \le r\)” for a point \(y\) of \(Y\) is read with the text’s convention \(N(y) = \infty\) off \(Y_{0,1}\): it means \(y \in Y_{0,1}\) and \(N(y) \le r\) Chapter5/CompactnessStrongBundle.AuxLe, a property of the point only Chapter5/CompactnessStrongBundle.AuxLe.congr. A section \(f\) is weakly proper if \(f^{-1}(0)\) is compact and for every auxiliary norm \(N\) there is an open \(U \supseteq f^{-1}(0)\) such that \(\{f = s\}\) is compact for every sc⁺-section \(s\) with support in \(U\) and \(N(s) \le 1\) Chapter5/CompactnessStrongBundle.IsWeaklyProper; proper if instead \(\operatorname{cl}_X\{x \in U \mid N(f(x)) \le 1\}\) is compact Chapter5/CompactnessStrongBundle.IsProper.

Proper implies weakly proper for a continuous \(f\) Chapter5/CompactnessStrongBundle.IsProper.isWeaklyProper. Take the \(U\) of properness. A solution of \(f(x) = s(x)\) outside \(U\) has \(s(x) = 0\), so \(f(x) = 0\) and \(x \in f^{-1}(0) \subseteq U\) after all; inside \(U\), \(f(x) = s(x)\) gives \(N(f(x)) = N(s(x)) \le 1\). So \(\{f = s\}\) lies in the compact closure, and it is closed because \(f\) and \(s\) are continuous and \(Y\) is Hausdorff. Weakly proper sections have compact solution sets by definition Chapter5/CompactnessStrongBundle.IsWeaklyProper.isCompact_solutionSet. The text’s “obviously” hides the continuity of \(f\).

V.5 Theorem 5.5: the local form for basic germs

Theorem 5.5 says that for sc-Fredholm sections a compact solution set already forces properness. The appendix proves it in the coordinates of a basic germ, and that local statement is the heart of the matter.

The setting. A basic germ (Definition 3.7, Part III) is \(h : \tilde C \oplus W \supseteq U_0 \to \mathbb R^N \oplus W\) whose \(W\)-component is \(w - B(a, w)\), where \(B\) is an sc⁰-contraction germ: on small balls, \(w \mapsto B(a, w)\) contracts with constant \(\le 1/2\) on level \(0\), uniformly in \(a\), and \(B(0, 0) = 0\). Part III built the parametrized fixed point \(\delta(a, z)\), the unique solution \(w\) in a closed ball \(\bar B(r)\) of \(w = B(a, w) - z\) for \((a, z)\) in a set \(\Sigma\) of small parameters, continuous in \((a, z)\) on level \(0\) Chapter3/LocalCompactnessIsSc0ContractionGerm.delta_continuousOn Chapter5/CompactnessIsSc0ContractionGerm.eq_delta_zero.

The local form Chapter5/CompactnessIsSc0ContractionGerm.exists_isCompact_bdd. Assume \(\tilde C\) closed. There is an open \(O \ni 0\), independent of \(c\), such that for every \(c\) the points \(x = (a, w) \in U_0 \cap O\) with \(w - B(a, w) \in W_1\) and \(|w - B(a, w)|_1 \le c\) lie in a compact set. The proof:

  1. A small ball. \(B(a, w) - w\) is continuous at \(0\) within \(U_0\) and vanishes there, so for \(|(a, w)|_0 < \rho_1\) it has norm \(< r/8\). Let \(\rho = \min(\rho_1, \rho'/2, r/2)\), with \(\rho'\) the radius of the parameter set, and \(O = B(0, \rho)\).
  2. The compact set of parameters. The inclusion \(W_1 \to W_0\) is compact, so the image of the closed level-\(1\) ball of radius \(c\) lies in a compact \(K_c \subseteq W_0\). The set \(L = (\tilde C \cap \bar B(\rho)) \times (K_c \cap \bar B(r/8))\) is compact (here \(\tilde C\) closed is used) and lies in \(\Sigma\).
  3. The candidate. The compact set is the image of \(L\) under the continuous map \((a, z) \mapsto (a, \delta(a, z))\).
  4. Every bounded point is hit. Let \(x = (a, w) \in U_0 \cap O\) with \(w - B(a, w) = \iota(z_1)\), \(|z_1|_1 \le c\). Put \(p = (a, B(a, w) - w)\). Then \(a \in \tilde C\) with \(|a| < \rho\); \(B(a, w) - w = \iota(-z_1)\) lies in \(K_c\) and has norm \(< r/8\) by step 1; so \(p \in L\). And \(w\) lies in the ball \(\bar B(r)\) and solves \(w = B(a, w) - (B(a, w) - w)\), so \(w = \delta(p)\) by uniqueness Chapter5/CompactnessIsSc0ContractionGerm.eq_delta_zero, i.e. \(x\) is the image of \(p\).

Only the level-\(0\) contraction is used. For a basic germ \(f\) itself the \(W\)-component of \(f(x)\) is \(w - B(a, w)\), so the same \(O\) works with the level-\(1\) bound \(|f(x)|_1 \le c\) Chapter5/CompactnessIsBasicGerm.exists_isCompact_bdd. This is the appendix’s (82)–(90), where the text writes “\(a \in \mathbb R^n\)” for \(a \in \tilde C\) (\(B\) is defined on \(\tilde C \oplus W\) only), “\(\mathbb R^n \oplus Y_1\)” for \(\mathbb R^N \oplus W_1\), and in (89) mixes the \(\mathbb R^N\)- and \(W\)-components; the \(t\) of its “\(h + t\)” and its estimates (83), (85) disappear in the next step.

V.6 Theorem 5.5: the local step and the covering

Uniform fibre bounds. A strong bundle map \(\Psi\) (Definition 2.47) is linear on the fibres and \(\Psi[1]\) is continuous; at \((u_0, 0)\), where \(\Psi[1](u_0, 0)_2 = 0\) Chapter5/CompactnessIsStrongBundleMap.shiftFiber_snd_zero, continuity gives \(|\Psi[1](u, k)_2|_1 \le 1\) for \(|u - u_0|_0 < \delta\), \(|k|_1 \le \eta\), and fibre linearity Chapter5/CompactnessIsStrongBundleMap.shiftFiber_snd_smul turns this into \(|\Psi[1](u, k)_2|_1 \le \eta^{-1}|k|_1\) for all \(k \in F_1\) Chapter5/CompactnessIsStrongBundleMap.exists_fiber_bound_one. The text uses this bound silently when it replaces \(N(f(x)) \le 1\) by a bound in basic germ coordinates.

The local step Chapter5/Compactnessexists_nbhd_isCompact_closure_bdd. Let \((f, x_0)\) be an sc-Fredholm germ (Definition 3.11) — \(x_0\) need not be a zero. Its data, in the text’s germ reading (§III.6): a strong bundle chart \(\Phi\) centred at \(x_0\), a filling germ \(g\) of the principal part \(\hat f\) on a germ inside the domain \(U\) of the retraction, an sc⁺-germ \(t_0\) on a germ \(G_s\), and a strong bundle isomorphism \(\Psi\) with base map \(\psi\) conjugating \(g - t_0\) to a basic germ \(h\): \(h(\psi(u)) = \Psi(u, g(u) - t_0(u))_2\) for \(u \in U\) near \(0\). The claim is an open \(V \ni x_0\), independent of \(C\), such that for every \(C\) the closure in \(X\) of \(Z_C = \{x \in V \mid |\Phi(f(x))_2|_1 \le C\}\) is compact.

  1. The neighbourhood. Near \(0\) the filler agrees with the principal part on \(O\) and the conjugation identity holds (a set \(N_1\)); \(t_0\) is continuous into \(F_1\) on level \(0\) of its germ, \((G_s)_0 = O_s \cap C\) with \(O_s\) open — not on \(U\) — so the neighbourhood is also cut with \(O_s\), and \(|t_0(u)|_1 \le |t_0(0)|_1 + 1\) for \(u \in U \cap O_s\), \(|u|_0 < \delta_2\) (with \(t_0\) sc-smooth on \(U\) the cut was not needed); the fibre bound of \(\Psi\) holds for \(|u|_0 < \delta_3\) with constant \(M\). On the side of the basic germ, the local form (§V.5) gives an open \(O'\); \(\psi\) maps a neighbourhood of \(0\) into a closed ball \(\bar B(r_0) \cap C'\) inside the domain \(U'\) of \(\psi^{-1}\) (relative openness of \(U'\)). \(V\) is the set of points of the chart domain whose image lies in all of these.
  2. The bound transported. For \(x \in Z_C\), \(u = \varphi(x) \in O\), \(g(u) = \hat f(u)\) lies in \(F_1\) with \(|g(u)|_1 \le C\), so \(|g(u) - t_0(u)|_1 \le C + |t_0(0)|_1 + 1\), and \(|h(\psi(u))|_1 = |\Psi[1](u, g(u) - t_0(u))_2|_1 \le M(C + |t_0(0)|_1 + 1) =: c'\). Subtracting the sc⁺-part before the conjugation is what makes the text’s \(t\) and its estimates unnecessary, and the neighbourhood independent of \(C\).
  3. Compactness on the side of the basic germ. So \(\psi(\varphi(Z_C))\) lies in the compact set \(K_{c'}\) of the local form, intersected with the closed ball \(\bar B(r_0) \cap C'\); its closure \(A\) is compact and inside \(U'\).
  4. Back to \(U\). \(\psi^{-1}\) is continuous on \(U'\), so \(T = \psi^{-1}(A)\) is compact, contains \(\varphi(Z_C)\) and lies in \(U\).
  5. Back to \(O\). The closure of \(\varphi(Z_C)\) lies in \(T \subseteq U\) and in the closure of \(O\); since \(O\) is the fixed point set of the continuous retraction \(r\) on \(U\), it is closed in \(U\), so the closure lies in \(O\).
  6. Back to \(X\). \(\varphi^{-1}\) is continuous on \(O\), so \(\varphi^{-1}\) of that closure is compact and contains \(Z_C\), hence its closure.

The text’s “it suffices to find in local coordinates an open neighborhood” leaves steps 4–6 implicit: its set \(\{(a, w) \in U \mid |(h + t)(a, w)|_1 \le c\}\) lives in the chart domain \(U\) of the filling, which contains points not in the retract.

Theorem 5.5 Chapter5/Compactnesstheorem_5_5. Let \(f\) be sc-Fredholm with compact solution set, and \(N\) an auxiliary norm. At each zero \(x\) the germ \((f, x)\) is sc-Fredholm, so the local step gives a chart \(\Phi\) and an open \(V(x)\); Lemma 5.2’s lower bound in that chart Chapter5/AuxNormStrongBundle.IsAuxNorm.exists_norm_liftOne_le gives \(V_1(x)\) and \(A\) with \(|\Phi(w)_2|_1 \le A\,N(w)\) over \(V_1(x)\), so on \(V(x) \cap V_1(x)\) the condition \(N(f(y)) \le 1\) implies \(|\Phi(f(y))_2|_1 \le A\), and \(\operatorname{cl}\{y \in V(x) \cap V_1(x) \mid N(f(y)) \le 1\}\) is a closed subset of a compact set. Finitely many of these neighbourhoods cover the compact \(f^{-1}(0)\); their union is \(U\), and the closure of \(\{y \in U \mid N(f(y)) \le 1\}\) lies in the finite union of the compact closures. That is the text’s last sentence, “since the solution set of \(f\) is compact, the proof is complete”. Tameness is not used, as in the appendix’s statement of the theorem.

The equivalence. For an sc-Fredholm section, which is continuous, proper ⇒ weakly proper (§V.4) ⇒ compact solution set ⇒ proper (Theorem 5.5) Chapter5/Compactnesstheorem_5_5_iff.

V.7 Theorems 5.6, 5.7 and Corollary 5.8

Theorem 5.6 is Theorem 3.12 at a zero: a zero of an sc-Fredholm section is a smooth point (regularizing), where \((f, x)\) is an sc-Fredholm germ, and Theorem 3.12 gives nested open \(U(i) \ni x\) with \(\operatorname{cl}\{y \in U(i) \mid f(y) = 0\}\) the image of a compact subset of \(X_i\) Chapter3/SectionCompactnessGtheorem_3_12 Chapter5/Compactnesstheorem_5_6.

The space \(X_\infty\). The text says “\(X_\infty\) is a metric space” but never gives it a topology. It is the set of smooth points with the initial topology of the inclusions \(X_\infty \to X_m\) Chapter2/MetrizableMPolyfold.smoothLevel_topology_eq, metrizable by Theorem 2.16 Chapter2/MetrizableMPolyfold.metrizableSpace_smoothLevel, and a sequence converges in it iff it converges on every level Chapter5/CompactnessMPolyfold.tendsto_smoothLevel_iff; the inclusions into \(X\) and into each \(X_i\) are continuous Chapter5/CompactnessMPolyfold.continuous_smoothVal Chapter5/CompactnessMPolyfold.continuous_smoothIncl.

Theorem 5.7 Chapter5/Compactnesstheorem_5_7. \(S = f^{-1}(0)\) lies in \(X_\infty\) because \(f\) is regularizing. Take a sequence \((x_k)\) in \(S\); a subsequence converges in \(X\) to some \(x\). The limit is a zero, since a limit of zeros of a continuous section is a zero Chapter3/SectionCompactnessStrongBundle.IsScSmoothSection.isZeroAt_of_tendsto, so it is smooth and \((f, x)\) is an sc-Fredholm germ. Now Corollary 3.13 at the point \(x\) gives the convergence \(x_k \to x\) on every level Chapter3/Chapter5BridgeGcorollary_3_13_section, hence in \(X_\infty\). The text cites Theorem 5.6, which gives compactness in \(X_i\), not the convergence of a given sequence. Tameness is not used.

Corollary 5.8, the compact solution set. The zeros in \(X_i\) are the image of the compact subset of \(X_\infty\) of Theorem 5.7 under the continuous inclusion \(X_\infty \to X_i\) Chapter5/CompactnessisCompact_solutionSet_level.

Corollary 5.8 in a chart. “It is a priori clear that \(f^i\) is sc-Fredholm” is not clear, and \(Y^i \to X^i\) is not defined in the text. What is formalized is the shift of the germ data. A basic germ \(f\) on \(\tilde C \oplus W\) shifts to a basic germ \(f^1\) on \(\tilde C \oplus W^1\) with contraction germ \(B^1\): the shifted neighbourhood germ Chapter5/CompactnessScNbhdGerm.shiftParam, the contraction estimates on the shifted levels Chapter5/CompactnessIsSc0ContractionGerm.shift, and sc-smoothness of \(f^1\) by Proposition 1.17 for germs, which needs \(\tilde C\) a partial quadrant Chapter5/CompactnessIsBasicGerm.shift. If \(k\) is conjugated to \(h\) by \(\Psi\), then \(k^1\) is conjugated to \(h^1\) by the index raise \(\Psi^1\) Chapter3/BasicClassCompositionIsStrongBundleIso.shift Chapter5/CompactnessIsConjugateToBasicGerm.shift. Hence, for an sc-Fredholm section with compact solution set, the zeros in \(X_1\) are compact, and at every smooth point, in the chart of the germ, \((g - s)^1\) is conjugated to a basic germ and \(s^1\) is an sc⁺-germ on the shifted germ \(G_s^1\) (Proposition 1.17 for germs, Chapter3/GermLevelsIsSckGerm.shift), the text’s setting Chapter5/Compactnesscorollary_5_8_chart. In the germ reading of Definition 3.11 (§III.48) \(g\) is a filling germ and \(g - s\) only an sc⁰-germ on the intersection of the two germs; the level shift of the conjugation needs no more, since the conjugation identity is used near \(0\) only Chapter5/CompactnessIsConjugateToBasicGerm.shift_germ. The statement changed with the switch: in the whole-chart reading \(s^1\) was an sc⁺-section of all of \(U^1 \triangleleft F^1\). The filler of \(g^1\) was the gap: its condition (3) on level \(1\) does not follow from level \(0\). It is closed, together with the shifted strong bundle and the whole corollary, in §V.29.

V.8 \(\mathbb R\) as an M-polyfold, and bump functions

\(\mathbb R\). “An sc-smooth map \(f : X \to \mathbb R\)” needs \(\mathbb R\) as an M-polyfold: the constant sc-structure Chapter5/BumpFunctionsrealSc and the single chart \(\mathrm{id}\) Chapter5/BumpFunctionsrealChart Chapter5/BumpFunctionsrealPolyfold Chapter5/BumpFunctionsisChart_realChart. Sc-smoothness of a map between M-polyfolds can be checked in one pair of charts around each point, continuity included, since the local representatives determine the map near the point Chapter5/BumpFunctionsMPolyfold.isScSmoothMap_of_local Chapter5/BumpFunctionsisScSmoothMap_real_of_local; an sc-smooth function read in any chart is sc-smooth on the retract Chapter5/BumpFunctionsMPolyfold.IsScSmoothMap.real_chart; constants are sc-smooth Chapter5/BumpFunctionsisScSmoothMap_real_const; a \(C^\infty\) function \(\sigma : \mathbb R \to \mathbb R\) is an sc-smooth self-map of \(\mathbb R\) (Corollary 1.20 in the constant structure) Chapter5/BumpFunctionsisScSmoothMap_real_of_contDiff, so \(\sigma \circ f\) is sc-smooth Chapter5/BumpFunctionsMPolyfold.IsScSmoothMap.comp_contDiff.

Definitions 5.9 and 5.29. \(X\) admits sc-smooth bump functions if every \(x\) and open \(U \ni x\) have an sc-smooth \(f\) with \(f(x) \ne 0\) and \(\operatorname{supp} f \subseteq U\) Chapter5/BumpFunctionsMPolyfold.AdmitsBumpFunctions. The text has two definitions: Definition 5.9 asks “\(f \ne 0\)”, Definition 5.29 “not identically zero”. The proof of Proposition 5.30 starts from “a bump function \(g\) with \(g(0) = 1\)”, i.e. \(g(x) \ne 0\) at the given point; on an M-polyfold there are no translations to move a bump to \(x\) (even on an sc-Banach space, translation by a non-smooth vector does not preserve the levels). So Definition 5.9 is read with \(f(x) \ne 0\); Definition 5.29 as written Chapter5/BumpFunctionsMPolyfold.AdmitsBumpFunctionsWeak is implied Chapter5/BumpFunctionsMPolyfold.AdmitsBumpFunctions.weak. How far apart the two readings are is §V.31.

Propositions 5.10 and 5.30. Given \(x\) and \(U\), take a bump \(g\) with \(g(x) \ne 0\) and let \(f = \tau(3g/g(x) - 1)\), \(\tau\) the smooth transition from \(0\) on \((-\infty, 0]\) to \(1\) on \([1, \infty)\) Mathlib/Analysis/SpecialFunctions/SmoothTransitionReal.smoothTransition. Then \(f\) is sc-smooth, \(0 \le f \le 1\), \(f(x) = \tau(2) = 1\), \(f \equiv 1\) on the open set \(\{g/g(x) > 2/3\} \ni x\), and \(f \ne 0\) only where \(g/g(x) > 1/3\), so \(\operatorname{supp} f \subseteq \operatorname{supp} g \subseteq U\) Chapter5/BumpFunctionsproposition_5_30 Chapter5/BumpFunctionsproposition_5_10. The text’s \(\sigma\) (“\(0\) for \(s \le 1\) and \(1\) for \(s \ge 1\)”) is not a function.

V.9 The calculus of sections, and Lemma 5.11

\(\Gamma^+(P)\) and its algebra. \(\Gamma^+(P)\) is the set of sc⁺-sections (Definition 2.52) Chapter5/BumpFunctionsStrongBundle.scPlusSections; their values lie in \(Y_{0,1}\), because in a chart their principal parts take values in \(F_1\) Chapter5/BumpFunctionsStrongBundle.IsScPlusSection.mem_oneSet. The text uses, and does not state, the rules that make \(\Gamma^+(P)\) a module over the sc-smooth functions. The zero section is sc⁺ Chapter5/BumpFunctionsStrongBundle.isScPlusSection_fiberZero. The product rule: for \(f\) sc-smooth and \(s\) sc⁺, the fibrewise product \(f \cdot s\) Chapter5/BumpFunctionssectionSmul is sc⁺: in a chart its principal part on level \(1\) is \((f \circ \varphi^{-1}) \cdot \hat s\), the product of an sc-smooth function and an sc-smooth map into \(F^1\), sc-smooth by the product rule of the sc-calculus Chapter3/ParamPerturbationIsScSmooth.smul Chapter5/BumpFunctionsStrongBundle.IsScPlusSection.smul_left. Sums are sc⁺, since principal parts add in a chart Chapter5/BumpFunctionsStrongBundle.IsScPlusSection.add, and by induction finite sums Chapter5/BumpFunctionssectionSum Chapter5/BumpFunctionsStrongBundle.isScPlusSection_sectionSum.

Cut-offs. Lemma 5.11 builds a section in one chart and “extends it by \(0\)”. For a chart \(\Phi\) of the atlas, \(\tau : O \to F_1\) with \(z \mapsto (z, \tau(z))\) sc-smooth into \(K[1]\), and \(\beta\) sc-smooth with \(\operatorname{supp}\beta \subseteq \operatorname{dom}\varphi\), the section \(y \mapsto \Phi^{-1}(\varphi(y), \beta(y)\tau(\varphi(y)))\) on \(\operatorname{dom}\varphi\), \(0_y\) outside Chapter5/BumpFunctionsStrongBundle.cutoffSection, is sc⁺ Chapter5/BumpFunctionsStrongBundle.isScPlusSection_cutoffSection: on \(\operatorname{dom}\varphi\) its representative in \(\Phi[1]\) is \(z \mapsto (z, \beta(\varphi^{-1}(z))\tau(z))\), sc-smooth by the product rule; on the open set \(X \setminus \operatorname{supp}\beta\) it is the zero section; the two open sets cover \(X\).

Lemma 5.11 Chapter5/BumpFunctionslemma_5_11. Let \(X\) admit bump functions, \(N\) be an auxiliary norm, \(x\) smooth, \(e\) a smooth point of \(Y\) over \(x\), \(\varepsilon > 0\) and \(U \ni x\) open. Take any chart \(\Phi\) of the atlas around \(x\) — neither a centred chart nor tameness is needed — and \(\hat e = \Phi(e)_2\), a smooth point of \(F\) because \(e\) is smooth. The constant \(\hat e\) is sc-smooth into \(F^1\) Chapter5/BumpFunctionsisScSmooth_const_of_mem_smooth, and \(R[1]\) is sc-smooth, so \(t(z) = R(z, \hat e)\) gives an sc⁺-section near \(x\) with \(t(x) = e\). Since \(N\) is continuous on \(Y[1]\) and \(t\) is continuous into \(Y[1]\), the set \(\{y \mid N(t(y)) < N(e) + \varepsilon\}\) is an open neighbourhood of \(x\). Proposition 5.30 gives \(\beta : X \to [0, 1]\) with \(\beta(x) = 1\) and support in that set, in \(U\) and in the chart domain, and the cut-off \(s = \beta \cdot t\) is sc⁺ with \(s(x) = e\) and \(\operatorname{supp}s \subseteq U\). Finally, at every \(y\), \(N(s(y)) = \beta(y)N(t(y)) \le N(t(y)) < N(e) + \varepsilon\), because \(N\) is a norm on the fibre and \(0 \le \beta \le 1\); off the support, \(N(s(y)) = N(0_y) = 0\). The text states the bound only at \(x\), where it is trivial; its proof gives, and §5.3 needs, the bound everywhere.

V.10 Allowable sections and Remark 5.12

\(\Gamma^{+,1}_U(P)\). For an auxiliary norm \(N\) and an open \(U\), the allowable sections are the sc⁺-sections with support in \(U\) and \(N(s(x)) \le 1\) at every point Chapter5/BumpFunctionsStrongBundle.allowableSections — a condition at every point because sc⁺-sections take values in \(Y_{0,1}\). The text’s metric \(\rho(s, s') = \sup_xN(s(x) - s'(x))\) is used through its pointwise form: \(N(s(x) - s'(x))\), the difference taken in the fibre \((Y_{0,1})_x\) Chapter5/TransversalityStrongBundle.sectionDistAt. The metric space itself is §V.30.

Remark 5.12 Chapter5/Compactnessremark_5_12. Let \(S_f \subseteq U\) with \(\operatorname{cl}\{x \in U \mid N(f(x)) \le 1\}\) compact (the \(U\) of properness), and let \(s\) vanish outside \(U\) with \(N(s(x)) \le 1\) everywhere — properties that pass to uniform limits of allowable sections, which is all the remark uses of the completion. At a zero \(x\) of \(f + s\): if \(x \notin U\), then \(s(x) = 0\) and \(f(x) = 0\), so \(x \in S_f \subseteq U\), a contradiction; so \(x \in U\), and \(f(x) = -s(x)\) gives \(N(f(x)) = N(s(x)) \le 1\) Chapter5/CompactnessStrongBundle.IsAuxNorm.auxLe_of_sectionAdd. So \(S_{f+s} \subseteq \{x \in U \mid N(f(x)) \le 1\}\), whose closure is compact. The remark claims the solution set compact, which needs it closed; for an allowable \(s\) this holds because \(f + s\) is sc-Fredholm (Theorem 3.15) Chapter3/FredholmSectionsGtheorem_3_15 and solution sets of continuous sections are closed Chapter5/TransversalityisClosed_solutionSet. This is how part (1) of Theorems 5.13, 5.18, 5.19, 5.25 is proved: \(U\) from Theorem 5.5, then Remark 5.12 and closedness.

V.11 Transversality and the parametrized section

Definition 5.15. \(g\) is transversal if at every zero its linearization is onto in a chart Chapter5/TransversalityStrongBundle.IsTransversal, hence in every chart Chapter3/GlobalIFTIndexStrongBundle.IsLinSurjAt.linAt_surjective Chapter3/LinearizationChartsStrongBundle.linAt_chart_independence. The kernel of \(\mathrm{Lin}(z)\) in a chart is a subspace of \(E_0\) inside \(T_zO\) Chapter5/TransversalityStrongBundleChart.linKer.

The parametrized section. For a section \(g\) and sections \(t_1, \dots, t_m\), Theorem 3.18 (Part III) makes \(F(\lambda, y) = g(y) + \sum\lambda_it_i(y)\) a section of the pull-back of \(P\) to \(\mathbb R^m \times X\), sc-Fredholm when \(g\) is and the \(t_i\) are sc⁺, and with tame germ data when \(g\) has them Chapter3/ParamPerturbationGtheorem_3_18_tame. Its slice at \(\lambda\) is the section \(g + \sum\lambda_it_i\) of \(P\) Chapter5/TransversalityparamSlice Chapter5/TransversalityparamSlice_eq_sectionAdd, and \((\lambda, y)\) is a zero of \(F\) iff \(y\) is a zero of the slice Chapter5/TransversalityisZeroAt_paramSection_iff. The slices are sc-Fredholm, since \(\sum\lambda_it_i\) is sc⁺ (§V.9, Theorem 3.15) Chapter5/TransversalityisScFredholmSection_paramSlice; slices of sc⁺-sections are sc⁺ Chapter5/TransversalityisScPlusSection_paramSlice with support in the union of the supports Chapter5/TransversalitysectionSupport_paramSlice_subset and vanish off it Chapter5/TransversalityisZeroAt_paramSlice_of_not_mem_support. Allowability: if \(N(s_0) \le 1 - \varepsilon\) and \(N(t_i) \le 1\), the triangle inequality on the fibre gives \(N(s_0 + \sum\lambda_it_i) \le 1 - \varepsilon + m|\lambda|\) Chapter5/TransversalityStrongBundle.IsAuxNorm.toOne_sum_le, which is \(\le 1\) when \(m|\lambda| \le \varepsilon\) Chapter5/TransversalityauxLe_paramSlice — the text’s “\(N(\sum\lambda_jt_j(y)) < \varepsilon/2\)”, with \(|\lambda|\) the maximum norm.

The linear algebra of “regular value ⇔ transversal”. Let \(M(a, u) = Lu + \sum a_ie_i : \mathbb R^m \oplus T \to K\) be onto. If the projection \(\ker M \to \mathbb R^m\) is onto, \(L\) is onto: given \(k = Lu + \sum a_ie_i\), choose \(u'\) with \((a, u') \in \ker M\), so \(k = L(u - u')\) Chapter5/Transversalitysurjective_of_forall_exists_ker_fst. Conversely, if \(L\) is onto, every \(a\) lifts to \(\ker M\) Chapter5/Transversalityforall_exists_ker_fst_of_surjective. In the product chart \((r \mapsto r - \lambda) \times \Phi\) of a chart \(\Phi\) centred at \(y\), the linearization of \(F\) at \((\lambda, y)\) is \(\mathrm{Lin}_F(0)(a, u) = \mathrm{Lin}_{g_\lambda}(0)u + \sum a_i\hat t_i(0)\) Chapter3/ParamPerturbationGlinAt_paramSection, the fibre of the product chart over its centre being the fibre \(K_0\) of \(\Phi\) Chapter5/Transversalitymem_K_ofProd_zero_iff. So if \(\mathrm{Lin}_F\) is onto at \((\lambda, y)\) and its kernel projects onto \(\mathbb R^m\), the slice \(g_\lambda\) is transversal at \(y\) Chapter5/TransversalityisLinSurjAt_paramSlice_of_ker_fst. In the other direction, if in a chart centred at a zero \(y\) of \(g\) the range of \(\mathrm{Lin}_g(0)\) and the \(\hat t_i(0)\) span \(K_0\), then \(F\) is transversal at \((0, y)\) Chapter3/ParamPerturbationGlinAt_paramSection_zero Chapter5/TransversalityisLinSurjAt_paramSection_zero_of_spanning; and adding sections keeps this, because a combination over a subfamily is one over the family Chapter5/Transversalityexists_sum_comp_eq Chapter5/TransversalityisLinSurjAt_paramSection_zero_of_comp. Only “regular value ⇒ transversal” is needed in Theorem 5.13.

V.12 Spanning sections

“For every \(x \in S_{f+s_0}\) we find finitely many allowable sc⁺-sections such that the range of \((f + s_0)'(x)\) together with the sections span \(Y_x\)”: the text does not say how. Two ingredients.

Linear algebra Chapter5/Transversalityexists_fin_mem_of_dense_of_closedComplemented. Let \(R \subseteq K\) be closed, complemented and of finite codimension, and \(D \subseteq K\) a dense subspace. With \(\pi\) a continuous projection onto \(R\), \(Q = \ker\pi\) is finite-dimensional, and \((1 - \pi)(D)\) is a dense subspace of \(Q\), hence closed, hence all of \(Q\); a basis of \(Q\) lifts to finitely many \(d_i \in D\), and \(K = R + \operatorname{span}\{d_i\}\).

The sections Chapter5/Transversalityexists_spanning_sections. Let \(g\) be sc-Fredholm, \(g(y) = 0\), \(U \ni y\) open. In the chart \(\Phi\) of the germ, centred at \(y\), \(\mathrm{Lin}(0) : T_0O \to K_0\) is \(Dg(0)|_{T_0O}\) for a derivative family \(Dg\) of the filling germ on its germ (the bridge for germs at the centre, Chapter3/LinearizationChartsGIsFillingGerm.fillerRestrict_eq_linAt), hence Fredholm (Proposition 3.52 for germs, which exposes the germ and \(Dg\)) Chapter3/FredholmGermLinearizationGproposition_3_52, so its range \(R\) is closed, complemented and of finite codimension in \(K_0 = \rho(0)F\). The smooth vectors \(\rho(0)F_\infty\) are dense in \(K_0\) — \(\rho(0)\) is continuous and preserves the levels at the smooth point \(0\), and \(F_\infty\) is dense — so finitely many smooth \(k_i\) span a complement. Each \(k_i\) is \(\Phi(e_i)_2\) for a smooth point \(e_i\) of the fibre over \(y\) Chapter5/Transversalitymem_smoothSet_toMPolyfold0_of_chart; Lemma 5.11 gives \(s_i\) with \(s_i(y) = e_i\), support in \(U\) and \(N(s_i) < N(e_i) + 1\), and \(s_i/(N(e_i) + 1)\) is allowable, with support unchanged Chapter5/TransversalitysectionSupport_sectionSmul_const_subset, \(N\) scaled Chapter5/TransversalityStrongBundle.IsAuxNorm.oneMk_sectionSmul_const and principal part scaled Chapter5/Transversalityprincipal_sectionSmul_const. The density of the smooth vectors is the point the text omits: Lemma 5.11 only reaches smooth points of the fibre.

V.13 Theorem 5.13: openness, and the omitted compactness step

No boundary on \(\mathbb R^m \times X\). “The interior case, Theorem 3.19” is applied to \(F\) on \(\mathbb R^m \times X\), so \(\partial(\mathbb R^m \times X) = \emptyset\) is needed: \(d_{\mathbb R^m} \equiv 0\) Chapter5/TransversalityrnPolyfold_degIndex and \(d_{\mathbb R^m \times X} \le d_{\mathbb R^m} + d_X\) Chapter2/FibredProductMPolyfold.degIndex_prod_le Chapter5/TransversalityisWithoutBoundary_prod_rn. At a point with \(d = 0\) good position is surjectivity Chapter3/GlobalIFTIndexGStrongBundle.isGoodPositionGerm_of_isLinSurjAt.

Transversality spreads. If \(g\) has tame germ data and \(F\) is transversal at \((0, x)\), \(x\) a zero of \(g\), then \((F, (0, x))\) is in good position, and Theorem 3.54 (1) gives an open \(V \ni (0, x)\) all of whose zeros are in good position, hence transversal; \(U(x) = \{y \mid (0, y) \in V\}\) is the text’s neighbourhood Chapter3/GlobalIFTNearbyOntoGtheorem_3_54_one' Chapter5/Transversalityexists_isOpen_isLinSurjAt_zero_near. Likewise, if \(F\) is transversal at every \((0, y)\), \(y \in S_g\), the union of these sets is an open \(V \supseteq \{0\} \times S_g\) all of whose zeros of \(F\) are in good position in a tame chart Chapter5/Transversalityexists_isOpen_goodPosition_of_isLinSurjAt.

The omitted step. The text passes from the neighbourhood \(U\) of \(\{0\} \times S_{f+s_0}\) to “\(U \subset \{|\lambda| < \delta_0\} \oplus X\)” without argument; what is needed is that every zero of \(F\) with \(|\lambda|\) small lies in \(V\). The topological core: if \(Z \subseteq \mathbb R^m \times X\) is compact and the open \(V\) contains \(Z \cap \{\lambda = 0\}\), then \(Z \setminus V\) is compact, its projection to \(\mathbb R^m\) is compact and misses \(0\), and any \(\delta\) below its distance to \(0\) works Chapter5/Transversalityexists_pos_forall_mem_of_isCompact. The compact \(Z\) is the set of zeros of \(F\) with \(|\lambda| \le \delta_1\): for such \(\lambda\) the perturbation \(s_0 + \sum\lambda_it_i\) is allowable (§V.11), so by Remark 5.12 its zeros lie in the compact \(\operatorname{cl}\{x \in U \mid N(f(x)) \le 1\}\) of Theorem 5.5 — \(Z\) is a closed subset of \(\bar B(\delta_1) \times\) (that compact set), closed because \(F\) is continuous.

V.14 Theorem 5.13: the Sard step

“\(\tilde S := F^{-1}(0)\) is a smooth manifold”; “taking a regular value \(\lambda_0\) for the projection \(\tilde S \to \mathbb R^m\), it is easily verified that \(f + s_0 + s(\lambda_0, \cdot)\) is transversal”. The formalization does not build \(\tilde S\); it proves the needed statement near each zero Chapter5/Transversalityexists_null_isLinSurjAt_paramSlice_near.

Claim. Let \(g\) have tame germ data, \(t_i\) be sc⁺, and \(z_0\) a zero of \(F\) in good position in a tame chart. There are an open \(W \ni z_0\) and a null set \(CV \subseteq \mathbb R^m\) such that for every zero \((\lambda, y) \in W\) with \(\lambda \notin CV\) the slice \(g_\lambda\) is transversal at \(y\).

  1. The chart of \(\tilde S\). Theorem 3.54 (2) gives at \(z_0\) a regular tangent germ chart \(D\) of the solution set of \(F\) (Definition 3.25 (2)): a chart \(D.\varphi\) of \(\mathbb R^m \times X\) with domain \(W\), a finite-dimensional \(N\), a relatively open \(V \subseteq N \cap C\) and an sc-smooth graph map \(\Gamma\) with \(D.\varphi^{-1} \circ \Gamma\) parametrizing \(\tilde S \cap W\) Chapter3/GlobalIFTTheoremsGtheorem_3_54_two.
  2. The projection. \(q = p \circ D.\varphi^{-1} \circ \Gamma : V \to \mathbb R^m\), \(p\) the projection to the parameter, is sc-smooth on a finite-dimensional space with the constant structure, hence \(C^\infty\) Chapter1/ExpositionLemmasisScSmooth_iff_contDiffOn_const.
  3. Sard on the strata. \(V\) is relatively open in a partial quadrant of \(N\); Sard’s theorem on each stratum of the quadrant (Part IV) makes the set \(CV\) of stratified critical values of \(q\) null Chapter4/FamiliesLocalmeasure_image_stratCritSet. Since \(\partial X = \emptyset\) the points over the zeros are interior and classical Sard would do, but proving that needs the degeneracy index of the induced structure; the stratified form makes the question unnecessary.
  4. The point. A zero \((\lambda, y) \in W\) is \(D.\varphi^{-1}(\Gamma(v))\) for some \(v \in V\) with \(q(v) = \lambda\). Let \(\Phi\) be a chart centred at \(y\) and \(\psi = (r \mapsto r - \lambda) \times \varphi\) the product chart. On a relatively open \(V' \subseteq V\) around \(v\), \(\mathrm{gmap} = \psi \circ D.\varphi^{-1} \circ \Gamma\) is sc-smooth (the transition between the two charts of \(\mathbb R^m \times X\) restricted to the overlap), and \(q = \mathrm{pr}_1 \circ \mathrm{gmap} + \lambda\) there.
  5. Kernel vectors. If \(\lambda \notin CV\), \(Dq(v)\) maps the stratum through \(v\) onto \(\mathbb R^m\). The values of \(D\,\mathrm{gmap}(v)\) lie in the tangent space \(T_0O\) of the product chart, and in \(\ker\mathrm{Lin}_F(0)\): the principal part of \(F\) vanishes along \(r \circ \mathrm{gmap}\), and the chain rule gives \(\mathrm{Lin}_F(0) \circ D\,\mathrm{gmap}(v) = 0\). So for every \(a \in \mathbb R^m\) there is a kernel vector with first component \(a\).
  6. Conclusion. \(F\) is transversal at \((\lambda, y)\) (good position near \(z_0\)), and §V.11 gives the transversality of the slice at \(y\).

Only \(\operatorname{range}D\,\mathrm{gmap}(v) \subseteq \ker\mathrm{Lin}_F\) is used, not “\(T\tilde S = \ker F'\)”.

V.15 Theorem 5.13: the assembly

The generic form Chapter5/Transversalitytheorem_5_13_generic. Let \(\partial X = \emptyset\), \(X\) admit bump functions, \(f\) have tame germ data and compact solution set, \(N\) be an auxiliary norm.

  1. \(U\) and part (1). Theorem 5.5 gives \(U \supseteq S_f\) with \(\operatorname{cl}\{x \in U \mid N(f(x)) \le 1\}\) compact Chapter5/Compactnesstheorem_5_5; for allowable \(s\), Remark 5.12 and closedness give \(S_{f+s}\) compact (§V.10).
  2. The section \(g = f + s_0\). For \(s_0\) sc⁺ with \(\operatorname{supp}s_0 \subseteq U\) and \(N(s_0) \le 1 - \varepsilon\), \(g\) has tame germ data Chapter3/TameGermsAddGtheorem_3_15_tame, a compact solution set (part (1)), and \(S_g \subseteq U\) (Remark 5.12).
  3. Local families. At every zero \(x\) of \(g\), spanning sections \(s^x_1, \dots, s^x_{k_x}\) supported in \(U\) (§V.12) make \(F_x\) transversal at \((0, x)\), and at \((0, y)\) for the zeros \(y\) in an open \(U(x)\) (§V.13).
  4. One family. Finitely many \(U(x_j)\) cover the compact \(S_g\); the families are united through an equivalence \(\Sigma_j\mathrm{Fin}(k_{x_j}) \simeq \mathrm{Fin}(m)\) into \(t_1, \dots, t_m\), allowable and supported in \(U\); adding sections keeps transversality (§V.11), so \(F\), whose slice at \(\lambda = 0\) is \(g\) Chapter5/TransversalityparamSlice_zero, is transversal at every \((0, y)\), \(y \in S_g\).
  5. Good position near the zero slice. An open \(V \supseteq \{0\} \times S_g\) of zeros of \(F\) in good position (§V.13).
  6. Allowability and compactness. For \(|\lambda| \le \delta_1 = \varepsilon/(m + 1)\) the slices \(s_0 + \sum\lambda_it_i\) are allowable, and the zeros of \(F\) over \(|\lambda| \le \delta_1\) form a compact \(Z\) (§V.13).
  7. The omitted step. \(Z \cap \{|\lambda| < \delta_0\} \subseteq V\) for some \(\delta_0 > 0\).
  8. Sard. With \(\delta = \min(\delta_0, \delta_1)\), the zeros \(Z_0\) of \(F\) over \(|\lambda| \le \delta/2\) are compact and lie in \(V\); the Sard step (§V.14) at each point of \(Z_0\) gives an open \(W_z\) and a null \(CV_z\); finitely many \(W_z\) cover \(Z_0\), and \(CV = \bigcup CV_z\) is null.
  9. The conclusions. For \(|\lambda| < \delta/2\), \(\lambda \notin CV\): \(s_\lambda = s_0 + \sum\lambda_it_i\) is allowable; every zero \(y\) of \(f + s_\lambda\) gives a zero \((\lambda, y) \in Z_0\), inside some \(W_z\), so \(f + s_\lambda\) is transversal at \(y\); \(S_{f+s_\lambda}\) is compact by part (1); and if it is non-empty, Theorem 3.56 for a transversal section over \(X\) without boundary, applied to \(f + s_\lambda\) with tame germ data, makes it a sub-M-polyfold whose induced structure is tame, a manifold without boundary of locally constant dimension, with regular tangent germ data of dimension the Fredholm index at every zero Chapter3/GlobalIFTIndexGtheorem_3_56_of_surjective Chapter5/TransversalityStrongBundle.SolutionSetIsManifold.

The dense form Chapter5/Transversalitytheorem_5_13. Given an allowable \(s'\) and \(\varepsilon > 0\), let \(\varepsilon' = \min(\varepsilon, 1)\) and \(s_0 = (1 - \varepsilon'/2)s'\), so \(N(s_0) \le 1 - \varepsilon'/2\). The generic form gives \(t\), \(\delta\), \(CV\); since \(CV\) is null and the ball \(\{|\lambda| < \min(\delta, \varepsilon'/(2m + 2))\}\) has positive measure, some \(\lambda\) in it avoids \(CV\). Then \(s = s_0 + \sum\lambda_it_i\) has \(N(s(x) - s'(x)) \le (\varepsilon'/2)N(s'(x)) + \sum|\lambda_i|N(t_i(x)) \le \varepsilon'\). The text’s “\(N(s_0(y) + s(\lambda_0, y)) \le 1 - \varepsilon/2\)” is a slip for \(\le 1\), its “\(N(f(x)) \le 1\)” in the statement is \(N(s(x)) \le 1\), and its “the germ \((f, x)\) is in good position” is \((f + s, x)\).

V.16 Definition 5.17 and Lemma 5.26

Definition 5.17, in a tame chart Chapter5/TransversalityStrongBundle.IsGeneralPositionGerm. \((f, y)\), \(f(y) = 0\), is in general position if in some tame strong bundle chart around \(y\) (Definition 3.50) Chapter3/TameGermsStrongBundle.IsTameChart, at the level-\(1\) point \(z\) over \(\varphi(y)\), \(\mathrm{Lin}(z)\) is onto \(K_z\), and for every presentation \(T\) of the partial quadrant the kernel has an sc-complement \(B\) in \(T_zO\) inside the reduced tangent space \(T^R_zO = T_zO \cap E_z\) Chapter2/TamereducedTangentSpaceWith, on every level: \((T_zO)_m = (\ker\mathrm{Lin}(z))_m \oplus B_m\). The chart is tame because \(T^R_xX\) is the reduced tangent space of a tame M-polyfold and the dimension count below needs it. General position includes transversality Chapter5/TransversalityStrongBundle.IsGeneralPositionGerm.isLinSurjAt.

The linear algebra of Lemma 5.26 Chapter5/TransversalityisInGoodPositionIn_of_scComplement_le_reduced. Let \(r\) be a tame retraction, \(z\) a smooth point of the retract, and \(N, B \subseteq T_zO\) with \(T_zO = N \oplus B\) and \(B \subseteq T^R_zO\).
